details: Pure Go (Go 1.25.0) module google.golang.org/adk. Sibling adk-python and adk-java exist as independent ports — adk-go has no Python/Node bridge.
Python 3.7+ single-language project (libs/agno/pyproject.toml). No .NET/Go/TS siblings; server extras add FastAPI/uvicorn on the same Python runtime.
Primary Rust workspace (edition 2024). PyO3/maturin bindings expose a thin Python wrapper (autoagents-py), but the canonical surface is Rust.
Python 3.10+ package that subprocesses a bundled Node.js Claude Code CLI. A TypeScript sibling (claude-agent-sdk-typescript) tracks parity.
TypeScript SDK targeting Node ≥18, Bun, or Deno. The subprocess it spawns is a Node binary; the consumer surface is pure TS.
Python-only (>=3.10, <3.14). Multi-package on PyPI (crewai, crewai-core, crewai-cli, crewai-tools). No TS/Go/Java SDKs.
Pure Go (Go 1.25 minimum). Two modules: cloudwego/eino and cloudwego/eino-ext for adapters. No Python/TS/Rust bindings.
Go module github.com/firebase/genkit/go. Same repo also ships canonical TypeScript and Python SDKs sharing a cross-runtime schema; Go SDK trails JS feature parity.
Python this repo; a sibling JS/TS SDK ships for HTTP-client use, but the JS graph runtime is a separate repo (langchain-ai/langgraphjs).
Python >=3.10, <4.0. A separate TypeScript port (LlamaIndex.TS) exists in a sibling repo but is out of scope for this report.
Strict TypeScript monorepo (pnpm + turborepo). No Python/Go/Rust components.
Primary Python (≥3.10). Near-parity .NET 8/9+ tree (Microsoft.Agents.AI*) released from the same monorepo; .NET hosting story is slightly more mature.
Python primary (3.10+, also 3.11–3.14). Vendor maintains an independent TypeScript sibling at openai/openai-agents-js.
TypeScript single-language project (Node 22+, Deno, Bun; experimental Cloudflare Workers). Python sibling is a parallel codebase, not a dependency.
Python 3.10–3.14 single-language project. No second runtime.
Rust workspace edition 2024 (Cargo.toml:47). No secondary language; everything ships as Cargo crates under the rig umbrella.
Python ≥3.10. Companion strands-agents-tools is also Python; no second-language runtime.
TypeScript primary, compiles to WASM and is consumed from a sibling Python guest via a WIT contract — a guest-runtime arrangement, not a separate implementation.
ESM-first TypeScript package ai on npm. Runs in Node.js or compatible runtimes (Edge, Bun, Deno).

Apache 2.0 (LICENSE) under github.com/google/adk-go; Google engineers review PRs and require CLA. Indirect commercial backing through Google Cloud (Vertex AI, Agent Engine, Cloud Run) but no paid support tier specific to adk-go itself. Community: GitHub issues and r/agentdevelopmentkit subreddit; no Discord/Slack of record.

Apache 2.0 (libs/agno/LICENSE) owned by Agno AGI, a small commercial company (founder Ashpreet Bedi). Operates a managed UI at os.agno.com pointing at self-hosted runtimes; framework is fully OSS. No enterprise SLA disclosed.

Dual MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml:24) under liquidos-ai/AutoAgents (Liquidos AI). No commercial backing or paid support surfaced in the README — community channels only (GitHub Issues, Discussions, Discord). Smallest governance footprint among the scored set.

MIT (pyproject.toml:11) owned by Anthropic PBC; first-party SDK for Claude Code. Commercial Terms apply and the SDK is gated on an Anthropic API key. Anthropic Enterprise paid support exists for the underlying platform; SDK itself uses GitHub issues for community support.

MIT (LICENSE.md) maintained by Anthropic PBC — the same org that builds the underlying Claude Code CLI. Paid Anthropic Enterprise support is available; the SDK itself is free/OSS. Multiple-per-week release cadence and active GitHub issue triage.

MIT (LICENSE) maintained by crewAI, Inc. (Delaware C-corp, founder João Moura). Series A in Oct 2024 from Insight Partners + Blitzscaling Ventures; paid AMP/CrewAI Enterprise SaaS wraps the OSS framework with SLA-backed support. Discord (~25k members), Discourse, and active GitHub issue triage.

Apache 2.0 maintained by CloudWeGo (open-source initiative inside ByteDance/Volcengine). Volcengine offers paid Ark LLM endpoints and APMPlus tracing for the underlying infra, but there is no managed Eino cloud nor enterprise SLA for the framework. Community runs on a Lark/Feishu group; English Discord exists but is materially less active.

Apache 2.0 (LICENSE) under firebase/genkit, maintained by Google/Firebase. Positioned as the AI SDK for Firebase apps deployable on Cloud Run, App Hosting, or Firebase Functions; paid support flows through Google Cloud / Firebase support tiers — no Genkit-specific SLA. Standard OSS governance: small Google team merges PRs, CLA required for community contributions.

MIT for everything in libs/ (libs/langgraph/pyproject.toml:11) maintained by LangChain Inc. Commercial backing through paid LangGraph Platform (server + cloud) and LangSmith observability; community support via GitHub Issues and Discord. Paid support tied to LangGraph Platform.

MIT (LICENSE:1) owned by LlamaIndex Inc., founded by Jerry Liu with five named co-maintainers in pyproject.toml. Commercial backing through paid LlamaCloud / LlamaParse / LlamaExtract / LlamaAgents managed offerings; OSS framework remains free. GitHub issues, active Discord (discord.gg/dGcwcsnxhU), paid LlamaCloud support contracts.

Apache 2.0 for everything outside ee/, with a Mastra Enterprise License covering the auth ee/ tree (free for dev, commercial use needs license). Maintained by Kepler Software, Inc. (Y Combinator W25); commercial backing via Mastra Cloud and paid enterprise support; dedicated security email. Mixed-license posture is unusual among scored frameworks but clearly disclosed.

MIT (LICENSE) owned and maintained by Microsoft (microsoft/agent-framework). Very strong commercial backing through Azure Foundry, Azure AI Search, Cosmos DB, Azure Functions, DurableTask, Hyperlight. Formal numbered ADRs, public Discord, weekly community office hours; explicit migration guides from Semantic Kernel and AutoGen.

MIT (LICENSE) maintained by OpenAI; underpins Codex and other OpenAI Agents products internally so the funding/maintenance signal is strong. Community-only for the SDK itself (GitHub issues, OpenAI Developer Community); paid backing is through the OpenAI API contract on the underlying LLM, no separate SDK SLA.

MIT (packages/agents-core/package.json:38) owned by OpenAI (support@openai.com). Hosted complementary services (Traces dashboard, Conversations API, hosted MCP, hosted built-in tools, sandbox tools) sit behind the OpenAI platform paywall; no managed agent runtime, no SDK SLA — community-supported via GitHub issues.

MIT (pyproject.toml:23) owned by Pydantic Services Inc., commercial steward of Pydantic Validation and Logfire. Five named maintainers including Samuel Colvin. Commercial support via Pydantic Logfire (observability, hosted) and Pydantic AI Gateway (managed multi-provider router) — both optional; OSS library is fully usable without either.

MIT (Cargo.toml:6, LICENSE) under 0xPlaygrounds — Discord-only community (discord.gg/playgrounds). No commercial backing, no paid support, no managed cloud, no SLA visible. Adopters listed in README but governance is the thinnest among scored frameworks alongside autoagents.

Apache-2.0 (LICENSE) maintained by AWS (pyproject.toml:14-15). Community/Discord (discord.gg/strands) and GitHub Issues; no commercial Strands cloud, but Bedrock is the default model provider, signalling AWS-led origin. No separately advertised enterprise SLA for the SDK itself.

Dual Apache-2.0 + MIT licensed (package.json declares Apache-2.0) under the AWS Strands Agents org. Default model provider is Amazon Bedrock (Agent ctor strands-ts/src/agent/agent.ts:325). Community-only support (Discord) — no managed cloud or paid SLA advertised in-repo; package is still at 0.0.1-development.

Apache-2.0 (packages/ai/package.json:7) maintained by Vercel Inc. with a sizable community contributor base. Vercel sells the AI Gateway (per-token routing, spend reports, key management) and Vercel hosting; SDK itself is free. Support via GitHub issues, community Discord, and Vercel commercial support for platform customers.

Go port of the older adk-python project; no tagged v1.x release in this clone and the module path google.golang.org/adk has no major-version suffix (v0.x by Go convention). README/CONTRIBUTING do not mark APIs as experimental/beta/stable; internal/ packages are unstable by Go convention. HEAD commit adds major new capability (bidi WebSocket streaming) — not in maintenance mode but still pre-1.0 with active churn.

Current version 2.6.7 (libs/agno/pyproject.toml:3) with classifier Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable. Active 2.x line with default_schema_version 2.0.0 and a managed migrations subsystem (libs/agno/agno/db/migrations/). Two published PyPI packages (agno, agno-infra).

Workspace version 0.3.7 (Cargo.toml:21) on Rust edition 2024 (bleeding-edge). README declares production-grade but the 0.3.x major-zero, absence of CHANGELOG/HISTORY/RELEASES files (verified), and lack of session/HTTP primitives all signal pre-1.0 maturity with breaking changes expected. Shallow-cloned submodule limits visibility of history.

Python package version 0.2.82 (pyproject.toml:7) released 2026-05-13 with Development Status :: 3 - Alpha classifier. Renamed from claude-code-sdk; semantic API has stabilized but recent releases still introduce material additions (skills option, SessionStore adapter, defer hook decision, strict_mcp_config). Bundled CLI version 2.1.143 bumps in lockstep with each release.

The 0.3.x line has shipped 100+ patch versions with frequent breaking changes documented in CHANGELOG.md (e.g. 0.3.142 removed v2 session API). @experimental APIs (taskBudget, criticalSystemReminder_EXPERIMENTAL, betas) signal active iteration.

Initial public release Nov 2023; v1.0 cut Oct 2024 (docs/en/changelog.mdx). Current version crewai==1.14.5a6 (released 2026-05-15) — alpha prereleases ship nightly and breaking changes still land within minor versions (e.g. v1.14.5a5's executor swap). A sizeable surface stays tagged experimental (the new default AgentExecutor lives under crewai.experimental.agent_executor).

Initial public release late 2024 (oldest tag v0.1.0); roughly 18 months old at analysis. Current major version v0.8.x for core eino; eino-ext sub-modules version independently. Still pre-v1 so APIs are not formally frozen; lower layers (compose, schema, callbacks) are more stable while the ADK layer is newest (v0.7) and middlewares are evolving.

Maintenance-mode signal: create_react_agent and AgentState are now @deprecated in favor of langchain.agents.create_agent — the prebuilt surface is being consolidated into the broader langchain package.

Initial public release November 2022 (originally GPT Index) — the oldest framework in the cohort. llama-index-core is at 0.14.22 with most APIs non-experimental and stable. Agent layer substantially rewritten in 2025 to live on top of workflows; Memory API is the marked replacement for deprecated ChatMemoryBuffer / SimpleComposableMemory.

@mastra/core@1.36.0-alpha.0 (packages/core/package.json:3); CLI mastra@1.9.4-alpha.0. Approximately 1.5 years public (launched 2024). Most APIs marked stable, but vNext/deprecated markers exist on a few HTTP routes (e.g. STREAM_GENERATE_VNEXT_DEPRECATED_ROUTE) — active churn at the HTTP layer.

First public release 2025 (preview); now at 1.4.0 (2026-05-14) for Python and similar for .NET via NuGet. Formal PACKAGE_STATUS.md classifies packages into alpha/beta/rc/released/deprecated: agent-framework core packages are released, most provider/adapter packages are beta, and azure-contentunderstanding + gemini are still alpha. Feature-level @experimental decorators on Skills/Evals/FileHistory; breaking changes still happen in experimental areas (skills restructured in 1.3.0/1.4.0).

Most public APIs stable enough for production with detailed breaking-change changelog, but beta features (sandbox surface introduced 0.14.0) can change in patch releases. First public release Spring 2025.

All five packages at 0.11.4 (packages/agents-core/package.json:5). Pre-1.0 with most constructs (Agent, tool, run) marked stable but Sandbox Agents explicitly labeled beta in README.md:38. Release cadence shows ~3 minor versions in 6 months (0.9.0 → 0.11.x) and heavy patch traffic.

v1.0.0 shipped 2025-09-04 (docs/changelog.md:15) with committed API stability until v2. Classifier Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable (pyproject.toml:30). Pre-1.0 history was active throughout 2025 with monthly minor releases; latest commit in submodule is 2026-05-15 — actively maintained on the post-1.0 line.

Pre-1.0 (rig v0.37.0, released 2026-05-13, CHANGELOG.md:9). README explicitly warns: "Here be dragons! As we plan to ship a torrent of features in the following months, future updates will contain breaking changes." Recent breaking change in 0.37 ("[breaking] make Chat append messages to caller history").

Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable in pyproject.toml:18 with dynamic version from VCS tags. Shallow-clone submodule limited release-history visibility; live release timeline should be confirmed on GitHub.

Multi-workspace monorepo (strands-ts, strands-wasm, strands-py, strandly) with deliberately ambitious WIT-based runtime architecture; many features marked experimental in code comments (A2A protocol, MCP tasksConfig, Skill.allowedTools). Interventions subsystem landed days before the analysed commit.

Several APIs still marked experimental_* (experimental_onStart, experimental_sandbox, experimental_createMCPClient).

Official docs at https://docs.agno.com (English). Docs under docs/content/ as Docusaurus markdown (docusaurus.config.ts) with sections getting-started/, core-concepts/, llm-providers/, developer/. Pages are short and conceptual — architecture.md is 36 lines, executors.md is 60 lines. English only (READMEs are translated but the docs site is not). A non-engineer cannot author content — every extension is a Rust trait implementation requiring compile cycles; no YAML/JSON config except MCP TOML.

Official docs at https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/sdk and platform.claude.com. In-repo: README (~360 lines), CHANGELOG (1k+ lines), RELEASING.md, CLAUDE.md. Code heavily docstringed (ClaudeAgentOptions got per-field docstrings in 0.1.69). Accessibility for non-engineers is low — every interaction is a Python coroutine, JSON wire frames, and CLI flags. SKILL.md authoring is approachable but the SDK does not help publish them.

Well-written, deep, English-only official docs. Quickstart is 5 minutes; API reference (code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript) is autogenerated from TypeScript types and comprehensive. Separate hosting/production guide page covers permissions and multi-tenant gotchas — a rare explicit deployment page. In-repo examples limited to three session-store adapters. A PM can author SKILL.md but cannot author hooks/sub-agents/tools without engineering.

Documentation in 4 languages: English (docs/en/, deepest), Arabic, Korean, Brazilian Portuguese. 21 concept pages, 17 enterprise feature pages, 25+ integrations (Gmail, Salesforce, Stripe, Notion), 18 observability integrations, ~70 individual tool pages. Crew Studio (AMP) is a no-code visual crew builder explicitly aimed at non-engineers; YAML-first project layout (@CrewBase + agents.yaml + tasks.yaml) is friendly to non-engineers editing prompts/roles. SKILL.md authoring is doable by Product/Data.

Official docs in English + Simplified Chinese (cloudwego.io/docs/eino/). Chinese pages frequently include longer code examples, more middleware-specific guidance, and faster-updated v0.8 ADK content; English versions are shorter. Source-level docs are bilingual (parallel *_chinese.go prompt files; SetLanguage(LanguageChinese) toggles internal prompts). A non-engineer can technically author SKILL.md markdown but the Chinese-richer docs gap makes cross-team contribution materially harder than English-only stacks.

Official docs at https://genkit.dev/docs/overview/ with ?lang=js|go|py toggle. Solid Go coverage: Generate, Tools, Flows, Prompts (dotprompt), Streaming, Plugins, Telemetry, Evaluators. Per-feature pages: agents, tools, sessions, guardrails, handoffs, MCP, realtime, sandbox, tracing, voice, visualization, REPL. Cross-team accessibility is medium — docs assume a Python developer comfortable with asyncio, dataclasses, Pydantic. No markdown-only authoring flow for non-engineers (skills bundled into Python code or pulled from a LocalDir).

Astro/Starlight site under docs/, multi-language (English + ja/zh/ko translations). Guides cover Agents, Running Agents, Sessions, Streaming, Tools, MCP, Handoffs, Human-in-the-loop, Guardrails, Tracing, Sandbox Agents, Voice Agents, Models, Context, Troubleshooting. Examples directory is large and runnable (22 sub-folders). A non-engineer would need TypeScript and CLI familiarity; no no-code surface.

Topic coverage: agents, capabilities, hooks, agent-spec (YAML), dependencies, output, message history, multi-agent, MCP client/server, durable execution, UI adapters, evals, models/providers. Official docs at https://docs.rig.rs + Rustdoc at https://docs.rs/rig/latest/rig/. Documentation is aimed at Rust engineers; non-engineers can read README and examples but cannot author content (no skills, no markdown configs, no playground). Thinnest non-engineer authoring surface alongside autoagents.

English docs at https://strandsagents.com/. In-repo docs/ contains HOOKS.md, MCP_CLIENT_ARCHITECTURE.md, PR.md, STYLE_GUIDE.md, README.md. No UI authoring layer in the SDK itself — that lives in the separate agent-builder repo.

In-repo: README.md (top-level usage), AGENTS.md (~600+ lines agent-specific contributor guide), CONTRIBUTING.md, COMPATIBILITY.MD, docs/{TESTING,DEPENDENCIES,DIVERGENCES,PR}.md. External: https://strandsagents.com/ (shared with Python sibling) + https://strandsagents.com/docs/api/typescript/. Non-engineer authoring is possible via SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter + markdown) through the Skills plugin (strands-ts/src/vended-plugins/skills/).

Docs at ai-sdk.dev/docs are deep with quickstarts and migration guides; source docs live at content/ in the repo. TypeScript-centric — a non-engineer (Product/Data) authoring agent behavior would need engineering help, with no "drop a markdown file" runtime path. (The skills/ directory in this repo is contributor-facing — telling Claude/Cursor how to author code with the SDK — not a runtime feature consumers use.) ADR pattern encouraged.

Go library that also ships first-party REST/A2A servers, web UI, and an Agent Engine emulator (server/adkrest, server/adka2a, cmd/launcher). One Go binary covers loop + HTTP, so it sits between thin library and platform.

Python library plus an opinionated AgentOS FastAPI server (50+ routers, JWT, RBAC, scheduler). Optional os.agno.com control-plane UI points at your self-hosted runtime. Behaves as a batteries-included platform you self-host.
Multi-crate Rust workspace (autoagents-core, llm, telemetry, etc.); no HTTP server, no CLI runtime. Optional ractor-based SingleThreadedRuntime for in-process actor pub/sub.
Python shim that subprocesses the bundled Claude Code Node CLI binary; the agent loop runs in the CLI, not in Python. Library-only, no HTTP server.
TypeScript shim that subprocesses a 207-233 MB per-platform native Claude Code binary (post 0.2.113). Library-only; loop, skills, sub-agents all live in the subprocess.
Pure Python library (Crew/Flow/Agent), no HTTP server. Enterprise AMP SaaS adds the managed runtime, automations, RBAC, marketplace — but that is a vendor cloud.
Go library (graph runtime + ADK) used as embedded import. No HTTP server, no CLI runtime, no platform layer; you assemble HTTP/auth/persistence around it.
Go library (flows, registry, plugins) with a dev-only Reflection HTTP server bound to :3100 driven by the Node genkit CLI. In production it is just your Go binary serving genkit.Handler routes.
OSS Python graph runtime (libs/langgraph) plus a closed-source HTTP server (langgraph_api / LangGraph Platform) that the CLI loads on langgraph dev/up. Hybrid OSS+SaaS.
Python library; agent loop runs in your asyncio event loop. No bundled HTTP server (llama_deploy is a separate repo) and deployment docs are still a TODO stub.
Full-stack TypeScript framework: @mastra/core (loop, registry, storage), @mastra/server (Hono HTTP), deployers, CLI/Studio, Mastra Cloud optional. Behaves as a platform.
Python and .NET libraries plus hosting helpers (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting, DurableTask, Azure Functions). Loop is in your process; deployment shape is your choice.
Pure Python library (~36 kLOC) built on the openai SDK. No subprocess, no server, no platform; host owns HTTP layer.
TypeScript library (agents-core + openai + realtime + extensions). No bundled server or CLI; you embed run() inside your own Node/Deno/Bun handler.

Provider-agnostic Python library built as a typed pydantic_graph state machine. Ships opt-in adapters (agent.to_web, AGUIAdapter, VercelAIAdapter) and durable execution integrations (Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate).
Rust workspace of Cargo crates (rig-core + 19 companions) — no server, no CLI, no managed cloud. Pure embedded library.
Python library; event_loop_cycle runs in your asyncio worker. Optional A2A FastAPI server is for agent-to-agent only, not user-facing.
TypeScript SDK (@strands-agents/sdk) with optional A2AExpressServer subpath. Loop is an async generator; no multi-tenant chat server.
Library only — generateText/streamText + provider adapters + UI helpers. No server, no session store, no runtime; the host owns everything around the loop.

runner.Runner.Run drives flow.Run/agent.Run/tool dispatch entirely inside the Go binary (internal/llminternal/base_flow.go). No subprocess, no sidecar — same OS process for loop + REST + A2A + WebUI. Simplest deployment shape in the benchmark.

Agent.run dispatches to _run.run_dispatch -> _run (libs/agno/agno/agent/_run.py:324-712), all in the uvicorn worker. Background memory threads run inline; no subprocess and no vendor cloud unless you opt into os.agno.com.
BaseAgent.run drives TurnEngine.run_turn loop on the host tokio runtime (crates/autoagents-core/src/agent/direct.rs). Optional ractor SingleThreadedRuntime stays in-process; LLM is just HTTPS out.

The actual model->tool->result cycle, skills, sub-agents, compaction all execute in the bundled Claude Code Node CLI (subprocess_cli.py:474-482). Python is only a transport + control-protocol shim. Adds JSON-RPC bridge, version checks, and a 20-30 s cold start (issue #333).

note: Loop runs in native CLI subprocess
details: Same architecture as the Python SDK: loop runs in a 207-233 MB per-platform Claude Code native binary spawned via stdio (sdk.mjs). TS query() is a transport shim; cannot fork the loop without forking Claude Code.
Crew.kickoff -> Task.execute_sync -> AgentExecutor (experimental/agent_executor.py) all live in-process. No subprocess, no vendor binary; AMP is a separate hosted runtime.
ChatModelAgent.Run spawns a goroutine inside your process that drives a compose.Graph (adk/chatmodel.go:948-995). No subprocess, no daemon; LLM calls go straight from the binary.

ai.GenerateWithRequest (go/ai/generate.go:211-510) iterates model->tools->loop inside your binary. The Node genkit CLI talks to your process only in dev via the Reflection server on :3100; production is one Go binary.

CompiledStateGraph.stream drives PregelLoop.tick directly in-process (libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_loop.py). The closed-source langgraph_api server merely wraps the same in-process loop with queue + auth + persistence.
FunctionAgent.run -> Workflow.run schedules @step methods on the asyncio loop (llama_index/core/agent/workflow/base_agent.py). No subprocess, no vendor round-trip.
loop() in packages/core/src/loop/loop.ts builds a Mastra workflow stream that runs entirely on Node/Bun/Edge. No subprocess, no external scheduler.
Python: agent.run -> BaseChatClient.get_response and _try_execute_function_calls in _tools.py:1632. .NET: ChatClientAgent.RunCoreAsync via FunctionInvokingChatClient. No subprocess, no bundled CLI.
Runner.run (src/agents/run.py:197) drives run_single_turn/execute_tools_and_side_effects on the host asyncio loop. No subprocess, no sister-repo runtime.
Runner.run() is a TS class with a single while(true) loop (packages/agents-core/src/run.ts:844) calling prepareTurn/model.doStream/processModelResponse in-process.
Agent.iter -> AgentRun wraps a pydantic_graph GraphRun (UserPromptNode -> ModelRequestNode -> CallToolsNode). All nodes run in your interpreter; only LLM calls go out over HTTPS.
PromptRequest::send and the streaming variant are plain Rust async functions on the caller's tokio runtime (crates/rig-core/src/agent/prompt_request/mod.rs:396-709). No subprocess, no IPC.
event_loop_cycle (src/strands/event_loop/event_loop.py:120) is a pure-Python async generator driven from Agent.stream_async. No subprocess, no bundled binary.
Agent.stream() is an async function* loop running on V8 (strands-ts/src/agent/agent.ts:608). WASM build exists for Python guest but the TS SDK runs natively in Node.
generateText/streamText runs in-process; ToolLoopAgent.stream() is just a method call wrapper. No daemon, no IPC, only LLM HTTPS calls leave the process.

Single Go binary; no Node, no Python, no bundled CLI. Optional Postgres/MySQL/SQLite/Spanner only if you use session/database. GCS/Vertex Agent Engine opt-in. Lightest runtime story alongside eino and rig.

Python 3.7+; for the server extra add FastAPI/uvicorn/SQLAlchemy/PyJWT/OpenTelemetry/croniter. Pulls 49 model adapters and 100+ tool modules — moderate footprint. Optional Postgres/MySQL/Redis/Mongo/DynamoDB depending on storage choice.

Rust 1.75+ and tokio are the only mandatory pieces; ractor is enabled by default for the actor runtime. No DB, no vendor service, no bundled binary. WASM/llama.cpp/mistral-rs are opt-in Cargo features.

Python 3.10 plus the bundled claude Node binary (or system-installed claude) is mandatory — the loop cannot start without it. Adds Anthropic credentials and a JSON-RPC bridge. Cold start dominated by Node startup.

Node 18+ plus a 207-233 MB per-platform native CLI as optionalDependencies (mandatory in practice — SDK throws on missing binary). Multi-arch deploys ship ~460 MB of binaries. Anthropic provider + optional bubblewrap for sandbox.

Python 3.10-3.13, pure Python — no Node/Go/CLI. LanceDB writes locally by default. LiteLLM pulls many provider SDKs. Optional E2B/Daytona/MCP if you use those tools. AMP path requires the vendor cloud.
Single Go binary; no bundled binaries, no required Postgres/Redis. Optional eino-ext modules pull in vector stores, MCP, tracing only when you adopt them. Lightest deployment story in the benchmark.
Go 1.25 with pure-Go modules. Node + genkit CLI is optional and dev-only (eval, dev UI). Optional GCP credentials / OTel / Firestore / Postgres only if you use those plugins.

Python 3.10 only for pure-OSS embed. But to get the HTTP server / auth / queue / multitask coordination you install closed-source langgraph-runtime-postgres plus a Redis pub/sub on top of Postgres. Self-host effectively means BYO Postgres+Redis.

Python 3.10. Core pulls SQLAlchemy, pydantic, tiktoken, nltk, banks, httpx, aiohttp, llama-index-workflows — non-trivial import graph. No mandatory infra; default Memory uses local SQLite. Production typically swaps in Postgres.

Node 18+ (or Bun/Cloudflare Workers/Vercel Edge). Default in-memory store is fine for dev but must be replaced for production (libsql/pg/d1/dynamo). Optional vector store, Redis pubsub, OTel exporter.
Python 3.10+ or .NET 8/9+; no bundled subprocess. Optional Redis/Cosmos/Azure AI Search/Foundry threads only if you opt into those persistence/hosting kits. Provider SDKs added on demand.
Python 3.10+, no bundled binaries, no native libs beyond pydantic-core wheels. Sessions default to in-memory; Postgres/Redis/Mongo/Dapr only when you pick those backends.
Node 22+ (Deno/Bun supported). No bundled binaries. Sessions in memory by default; tracing exporter calls OpenAI Traces unless disabled. Optional MCP subprocesses.
Python 3.10+, pydantic / pydantic-graph / genai-prices / opentelemetry-api / anyio. No bundled binaries, no required infra. Durable execution opts into Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate as extras.
Rust edition 2024, tokio + reqwest by default. No bundled subprocess; provider crates are individual features. WASM-compatible. Persistence/vector stores are companion crates you pull as needed.
Python 3.10. Core deps include boto3 (Bedrock default), pydantic. No bundled binary, no required infra; S3 only if you use S3SessionManager. Provider extras under pyproject.toml:46-79.

Node 20+, @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime, uuid, yaml. Other providers (@anthropic-ai/sdk, openai, @google/genai, @ai-sdk/provider) are peer-deps you install on demand. No subprocess, no mandatory DB.
Node 18/20/22, pure JS/TS. No native libs, no bundled CLI, no database required. Add @ai-sdk/<provider> packages only for what you use.

README explicitly recommends Cloud Run / GKE deployment; cmd/launcher/full composes web UI + REST + A2A + Agent Engine emulator. Sessions persist to Cloud SQL Postgres or Vertex Agent Engine. Multi-tenant via AppName/UserID/SessionID composite key.

Canonical pattern is agent_os.serve() uvicorn (libs/agno/agno/os/app.py:1466). Horizontal scale by pointing multiple workers at the same BaseDb. Auth/RBAC/SSE/scheduling/tracing all in-process. Detailed in docs.agno.com/runtime/deploy.

docs/architecture only describes 'direct agents' vs 'actor agents' inline; no container-per-tenant or shared-process guidance. You embed AutoAgents in your own Axum/Actix binary and decide topology entirely yourself.

Not stated in repo. Implicit: every query()/ClaudeSDKClient connection spawns a CLI subprocess, so natural shape is container-per-tenant or one-Python-process-many-CLI-subprocesses. Ships only Dockerfile.test, no production Dockerfile.

Vendor hosting doc recommends one CLI subprocess per session. assistant.mjs/bridge.mjs expose a worker-per-session blueprint with userIdleMs despawn. No first-party queue or scheduler. N session workers per pod is the practical pattern.

OSS docs assume one Python process running a Crew per request; no first-party multi-tenant pattern. production-architecture.mdx covers crew design, not horizontal scaling. AMP recommends container-per-crew-automation on the managed runtime.

CloudWeGo docs do not prescribe a topology; implicit one-process-many-tenants with horizontal pod scaling and BYO ingress. In practice (e.g. ByteDance, Dailymotion Ray) Eino is embedded in a single Go process per pod behind your own router.

Go samples target Google Cloud Run as the canonical hosting model — stateless container behind a load balancer with one Go binary serving genkit.Handler routes. Multi-tenancy via context provider; no tenant pinning recommended.

Platform docs recommend one-process-many-tenants with a fleet of API pods sharing Postgres + Redis pub/sub between API and worker pods. Self-host follows the same pattern via langgraph up Docker compose and the langchain-ai/helm chart.

Official deployment tutorial is a literal TODO stub (docs/.../deployment.md:1-6). Vendor punts production multi-agent serving to the separate llama_deploy project (out of scope here). No first-party hosting guidance for FunctionAgent.

@mastra/server (Hono) is stateless across requests; multiple replicas behind LB share storage backend. Resumable streams remove the need for session affinity. Ships deployers for Vercel/Netlify/Cloudflare Workers and deployers/cloud.

Vendor recommends: Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting (AddAIAgent + AgentSessionStore + AIHostAgent) for ASP.NET multi-tenant; FoundryHostedAgents for container-per-agent; DurableTask + AzureFunctions for durable orchestration. Each path has samples.

SDK has no vendor opinion; examples assume one Python process per host with sessions isolated by session_id. Horizontal scaling by N stateless workers + shared SQLAlchemy/Redis/Mongo store. No first-party container-per-tenant recommendation.

Docs do not prescribe topology; examples/nextjs shows in-process Next.js route handler. Each run() is request-scoped; no built-in worker pool, queue, or cluster mode. Cloudflare Workers documented as experimental.

Not opinionated; docs treat Agent like a FastAPI App reused across requests. UI adapter docs assume one agent per ASGI app, one route per agent endpoint. Production durable patterns documented for Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate.
Library only; docs offer zero production deployment guidance. You ship a Rust binary (typically axum + tokio) and embed Rig. Container-per-tenant vs one-process-many-tenants is entirely your call.

Concurrency lock (agent/agent.py:823) refuses concurrent invocations, pushing you to one Agent instance per active session. Many sessions per process are fine. Official guide at strandsagents.com/.../operating-agents-in-production.

README/examples treat the SDK as a normal Node library — no shipped agent runtime daemon. Practical patterns: one-process-many-agents or container-per-tenant if you want strong isolation. No documented multi-tenant blueprint.

SDK ships no hosting recipes; vendor examples/next-agent recommend createAgentUIStreamResponse in a Next.js API route (one process per Node instance, many tenants per process). State lives in your external DB.

Fastest in the benchmark. Sub-second from main() to first r.Run(); tens of MB RAM (Go runtime + gorilla/mux + genai client). 20-40 MB binary depending on whether you embed the Web UI. No interpreter/vendor binary penalty.

Cold start includes uvicorn + FastAPI app + AgentOS init (db_lifespan, _initialize_sync/async_databases, optional MigrationManager). Pydantic v2 + 100+ tool modules + 49 model adapters give a moderate footprint. Not measured in repo.

Not benchmarked, but a Rust release binary cold-starts in <100ms with small RAM baseline (no embedded vector store / LLM weights unless you enable those Cargo features). Compile time is the real cost, not runtime.

Every connect() runs _check_claude_version() (2 s timeout), spawns the CLI binary, then a 60 s initialize control-protocol roundtrip. Issue #333 reports 20-30 s cold start. 200-500 MB RAM per active session including model context.

Binary footprint 207-233 MB per platform in node_modules (multi-arch Docker adds up). 5-20 s warm-process resolve + initialize handshake; startup()/WarmQuery exists explicitly to amortize this. listSessions() can use 900 MB+ RAM (issue #268).
Fresh import crewai + Crew(...).kickoff() dominated by openai + LiteLLM imports (~0.5-1 s) and LanceDB index init (~100 ms). ~150 MB RAM baseline. No 20-30 s startup like Claude Agent SDK.

Runner construction is just struct allocation (adk/runner.go:63-69). Eino package is ~12k LOC of Go code; per-session memory dominated by runSession.Events. Massive cold-start advantage vs Claude Agent SDK Python.

Cloud Run Go binary cold-boots well under 1 s after image pull. RAM baseline ~30 MB for a minimal binary; Vertex AI client + gRPC adds ~50 MB on first call. No documented startup ceremony — heavyweight pieces live in the JS CLI.

Pure-OSS embedding: a few hundred ms to import the package; tens of MB RAM baseline beyond model client. Platform deployment: Starlette+Uvicorn worker pods with Postgres pool dominating RAM — exact numbers not visible (closed-source server).

Pure-Python import overhead pulls in SQLAlchemy, pydantic, tiktoken, nltk, banks, httpx, aiohttp — non-trivial. No published RAM baseline. Cold start ultimately dominated by LLM SDK warm-up, not framework code.

No public benchmark in repo. Realistic baseline for a 5-agent app: tens of MB RAM, sub-second cold start on Node, longer (~1-2 s) on Cloudflare Workers due to bundle size. @mastra/core is heavy (>200 source files).

Not advertised. Thin .NET assembly / Python package — startup dominated by provider SDK initialisation (AzureCliCredential, OpenAIClient) and context-provider loading. No documented multi-second cold-start surcharge.
Cold start low — lazy SQLiteSession import, lazy-imported extension backends. ~100-150 MB RAM for interpreter + pydantic + openai SDK. SQLiteSession defaults to :memory: (zero disk).
No bundled binary; SDK is pure JS/TS. Startup is whatever your Node process takes (~200-400 ms typical). RAM minimal beyond Node baseline. No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK issue #333.
Sub-second once Python is warm. No bundled binaries, no LLM subprocess. RAM baseline = pydantic + chosen provider SDK (tens of MB). No documented 20-30 s startup.
Rust binary startup typically <500 ms once compiled — no JIT, no Python interpreter. Memory baseline small: Agent is a few Arcs plus a RwLock-wrapped ToolServerState. No vendor binary download.
Construction initializes ToolRegistry, HookRegistry, EventLoopMetrics, OTel tracer (agent/agent.py:271-302); a few hundred ms cold from boto3/pydantic imports. No 20-30 s subprocess warm-up.
Not measured but expected to be light because no subprocess starts. Lazy-loaded peer-deps keep tree-shaken bundles small. Browser bundle check in CI suggests modest baseline.
Cold start is just a JS import — tens of milliseconds. No bundled binaries or large native deps. Footprint is essentially Node baseline; first LLM call latency is provider-dominated.

LLM: medium-high de-facto — model.LLM interface is open but LLMRequest is shaped around genai.Content; only first-party impls ship for Gemini/Vertex. Hosting: low-medium; README pushes Cloud Run. Session backend Vertex Agent Engine is GCP-only. Eval Python-only. Observability OTel-portable.

LLM: 49 providers under libs/agno/agno/models — minimal lock-in. Hosting: none, just a uvicorn Python process. Eval: BaseEval/Scorer classes in-repo; OTel tracing is provider-neutral. os.agno.com UI is optional viewer for self-hosted runtime.
LLM: unified LLMProvider trait with 10+ cloud + 3 local providers. Hosting: none — runs anywhere Rust runs. Eval: none shipped. Observability: OTel via autoagents-telemetry + optional Langfuse.

LLM: strongly Anthropic-locked — CLI talks to the Messages API directly; Bedrock/Vertex routed through Anthropic. Hosting: portable as a library. Eval/observability: only OTel forwarding. CLI binary itself is closed-source and version-specific — you cannot swap the loop.

LLM: high-medium — Anthropic native; Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry/anthropicAws/mantle/gateway enumerated as AccountInfo.apiProvider. 3P providers require gateway adapters. Hosting: low (self-host) but high if you adopt the claude.ai bridge. Skill/sub-agent format is CC-shaped (high migration cost).

OSS path: zero lock-in — LiteLLM gives 100+ providers, runs anywhere, OTel exporter free. AMP path: heavy — Agent Repositories, Automations, Triggers, Studio, RBAC, SSO, Traces dashboard, hallucination guardrail are AMP-only. Score reflects the OSS path used in this benchmark.

LLM: low — model.BaseChatModel/ToolCallingChatModel abstract 11+ providers; trivial to add your own. Hosting: none, library only. Eval: none shipped (BYO). Persistence: CheckPointStore is two methods on []byte. Cloud-vendor lock-in zero; CloudWeGo/ByteDance only drive roadmap priorities.

LLM: green — first-party plugins for googlegenai, vertexai, anthropic, compat_oai, ollama, modelgarden + Fallback middleware. Hosting: slight GCP tilt (samples target Cloud Run; telemetry plugin is GCP-only) but nothing GCP-required. Eval: BYO interface. Brand-level lock-in is Firebase repo + googlegenai default.

LLM: low — any langchain-* chat model works, init_chat_model for string routing. Hosting/platform: medium — HTTP server, auth, run queue, multitask coordination, /mcp routes ship only via LangGraph Platform (closed-source). Eval: medium — USD cost requires LangSmith (paid).

LLM: none — pluggable LLM abstraction with 104 implementations. Hosting: none for the OSS framework (llama_deploy is OSS, LlamaCloud is for parse/ingest). Eval: none — any of LangSmith/Arize/Langfuse/Opik/Phoenix integrate via callbacks.

LLM: low — Vercel AI SDK v5/v6 adapters across 40+ providers. Hosting: low — deployers for Vercel/Netlify/Cloudflare Workers; Hono server runs anywhere. Storage: low (15+ adapters). Eval/observability: medium — MastraScorer API and Mastra spans are house-shaped; OTel/Langfuse exporters exist but are not default.

LLM: open — Azure OpenAI / Foundry / OpenAI / Anthropic / Bedrock / Gemini / Ollama / GitHub Copilot / Foundry-Local / Copilot Studio adapters. Hosting: Microsoft Azure stack is clearly first-class (Foundry, Azure Functions, Cosmos, AI Search) but core has no hard Azure dep. Eval/observability OTel-native.

LLM: low — MultiProvider supports openai/ litellm/ any-llm/ prefixes (100+ providers). Hosting: none — runs anywhere Python 3.10+ runs. Eval/observability: none — default exports to free OpenAI Traces but 25+ partner exporters replace it. Session-store: 10 first-party backends + Protocol for BYO.

LLM: medium — default is OpenAI Responses API; Anthropic/Gemini/Bedrock/Vertex via @openai/agents-extensions/ai-sdk bridge or hand-rolled Model impl. Hosted tools (webSearchTool, fileSearchTool, codeInterpreterTool, imageGenerationTool, toolSearchTool) are OpenAI-only. Tracing defaults to OpenAI Traces.

LLM: low — ~14 providers + FallbackModel chain + pydantic-ai-litellm direction; custom Model implementable. Hosting: none. Eval: low — pydantic-evals optional; LangSmith/Braintrust via OTel. Observability: OTel-first; Logfire is one backend among many.
LLM: low — 26 native providers (Anthropic/Azure/Cohere/Gemini/Groq/Ollama/OpenAI/OpenRouter/Mistral/...). Hosting: none. Eval: in-tree evals.rs, no platform lock. No managed cloud, no marketplace.

LLM: low — 12+ providers in src/strands/models (Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, LiteLLM, Llama, Mistral, Ollama, SageMaker, Writer, Llama.cpp). Hosting: low — pure Python. Eval: low — no built-in. Default-Bedrock biases AWS shops but nothing about the SDK is AWS-only.

LLM: low — Bedrock default but Model base class is provider-agnostic; adapters for Anthropic, OpenAI Chat+Responses, Google, plus VercelModel shim around the AI SDK. Hosting: none. Eval/observability: OTel-native so any OTLP backend works.

LLM: low — 50+ provider adapters behind LanguageModel interface, swap providers in one line. Hosting: low, library-only — Vercel hosting + AI Gateway are conveniences, not requirements. Eval: N/A — SDK does not ship eval.

Bundles loop + session store (3 backends) + memory + artifact store + REST + A2A + Agent Engine emulator + WebUI + plugin system + skill loader + MCP client + configurable YAML + replay plugin + CLI. Comparable in scope to Mastra, heavier than Vercel AI SDK, lighter than LangGraph.

~50 subpackages in libs/agno/agno/: agent, team, workflow, tools (130+ files), models (49), db (10), knowledge, memory, learning, eval, guardrails, hooks, skills, scheduler, tracing, os (7k LOC FastAPI server). Agent constructor has 80+ parameters. Platform-tier surface.

Heavy by total LOC across multi-crate workspace (speech, vector stores, derive macros, guardrails, WASM sandbox), but the core autoagents-core surface is focused: agent/executor/memory/tool/context/hooks/runtime. You pay via Cargo features only what you use.

Thin Python SDK (~5 kLOC across src/claude_agent_sdk/): types.py 2043 lines, _internal/query.py 899, transport/subprocess_cli.py 762, client.py 627. Heavy lifting is in the bundled CLI binary (megabytes of Node bundle, not source-distributed).

TS shim ~862 KB sdk.mjs + ~1.1 MB bridge.mjs + 31 KB assistant.mjs + 17 KB browser-sdk.js (<= 2 MB pure JS). sdk.d.ts is 5722 lines. Bundled native CLI 207-233 MB per platform makes this the heaviest of the benchmark on disk.

Heavy framework: ~70 kLOC in core (agent classes, executors, memory, knowledge, RAG, MCP, A2A, event bus, hooks, checkpoint engine, CLI, skill loader, tool catalog, training data, guardrails, planning). 5 sub-packages under lib/, 151 event classes. But no HTTP server.

Medium-heavy library: 12k+ LOC across compose/, adk/, schema/, callbacks/, components/. ADK alone is ~40 files + 7 middlewares + 3 prebuilts. Zero platform code (no HTTP, no UI, no eval, no marketplace) — OSS runtime philosophy.

~317 Go files in go/. Core packages genkit/ai/core/api/tracing/logger/session/streaming (~25 dirs). 18 first-party plugins. Heavier than Anthropic Claude Agent SDK wrapper, lighter than Mastra. Each piece is opt-in and Generate call remains a single function.

Heavy: graph runtime ~2k LOC, but ToolNode + prebuilt + checkpointers + SDK add ~10k more, and BaseStore/BaseCheckpointSaver interfaces invite significant ecosystem packages. Platform-shaped via langgraph_api closed-source server.

Heavy ecosystem (300+ integration packages) but core is modular — install only what you need. Agent layer in llama-index-core/.../workflow is ~2000 lines across 9 files (base_agent.py 825, multi_agent_workflow.py 888).

Heavy framework: @mastra/core 200+ files; packages/core/src/agent/agent.ts is 6992 lines. Bundles agents + workflows + memory + storage + RAG + voice + MCP + deployer + scheduler + scorers + RBAC/FGA + playground + Studio. Tight coupling but consistent platform.

Heavy — Python core alone is ~27 kLOC; comparable to LangGraph in scope but broader. Bundles agents, workflows, sessions, compaction, mcp, middleware, observability, skills, security/labelling, evaluation, harness providers (memory/todo/mode), serialization, 20+ provider connectors.

Ships agents, sessions (10 backends), guardrails (4 types), MCP client + server-bridge, sandbox runtime with 7 providers, tracing, realtime (voice), Codex extension, hosted-tool wrappers, REPL. No dev UI, no frontend, no scheduler, no deployer, no eval harness.

Lean. Umbrella @openai/agents re-exports agents-core (~60 files), agents-openai (~15 files), agents-realtime (voice), agents-extensions (AI-SDK/Cloudflare/Twilio adapters). No bundled storage, eval, dev UI, or plugin system.

pydantic_ai_slim is ~50 modules; Agent class ~2885 LOC; graph engine ~2229 LOC. Optional evals/graph/durable-exec packages are clean separations. No bundled storage, no dev UI beyond clai/to_web, no marketplace. Library-first by design.

Medium-thick Rust library: ships Agent, AgentBuilder, Extractor, Pipeline, multi-turn loop, streaming loop, 26 provider integrations, 10+ vector stores, MCP client, CLI chatbot helper, telemetry helpers. No HTTP server, no dev UI, no marketplace.

Medium-light. ~30 sub-modules under src/strands/. Bundles tool registry hot-reload, MCP client, three multi-agent orchestrators (Graph/Swarm/A2A), OTel-native telemetry, FileSession+S3Session, sliding+summarizing conversation managers, two checkpoint mechanisms, interrupt system, AgentSkills plugin.

StreamManager-based durable streaming (experimental): first call writes X-Genkit-Stream-Id response header; reconnecting client supplies it and subscribeToStream replays from durable store (in-memory or Firestore impl shipped, samples/durable-streaming-firestore). No general 'session reopen' endpoint though.

GET /threads/{id}/runs/{run_id}/stream?last_event_id=... resumes SSE from the last delivered event id when stream_resumable: true. GET /threads/{id}/state and /state/{checkpoint_id} expose historical snapshots. HITL resume via POST /runs/stream with command: {resume: ...}.
Pattern: serialize Context to your store keyed by session_id, look it up on next request, pass ctx= to workflow.run. No endpoint shipped (docs/agent/state.md).

Three endpoints: GET /agents/:id/observe-stream (mid-stream attach, resumable, multi-client), POST /agents/:id/resume-stream (resume suspended runs from tool.suspend), GET /agents/:id/subscribe-thread (SSE subscription to thread's runs). Best-in-class resume surface.

DevUI: re-send the same conversation ID and the server automatically pulls thread history (README.md:175-196). AG-UI: availableInterrupts and resume metadata propagated through AGUIChatClient. No event-id replay.
Persist RunResult.to_state().to_json() on interruption; POST /runs/{id}/resume loads JSON, calls RunState.from_json(agent, json), applies approvals, re-runs. Primitive exists; endpoint is yours.
RunState.toString() → store keyed by conversationId → RunState.fromString(agent, str) → run(agent, state). Recipe in examples/nextjs; no endpoint shipped.

No dedicated endpoint — Vercel-AI / AG-UI design sends full messages history each request. For server-authoritative history, persist by conversation_id and pass message_history to the adapter (docs/ui/overview.md:107).
Not provided. With ConversationMemory you can resume by calling agent.prompt(...).conversation('user-123') again, but no HTTP surface.
Persistence: Agent(session_manager=FileSessionManager(session_id=...)) restores prior messages. Agent.take_snapshot/load_snapshot are the building blocks. No endpoint.
SessionManager.restoreSnapshot({ target: agent }) hydrates from snapshot_latest; agent.invoke([interruptResponseBlock]) resumes. Replay of past events not a primitive. No endpoint.
examples/next/app/api/chat/[id]/stream/route.ts uses third-party resumable-stream package + Redis to re-attach to in-flight streams. Not part of ai package — it's a recommended add-on.
SSE handler reads req.Context() (runtime.go:130) — closing the client connection cancels the context which propagates into Runner.Run and stops the iterator. No explicit DELETE /run/{id} endpoint.

POST /agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel?session_id=... (router.py:824-906) calls agent.acancel_run which sets a flag observed by raise_if_cancelled checkpoints inside _run (multiple checkpoint locations). First-class HTTP cancel.
No cancel primitive at all. Internally you can drop the JoinHandle or call Environment::shutdown to drain the whole runtime. For per-task cancel you'd build your own CancellationToken inside a hook.

ClaudeSDKClient.interrupt() (client.py:313-317) sends a control_request {subtype: 'interrupt'}; stop_task(task_id) cancels a sub-agent task. HTTP exposure: BYO — pattern is DELETE /chat/{sid} → call client.interrupt().
Query.interrupt() / Query.close() (sdk.d.ts:2062, 2278) plus Options.abortController. HTTP: BYO pattern DELETE /v1/sessions/:sid/turn → q.interrupt() on the stored handle.
OSS has no in-process cancel API — Crew.kickoff runs to completion. Only OS-signal events emitted by telemetry; no Crew.cancel/abort. AMP has no documented cancel endpoint either.

Not first-class. You cancel via context.CancelFunc in your host code — closed HTTP request → r.Context().Done() → goroutine sees cancel → agent's in-flight model/tool calls receive ctx cancellation. No 'abort run' API or route.

Standard http.Request cancellation propagates via context. Closed connection → cancelled ctx → tools see ctx.Err(). For durable streaming the flow runs on context.WithoutCancel so disconnect does NOT cancel. Dev UI reflection API has a cancel endpoint but it's dev-mode only.

POST /threads/{id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel?action=interrupt|rollback&wait=0|1 (runs.py:936-991). action=interrupt halts and persists marker; action=rollback discards and reverts state. on_disconnect: 'cancel' creation flag also wires SSE disconnect to cancel.
WorkflowHandler.cancel_run() exists per upstream workflows API. Wired into your route by you — no shipped endpoint.

Server-side AbortSignal wired from HTTP layer into agent.stream({abortSignal}) (agents.ts:1500). Dropping the SSE connection cancels. POST /agents/:id/signals can send application-defined stop signals. No explicit DELETE /runs/:id.
POST /v1/responses/{response_id}/cancel on DevUI (_server.py:886-908) plus automatic cancel on client disconnect. Explicit endpoint with bearer auth.
RunResultStreaming exposes _cancel_mode (none/immediate/after_turn) and result.cancel() (src/agents/result.py:496). Public HTTP surface is yours; SDK gives the primitive.
options.signal: AbortSignal (run.ts:324) propagates into model call and tool executions via details.signal. Pattern: attach request.signal to options.signal. No DELETE endpoint shipped.
StreamedRunResult.cancel() interrupts streaming and yields ModelResponseState='interrupted'. HTTP-side: closing the SSE connection cancels the asyncio task (Starlette). No explicit DELETE endpoint.
In-process, drop the Stream or use AbortHandle/Abortable from streaming.rs. No HTTP cancel endpoint shipped.
Agent.cancel() (agent/agent.py:371-401) sets a threading.Event checked at safe points; returns stop_reason='cancelled'. DELETE /runs/{id} handler calling agent.cancel() is your job.

Three primitives: agent.cancel() flips internal AbortController; InvokeOptions.cancelSignal: AbortSignal composes external signals (bind to req.signal); context.agent.cancelSignal.aborted inside tools. Endpoint is BYO.

Two BYO patterns: (a) same-server chat.stop() aborts local fetch → request.signal propagates to streamText abortSignal; (b) multi-server DELETE /api/chat/:id/stream writes canceledAt to DB; running POST polls every 1s via onChunk and aborts its own signal. Reference recipe in examples/next.

Inherits Gemini's partial FunctionCall streaming. Frames are models.Event with partial: true and FunctionCall.Args as a partial map. event.go:128-178 ensures Args marshals as {} not null when nil so client decoders see a stable field.

ToolCallStartedEvent carries the complete tool call at parse time. Partial-JSON tool-arg streaming is the provider-side feature (OpenAI/Anthropic); Agno surfaces the final tool_args on ToolCallStarted rather than emitting tool-arg deltas. Adapter-dependent.

StreamChunk::ToolUseInputDelta { index, partial_json } (autoagents-protocol/src/llm.rs:78) is emitted in the in-process event stream when providers stream tool args. Wrapped in Event::StreamChunk. HTTP framing is BYO.
include_partial_messages=True emits StreamEvent carrying raw Anthropic SSE input_json_delta events. HTTP-level exposure is BYO — re-emit StreamEvent.event frames over your own SSE channel.

includePartialMessages: true emits SDKPartialAssistantMessage (type: 'stream_event') wrapping BetaRawMessageStreamEvent with input_json_delta. Consumers render partial 'topicSearch({ query: 'young'...' in real time. Wire format is BYO.
In-process LLMStreamChunkEvent carries tool_call.function.arguments accumulated incrementally. AMP webhook llm_stream_chunk event ships the same shape. OSS HTTP framing BYO.

Tool-call deltas come through in the model's streamed *schema.Message chunks (ToolCalls partial fields with Index for merging via schema.ConcatMessages). No separate 'tool-arg-fragment' wire event — extract and forward in your own format.

ToolRequest.Partial bool field (ai/gen.go:543); plugins like googlegenai emit ModelResponseChunk with toolRequestPart Partial=true and Input as in-progress JSON. Same shape Vercel surfaces via tool-input-delta. Provider coverage varies — solid for Gemini.

AIMessageChunk events stream tool arguments as the LLM generates them — visible on stream_mode='messages' via the tool_call_chunks field. Final validated args appear on assembled AIMessage.tool_calls[*].args.
LLM's streamed delta of a tool call comes through on AgentStream.tool_calls as model emits it; granularity depends on the LLM integration. No typed delta event taxonomy.

note: Typed delta chunks on the wire
details: Three explicit chunk types: tool-call-input-streaming-start {toolCallId, toolName}, tool-call-delta {toolCallId, argsTextDelta}, tool-call-input-streaming-end {toolCallId}. Client renders partial args in real time.
DevUI streams response.function_call_arguments.delta (README.md:265); same for AG-UI. OpenAI-Responses-compatible wire.

response.function_call_arguments.delta events from the Responses API flow through RawResponsesStreamEvent directly (examples/basic/stream_function_call_args.py). Client sees argument tokens before tool call finalizes. SSE serialization is BYO.

Provider-dependent. RunRawModelStreamEvent surfaces underlying provider event under event.data.event, so partial tool args appear if the provider streams them. SDK does not normalize into a typed tool-call-delta event.
ToolCallPartDelta (messages.py:2528) emits incremental args_delta strings/dicts; PartDeltaEvent carries them. Vercel AI and AG-UI adapters surface these in their respective dialects.
In-process: StreamedAssistantContent::ToolCallDelta {id, internal_call_id, content} where content is ToolCallDeltaContent::Name(String) or Delta(String) (streaming.rs:71-77). Over the wire: BYO.
Yes in-stream. ToolUseStreamEvent (types/_events.py:145-150) yields {type: 'tool_use_stream', delta: {...}, current_tool_use: {toolUseId, name, input}} as model builds tool args. Wire framing BYO.

Model providers yield ModelContentBlockDeltaEvent with delta: {type: 'toolUseInputDelta', input: '<partial json>'}. Wrapped as ModelStreamUpdateEvent. UI can render 'calling topicSearch with {q: surf...' before dispatch.

First-class wire format: tool-input-start, tool-input-delta (with inputTextDelta), tool-input-available (final input), tool-input-error chunks. useChat auto-updates ToolUIPart.state from input-streaming to input-available. Partial UIs work without custom plumbing.

Wire: tool emits FunctionCall {name: adk_request_confirmation, id, args: {originalFunctionCall, hint, payload}}. Client follows with POST /run_sse carrying FunctionResponse for the same id with {confirmed: bool, payload}. Runner.findAgentToRun matches by id and resumes the tool. No separate /approve endpoint; reuses run-message endpoint. Pause inferred from LongRunningToolIDs.

@tool(requires_confirmation=True / requires_user_input=True / external_execution=True) pauses the model loop; RunPausedEvent emitted with status=RunStatus.paused. POST /agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/continue accepts tools form field with per-tool verdicts and resumes. Separate /approvals/... admin track with its own DB table for cross-tool approvals.
Partial. AgentHooks::on_tool_call returning HookOutcome::Abort skips the call. No 'pause and wait for external approval' state — run cannot be persisted and resumed. Surfacing to HTTP is BYO.

CLI sends control_request: can_use_tool; Python read loop awaits the can_use_tool callback and writes back PermissionResultAllow/Deny. Cross-request HITL requires keeping the ClaudeSDKClient alive across the HITL window. Weaker form: PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision: 'defer' (0.1.74) ends turn with ResultMessage.deferred_tool_use.

canUseTool callback returns a Promise resolved when your operator UI posts a verdict; correlated via toolUseID. No separate pause-state observable — full HITL flow mediated by your SDK consumer. Client-visible pause requires emitting a custom SSE frame from your handler when canUseTool awaits.

Three surfaces: Task(human_input=True) is console-blocking (not API-friendly); Flow-level @human_feedback with pluggable HumanFeedbackProvider supports async raise HumanFeedbackPending → auto-persist flow state → resume via flow.resume(feedback) when external verdict arrives. Tool-level ToolCallHookContext.request_human_input is console-only. AMP ships a Flow HITL Management UI.

Tool calls adk.Interrupt/StatefulInterrupt to pause; Runner saves checkpoint, sends InterruptedAgentEvent. Caller resumes via runner.ResumeWithParams(ctx, checkpointID, &ResumeParams{Targets: {<interrupt-address>: <data>}}). No shipped HTTP route; you wire POST /v1/runs/{id}/approve yourself.

Two-call protocol: first call returns ModelResponse with FinishReason='interrupted' and interrupt metadata; second call resumes via ai.WithToolResponses(tool.RespondWith(...)) or ai.WithToolRestarts(tool.RestartWith(...)). Pause state observable via FinishReason. Client persists messages + interrupted parts.

POST /threads/{id}/runs/stream with {assistant_id, command: {resume, update, goto}}. For multi-interrupt threads, resume can be {interrupt_id: value} mapping. State-edit pattern: POST /state first then /runs/stream with command. Pause state observable as StateSnapshot.interrupts non-empty.

First-class via Context.wait_for_event(HumanResponseEvent, waiter_id, waiter_event=InputRequiredEvent(...), requirements={...}). Client receives InputRequiredEvent on stream and replies via handler.ctx.send_event(HumanResponseEvent(...)). HTTP endpoint shape is yours.

POST /agents/:agentId/approve-tool-call body {runId, toolCallId} returns a new SSE stream resuming execution; /decline-tool-call symmetric; non-streaming variants also exist. Wire emits tool-call-approval chunk with {toolCallId, toolName, args, resumeSchema}. Client can also call /observe-stream for shared visibility.

approval_mode='always_require' causes agent to emit function_approval_request content and return with result.user_input_requests. Client builds function_approval_response (approved=True|False) and POST /v1/conversations/{id}/items with the item, or re-invokes agent.run(approval_response). DevUI surfaces this as response.function_approval.requested/responded events.

function_tool(needs_approval=True) or MCP require_approval. result.interruptions: list[ToolApprovalItem]; state.to_json() to persist; state.approve(interruption) / state.reject; Runner.run(agent, state) to resume. Wire format (endpoint, payload) is yours.

needsApproval: true tools → result.interruptions: RunToolApprovalItem[]. Serialize state, present approvals, then state.approve(interruption) / state.reject and re-run. Reference at examples/agent-patterns/human-in-the-loop.ts. Next.js example uses decisions: {callId: 'approved'|'rejected'} payload on same POST.

First-class. @agent.tool(requires_approval=True) or raise ApprovalRequired returns DeferredToolRequests output. Client gathers approvals and calls a new run with deferred_tool_results=DeferredToolResults(approvals={call_id: True}, calls={call_id: ...}). Or HandleDeferredToolCalls for inline resolution. UI adapters surface deferredToolResults via RunAgentInput extensions.

Only 'pause' primitive is PauseControl (crates/rig-core/src/streaming.rs:33-67) — pauses polling of a stream, does not expose a 'tool approval verdict' channel. For HITL you use on_tool_call → Skip { reason } to reject and ask user to re-submit.

First-class in the loop. BeforeToolCallEvent is _Interruptible; hook raises InterruptException(Interrupt(name, reason)) to pause. Agent yields EventLoopStopEvent with stop_reason='interrupt' and Interrupts list. Client re-invokes agent('...') with list[InterruptResponseContent]; _interrupt_state.resume() unpacks. State persisted via session manager. HTTP endpoint shape is your design.

context.interrupt({name, reason}) throws InterruptError; agent stops with stopReason: 'interrupt' and AgentResult.interrupts. Resume via agent.invoke([{type: 'interruptResponseContent', toolUseId, name, response}]). New interventions subsystem ships Confirm action with inline-or-external response. HTTP wiring BYO.

Wire emits tool-approval-request chunk → client gets ToolUIPart.state='approval-requested' → chat.addToolApprovalResponse({id, approved, reason}) → state='approval-responded' → with sendAutomaticallyWhen the chat re-POSTs messages. Server's next agent.generate sees approval responses in tool messages and resumes. No dedicated /approve endpoint; same POST /api/chat carries everything.

Session state is externalized to GORM-backed storage with per-write optimistic concurrency control (stale-session error at session/database/service.go:373-382). Runner and Flow hold no per-session global state. In-memory sessions use sync.RWMutex. Live bidi sessions require sticky routing but interactive sessions are well-isolated.

Each run()/arun() creates its own RunContext (_run.py:1323-1339) and reads/writes its own AgentSession from the DB. Agent objects are shared but mostly immutable post-construction; per-call mutable state lives in RunContext. AgentOS is explicitly designed to host many concurrent sessions.

AutoAgents has no Session type at all; isolation only works if you spawn one BaseAgent per logical session since memory is per-agent-instance (base.rs:63). Sharing a single agent across sessions will bleed memory. No tenant-scoped isolation primitives ship.

Each ClaudeSDKClient or query() invocation spawns its own claude CLI subprocess with isolated cwd, env, JSONL path, and MCP server connections. Strong OS-level isolation, but the host is BYO (no built-in multi-session manager). State only bleeds via shared filesystem or shared SessionStore adapter.

Each subprocess is single-tenant; state explicitly bleeds if you reuse a subprocess across tenants (working-directory caches, JSONL append target, active model setting are process-global). The SDK does not enforce isolation. Open issue #122 documents an SDK MCP server concurrency hazard between concurrent query() calls in the same Node process.

Each Crew instance has its own id, memory, and tools list, but the event bus is a process-wide singleton (CrewAIEventsBus._instance) and llm hooks are registered globally at module scope (hooks/llm_hooks.py:120). A hook registered for tenant A fires for tenant B. There is no (tenant, hook) scoping primitive.

ctxWithNewRunCtx (adk/runctx.go:387-401) seeds a fresh runContext with its own runSession per Runner.Run call; runSession.valuesMtx and runSession.mtx guard internal maps. Parallel sub-agents fork the context with per-lane events that join back to the parent. Risk: shared state outside runSession.Values (e.g. closure-captured singletons) is not isolated.

Each request gets a fresh context.Context with no shared mutable session state on the Genkit object. The registry is concurrency-safe for reads after Init, sessions live in your session.Store[S] implementation. Standard Go HTTP isolation model — clean but no first-party session semantics enforced.

Isolation is per-run by thread_id with one PregelLoop Python instance per run; no globals leak. State lives in the checkpointer keyed on thread_id. Inside langgraph_api, every Postgres query goes through the @auth.on.* filter chain so resource-scoping is enforced at the data layer.

Each workflow.run(...) call creates a new Context with no global sharing; sessions are isolated by construction. The Context.store is a per-context KV store. No formal Session/tenant concept — isolation is purely by Python object boundary.

RequestContext, MessageList, and RunState are all instantiated per agent.stream() call. SaveQueueManager keys persistence by threadId (save-queue/index.ts:6-49). Reserved requestContext keys (MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY, MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY) are server-controlled and cannot be spoofed at the HTTP layer.

AgentSession holds session_id, service_session_id, and a mutable state dict shared with providers (Python _sessions.py:711); .NET uses AgentSessionStateBag of concurrent-dictionary entries. Agents are typically singletons; only sessions are per-conversation. State bleed only if you store conversation state on the agent (anti-pattern).

Session Protocol binds one session_id per instance; messages are scoped to that id at the store layer (SQLiteSession puts session_id in every row). RunContextWrapper is a fresh dataclass per Runner.run invocation. Approvals are per-RunContextWrapper. Cross-session bleed is impossible inside the SDK unless callers explicitly share mutable TContext.

Each run() invocation constructs a fresh RunState (run.ts:769-780); RunContext<TContext> carries app context and is mutable but per-call. Because no shared runtime exists, isolation is trivially correct provided callers do not share mutable objects across runs. Approvals/usage are shared between parent and forked contexts intentionally.

Fresh RunContext per run() with deps, usage, metadata, conversation_id, run_id (_run_context.py:32). A ContextVar _CURRENT_RUN_CONTEXT (_run_context.py:122) is scoped via set_current_run_context so concurrent run() calls in the same process do not bleed. Toolset for_run lets toolsets spawn fresh instances per run for state isolation.

PromptRequest clones agent data into local fields per call (agent/prompt_request/mod.rs:101-123) so two concurrent prompts don't see each other's new_messages. However, ToolServerHandle is an Arc<RwLock<...>> shared across all uses of the agent, and tool/memory backends are caller-managed. No first-party session/tenant isolation primitive.

Each Agent instance owns its own messages, state, tool_registry, hooks, interrupt_state. Agent.stream_async holds a threading.Lock that throws ConcurrencyException if two invocations enter the same instance (agent/agent.py:823-828). ConcurrentInvocationMode.UNSAFE_REENTRANT is an opt-in foot-gun. Two Agent instances do not share state by construction.

Each Agent instance has its own messages, appState, modelState, toolRegistry, hooksRegistry, interruptState. acquireLock() throws ConcurrentInvocationError if invoke() runs while another invoke() is in flight (agent.ts:460). Multi-tenant fan-out must always be per-request new Agent(...) — sharing a single agent across tenants is explicitly unsafe.

No in-process session bag exists; isolation is whatever the HTTP handler provides. Each request has its own JS scope, its own messages: UIMessage[], and its own runtimeContext. There is no shared mutable state in the ai package that one tenant could leak to another — provided messages and runtimeContext come from external storage and the request.

Session state is externalized to GORM database or Vertex Agent Engine, so N pods share the same session pool. The stale-session check (service.go:373-382) prevents lost updates in racing pods. No leader election; every pod is equal. Live bidi sessions are pod-local (runnerLiveSession holds a Go channel) so /run_live requires sticky sessions.

Stateless workers point at the same PostgresDb/AsyncPostgresDb; sessions keyed by UUID session_id. The scheduler uses DB-backed leader election via agno_schedules rows and SchedulePoller claiming locks (libs/agno/agno/scheduler/poller.py). No agent-level leader election but the scheduler coordinates itself.

The SingleThreadedRuntime has no leader election, distributed lock, shared store, or N-pods-serve-one-session-pool pattern. Horizontal scaling is entirely BYO; the framework does not even acknowledge the concern.

No leader election, no shared coordinator. N Python pods can spawn CLI subprocesses for different sessions but the SessionStore adapter is append-only — concurrent writes to the same session from two pods would interleave unsafely (the SDK assumes one process owns one session at a time). SessionKey.project_key is the documented sharding lever.

The SessionStore interface (sdk.d.ts:3738) plus the Postgres adapter (examples/session-stores/postgres/) lets any pod resume any session by reading from the shared store. forkSession is also store-aware. No leader election; the local ~/.claude JSONL cache is no longer authoritative when sessionStore is set. Still no first-party session coordinator.

OSS has no shared-state, no leader election, no message-queue support — two pods running the same crew code do not share session state (LanceDB/SQLite are local). The CheckpointConfig only supports JSON-on-disk and SQLite. Scaling requires BYO worker pool plus externalizing memory and checkpoint stores via custom BaseProvider implementations. AMP solves this but is out-of-tree.

Eino is a stateless Go binary so pods scale trivially. The CheckPointStore implementation is the shared-state seam — point all pods at the same Postgres CheckPointStore and any pod can resume any session. Leader election, locking, and partition assignment are explicitly not provided; you must layer optimistic concurrency or advisory locks on top.

Cloud Run / GKE replication is the canonical scale model. Genkit has no leader election, no shared lock, no cross-instance coordination. Adopt FirestoreSessionStore for plug-and-play multi-instance, or your own session.Store[S] against Postgres while owning the locking semantics.

All N workers point to the same Postgres PostgresSaver (libs/checkpoint-postgres); thread_id is the partition key. The Pregel loop on any worker can replay from any persisted checkpoint. Leader election is not required — the langgraph_api run queue serializes work per thread via multitask strategy. Pure-OSS embedding needs a BYO queue, but the Platform ships the full distributed coordinator.

In OSS, you serialize a Context (ctx.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer())), stash it in Postgres/Redis/etc., and re-hydrate on the next request from any worker. No leader election, no coordinator. The separate llama_deploy project provides this out-of-tree.

Multiple Mastra processes behind a load balancer share the storage backend; no leader election. Resumable streams (/agents/:id/observe-stream) let any worker pick up an in-progress run because the workflow snapshot lives in storage. Suspended HITL state is durable via workflow snapshots.

Stateless workers share a Cosmos/Redis store via AgentSessionStore (CosmosCheckpointStorage and CosmosChatHistoryProvider in Microsoft.Agents.AI.CosmosNoSql). Leader election and sticky routing are not provided in the vanilla agent, but Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask offers leader-elected, queue-backed orchestration with replay-on-crash.

Stateless workers + shared store; route the same session_id to any worker (sticky routing not required if your store is consistent). SQLAlchemySession, RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, OpenAIConversationsSession all live in a shared external store. No leader election, no consensus, no langgraph_api-style centralized run scheduler. Some retry logic for OpenAI-managed conversation locks but app-level concurrency control is the caller's job.

As long as session state lives in an external store (custom Session impl backed by Postgres/Redis), any number of pods can serve the same session pool. No leader election, no shared in-process state. RunState.toString()/fromString() lets you serialize a paused run to any KV store.

N Python workers all serve the same logical Agent instance; the user owns message_history storage and re-passes per request. Durable execution (Temporal/DBOS/Prefect) provides per-workflow horizontal recovery. No leader election, no shared session pool in-tree.

Multi-pod scaling is the responsibility of the caller's deployment (e.g. axum behind a load balancer); shared state goes through whatever ConversationMemory backend you ship. Rig itself provides nothing — no shared coordinator, no leader election, no shipped distributed store implementations.

Stateless workers are the obvious pattern: keep Agent instances ephemeral and rehydrate from a shared SessionRepository. The SDK ships FileSessionManager, S3SessionManager, and RepositorySessionManager. No leader election or cluster-aware coordination — the SDK is unopinionated about the cluster layer.

N stateless Node processes behind a load balancer each load session state from S3Storage (or another SnapshotStorage) on-demand. No leader election, no built-in worker registration, heartbeat, or queue.

Standard stateless-worker model: spin up N Node processes (Next.js / Fargate / Cloud Run / Vercel Functions), each pulls session state from a shared store. The SDK has no leader election, no shared in-memory map. The chat example uses the third-party resumable-stream package + Redis for durable streams.

First-party in the REST server: PubSubController accepts Cloud Pub/Sub HTTP push messages and runs the agent with a semaphore-throttled concurrency limit (server/adkrest/controllers/triggers/pubsub.go:33-77); Eventarc has an analogous controller. TriggerConfig includes MaxRetries, BaseDelay, MaxDelay, MaxConcurrentRuns. RetriableRunner wraps for exponential backoff. No cron scheduler ships in the box; Cloud Scheduler -> Pub/Sub -> ADK trigger is the documented pattern.

ScheduleManager + SchedulePoller + ScheduleExecutor with croniter-driven cron schedules persisted in agno_schedules tables. agent.arun(..., background=True, stream=True) produces a resumable SSE stream that survives client disconnect and can be resumed via /agents/{agent_id}/runs/{run_id}/resume. @hook(run_in_background=True) decorator schedules FastAPI background tasks. Memory/learning futures run in threads/asyncio tasks during _run.

No cron, no schedulers, no webhook receivers. Long-running background work can be done by spawning your own tokio::spawn and routing tasks through a Topic<Task>, but there is no first-party primitive at all.

No cron, no webhook trigger, no agent-as-background-worker primitive. The closest first-party thing is AgentDefinition.background: bool (types.py:99), but that's a sub-agent hint for the CLI, not a host-level scheduler. All long-running and scheduled work is BYO.

Background sub-agents (AgentDefinition.background: true, sdk.d.ts:79) and background Bash commands (BashInput.run_in_background) emit task_notification events when done. AssistantWorkerOptions.scheduling.dir polls a local scheduled_tasks.json every 10s — local-only, not distributed cron. No webhook intake. BYO for distributed scheduling.

OSS provides nothing — Crew.kickoff() is a blocking call. AMP (closed-source) ships rich first-party Automations + Triggers including Gmail, Calendar, Drive, HubSpot, Salesforce, Slack slash commands, Zapier, webhook/API kickoff, and cron — but none of this lives in the OSS repo. No crewai schedule command, no scheduler module.
Eino has no cron, no webhook trigger system, no scheduled-job framework. Use Go's stdlib (time.AfterFunc, time.Ticker) or an external job library (Asynq, Temporal, Cloud Tasks) in your host.

BackgroundModel abstraction (go/ai/background_model.go) and genkit.GenerateOperation for long-running model ops (video, Imagen) with CheckModelOperation polling — for long model calls only, not general scheduled tasks. core/x/streaming.StreamManager + genkit.WithStreamManager enables resumable long agent runs (experimental per servers.go:79). Cron/webhook triggers are BYO via Cloud Scheduler + a webhook flow.

Pure OSS provides nothing — BYO Celery/arq/Temporal/cron. LangGraph Platform (closed-source langgraph_api) ships crons (crons.create/search/delete in libs/sdk-py/langgraph_sdk/_async/cron.py) and webhooks (run create accepts webhook: str URL). The Platform queue persists scheduled runs in Postgres. Score weighted because OSS-only deployments do not get this.
Not provided in llama-index-core — BYO Celery, Temporal, RQ, or your own asyncio task. The separate llama_deploy project offers richer runtime semantics but is out-of-tree.

Three first-party mechanisms: Schedulers (Mastra({ scheduler }) registers cron-like jobs under /api/scheduled-jobs); Background tasks (disableBackgroundTasks option + backgroundTaskCheckStep + background-task-* chunk family); Webhooks/channels (channels/slack and channels/discord packages wire agent runs into chat events). All are first-class and shipped in the box.

Cron/trigger via Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.AzureFunctions exposing Timer/HTTP/MCPTool triggers. Long-running background via Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask (DurableAIAgent, AgentEntity with EntityAgentWrapper.cs) treating each agent run as a durable orchestration with replay-on-crash. Python has agent-framework-durabletask in beta. All ride on Azure-native primitives.

No scheduler, no cron, no webhook trigger, no long-running background-agent runtime. The optional temporal extra (pyproject.toml:57) integrates Temporal workflows for durable orchestration, but Temporal is a separate runtime you stand up yourself. Report calls this the single biggest architectural gap vs Mastra and LangGraph.
