No cron, no webhook trigger primitives, no queues. Run a worker process (BullMQ, AWS SQS, etc.) and call run() from inside it.

Not provided directly — BYO via Temporal scheduling, Prefect deployments, DBOS workflows, or any external scheduler. The framework only provides the agent runtime; durable_execution docs cover the integration patterns.
No cron, no webhook trigger, no background agent. The Tokio runtime can spawn your own tasks but Rig offers no scheduling abstraction.
The library is invocation-driven; nothing schedules cron or webhook triggers. strands-agents-tools ships a cron.py tool that the agent can use, but that's tool-side, not runtime-side.
No cron primitive, no webhook trigger surface. Use BullMQ / Cloudflare Queues / etc. and call agent.invoke() inside the worker handler.
The SDK has no cron, no scheduler, no webhook trigger primitive. Use your host (Vercel Cron, Cloud Scheduler, Trigger.dev) and invoke agent.generate(...) from there.

The Pub/Sub trigger ships a semaphore-based concurrency limiter (pubsub.go:41: semaphore: make(chan struct{}, MaxConcurrentRuns)), a thin worker-pool. Beyond this the runtime assumes short-lived HTTP request scope. For long runs you either use IsLongRunning() tools that pause/resume on HITL or fire-and-forget via Pub/Sub. No explicit queue or durable dispatcher.

No first-party in-process queue (no Celery integration). The scheduler is DB-polling. For long-running runs: background=True for fire-and-forget with later /resume; Schedules for cron-driven runs; BYO Celery/RQ/Arq if you need a richer queue model.

Tasks are delivered to actors via actor_ref.cast(message) (in ractor). No durable queue, no retry semantics at the queue layer (LLM-level retries exist in optim::RetryLayer, but that's per-call, not queue-level).

The runtime model is one CLI subprocess per active session, lifetime owned by the calling Python coroutine. For queue-shaped workloads you must layer your own (Celery, RQ, Temporal, AWS SQS workers — pick your poison).

The Query interface includes streamInput() and stopTask() (sdk.d.ts:2251, 2256) which give primitives for a long-running streaming session, but there is no shipped queue, no enqueue() API, no leasing semantics. For long-running fan-out agents you build on top with BullMQ/Cloud Tasks/etc.
OSS provides no queue at all. AMP's queue model is implicit — each Automation is a separate managed deployment that receives trigger events and runs the crew. None of that is exposed via OSS code.

The framework assumes short-lived calls into Runner.Run from your HTTP handler. Long-running background work is your responsibility — typical pattern: enqueue externally and have a worker pool call Runner.Run.

No built-in job queue. The expected model is HTTP request -> run flow synchronously -> respond. For async work, place the request on Cloud Pub/Sub / SQS / etc. yourself and have a separate worker process call genkit.Generate on dequeue.

langgraph_api ships a Postgres-backed work queue with one logical lane per thread_id. Long-running agent work is the default expectation: runs can take minutes/hours and a re-attaching client picks up via GET /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/stream?last_event_id=... (requires stream_resumable: true). OSS has no queue and assumes short-lived HTTP request scope. Score reflects Platform-only availability.
Not provided in core. llama_deploy provides this in a separate project — control plane + queue runtime around Workflows — but that's out-of-tree.

Not first-party. Mastra assumes you put it behind your normal Node/Edge HTTP infra. The pubsub/ directory contains a pub/sub abstraction used internally; for production queues you bring your own (BullMQ, SQS, etc.).

DurableTask is the explicit queue/orchestrator model (Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask wraps each agent run as a durable orchestration). Azure Functions triggers fan out to a worker pool. The vanilla in-process agent does NOT expose a queue API, but the production deployment story has first-class Azure-native worker semantics.

The SDK assumes you embed the loop in your own HTTP request scope (or any async task). No internal task queue, no worker pool. For long-running agents typically: expose streaming endpoint over run_streamed(), or persist RunState.to_json() and resume later from a worker pulling jobs off your own queue (Celery/RQ/SQS).

Not provided. The SDK assumes short-lived HTTP request scope by default. Long-running agents need a serialized RunState checkpoint pattern (HITL example at examples/agent-patterns/human-in-the-loop.ts:81-106).

No built-in queue. pydantic_ai.capabilities.ThreadExecutor lets you supply your own concurrent.futures.Executor for sync tool functions in long-running servers (docs/capabilities.md:83-95). Otherwise short-lived HTTP request scope is assumed.

The harness assumes short-lived agent.prompt(...).await usage. No queue, no worker pool. Long-running runs can stream via agent.stream_prompt(...) to keep the client connected but that is not a queue.
Not provided — BYO. There is a ConcurrentToolExecutor (tools/executors/concurrent.py:19) that parallelizes tool calls within one cycle, but no inter-session queue or durable worker pool.

Not provided — BYO. The SDK assumes you wrap agent.stream() in whatever request-scoped wrapper your host uses. The lone exception is the optional A2AExpressServer which assumes one-task-at-a-time per TaskStore — not a general queue model.

Not provided — BYO. No queue. The SDK assumes the request scope is whatever your host gives you (typically HTTP). The new @ai-sdk/workflow package (packages/workflow/src/) provides a WorkflowAgent abstraction wrapping streamText with serializable step IO — but it is not a horizontal multi-tenant runtime.

`session.Session` interface plus `storageSession` GORM model with composite `(AppName, UserID, ID)` primary key, event-sourced `storageEvent` rows carrying messages, tool calls, usage, grounding metadata. Side tables for app/user state scoping. No `tenant_id` but composite identity covers it.

Rich `AgentSession` dataclass with `runs`, `session_data`, `metadata`, `agent_data`, `summary`, `created_at`, `updated_at`. Sibling `TeamSession` and `WorkflowSession`. Storage is per-run rather than per-message, which is coarser than event-sourced peers.

No Session type at all. Closest equivalents are `Task` (input only), `AgentState` (in-memory per-run), and `MemoryProvider` (sliding window). No `id`, `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `metadata`, `usage`, or `model` fields.

`SessionKey` TypedDict with `project_key` for tenant scoping plus `session_id` and optional subpath for subagent transcripts. `SDKSessionInfo` provides rich listing metadata (summary, gitBranch, cwd, tag, createdAt). Per-message rows are intentionally opaque pass-through dicts.

Same model as the Python SDK with `SessionKey { projectKey, sessionId, subpath? }`. The `projectKey` field is explicitly documented as the multi-tenant scope. `SDKSessionInfo` carries summary, gitBranch, cwd, tag, createdAt — closest thing to a tenant-aware session model in the benchmark.

No chat-session abstraction. Closest is a `Crew`/`Flow`/`Agent.kickoff` identified by frozen UUID4 `id` fields. No `tenant_id`, `user_id`, or `created_at` on the Crew. Per-execution state is on `Crew._inputs` and agent executor messages, durable only when checkpoint enabled.

No persistent Session type. `runSession` lives only for one `Runner.Run` call carrying Values/Events/LaneEvents. The persisted checkpoint is `serialization` bytes wrapping RunCtx + interrupt state. Traditional session fields (tenant_id, user_id, created_at, summary) are not in the framework.

`Session[S any]` carries `{ id, state S, store }` — a user-defined typed state struct with no built-in message array. Caller embeds messages, tenant_id, user_id into their own state type. Minimal contract but you build everything yourself.

Typed `Checkpoint` TypedDict with `channel_values`, `channel_versions`, `versions_seen`, plus `CheckpointMetadata` containing `parents`, `writes`, `source` (`input|loop|update|fork`), `step`. On-disk row is `CheckpointTuple` with parent_config and pending_writes. The most expressive session data model in the benchmark.

`Memory` class carries `session_id`, `token_limit`, `memory_blocks`, `sql_store`. Tracks chat history in `SQLAlchemyChatStore` with per-memory table. Workflow `Context` is a separate serializable bag. No tenant fields built in.

Threads are `{ threadId, resourceId }` paired explicitly so resourceId scopes the thread (user or tenant). `MastraDBMessage` shape carries `id, threadId, resourceId, role, content, createdAt, metadata` plus HITL fields. Strong native multi-tenant fit.

`AgentSession` carries `session_id`, optional `service_session_id` (for provider-managed threads like Foundry/OpenAI Responses), and namespaced `state` dict. .NET mirrors with `AgentSessionStateBag`. No first-class `tenant_id`/`user_id` — those go in the state bag.

Intentionally minimal `Session` Protocol with `session_id` + `session_settings` only. Concrete `SQLiteSession` adds `created_at`/`updated_at` columns. Composite tenant IDs are a string-prefix convention, not a typed field.
Interface is just `{ sessionId, items }` with seven methods. Items are full `AgentInputItem[]` history. No first-class tenant/user/metadata — caller composes the id and stores tenant in context.
No Session object. `RunContext` carries `conversation_id` (UUID7), `run_id`, and free-form `metadata` dict; `message_history` is passed in/out of each `run()`. Persistence is fully caller-owned.
Only abstraction is `ConversationMemory` keyed by `conversation_id: &str` to `Vec<Message>`. No `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `parent_session_id`, or metadata anywhere on the trait.

Three dataclasses: `Session(session_id, session_type, created_at, updated_at)`, `SessionAgent(agent_id, state, conversation_manager_state, _internal_state, ...)`, `SessionMessage(message, message_id, redact_message, created_at, updated_at)`. Rich shape but no tenant_id — BYO via `agent.state`.

`Snapshot { scope, schemaVersion, createdAt, data, appData }` with strict separation between framework `data` and user `appData`. `SnapshotLocation { sessionId, scope, scopeId }` ties it to an agent or multi-agent orchestrator. Schema-versioned envelope.
The SDK provides no Session or Thread type. The only persistable shape is `UIMessage[]`/`ModelMessage[]`, which the host owns. No interface, no fields, no metadata in the SDK.

Three first-party `session.Service` impls: `InMemoryService`, `database.NewSessionService` (Postgres/SQLite/MySQL/Spanner via GORM), and `vertexai.NewSessionService`. No JSONL/Redis/S3 first-party adapters but the GORM path covers most production needs.

Adapters under `libs/agno/agno/db/`: Postgres (sync+async), MySQL, SQLite (sync+async), Redis, Mongo, DynamoDB, Firestore, Singlestore, SurrealDB, GCS JSON, JSON file, in-memory. Tables auto-provisioned with `agno_sessions`, `agno_memories`, etc. Widest coverage in the benchmark.
No JSONL, no SQLite, no Postgres, no Redis, no S3. The `MemoryProvider` trait has hooks (`preload`, `export`) but you BYO every backend.

Default is local-disk JSONL written by the CLI at `~/.claude/projects/<cwd>/<session>.jsonl`. `InMemorySessionStore` shipped for tests. Postgres/Redis/S3 reference adapters under `examples/session_stores/` but not in the wheel — copy-in.

Same as Python SDK: local JSONL default, `InMemorySessionStore` for tests. Postgres/Redis/S3 reference adapters in `examples/session-stores/` are conformance-tested but vendored as copy-in. Local-disk is the source of truth, external store is mirror.

Two checkpoint providers ship: `JsonProvider` (one JSON file per checkpoint) and `SqliteProvider` (single DB with WAL). `SQLiteFlowPersistence` for flows. Memory layer ships LanceDB and Qdrant edge. No Postgres/Redis/S3 checkpoint backends in-tree.
`CheckPointStore` interface only — `Get([]byte)`/`Set([]byte)`. eino-ext ships zero implementations (only the framework-internal `bridgeStore` for agent-tool boundaries). Every backend is BYO.
Only `InMemoryStore[S]` (experimental, process-local) and `FirestoreSessionStore[S]` (production-ready). No Postgres, no SQLite, no JSONL, no Redis, no S3 first-party.

Four shipped savers: `InMemorySaver`, `PostgresSaver`/`AsyncPostgresSaver`, `SqliteSaver`/`AsyncSqliteSaver`. Postgres saver also implements `BaseStore` for namespaced KV with vector search. No Redis/S3/Mongo first-party but coverage of the production sweet spot is strong.

`SQLAlchemyChatStore` works against any SQLAlchemy DB (SQLite default, Postgres, MySQL). Additional community chat stores under `core/storage/chat_store/` (Postgres, Redis). Context serialization is BYO storage.

Adapters under `stores/`: libsql, pg, mysql, mssql, dsql, cloudflare/d1, dynamodb, mongodb, opensearch, couchbase plus vector stores (pinecone, qdrant, chroma, astra, lance, elasticsearch). Multiple storage domains (agents, memory, workflows, observability, scores, etc.) per adapter.

Python: `InMemoryHistoryProvider`, experimental `FileHistoryProvider`, Redis package, Cosmos NoSql (`CosmosChatHistoryProvider`+`CosmosCheckpointStorage`), Foundry server-side. .NET: in-memory, Cosmos NoSql, Foundry persistent. Strong cloud coverage; no first-party Postgres.

SQLiteSession (default with WAL+file-lock), OpenAIConversationsSession, OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession, AdvancedSQLiteSession, AsyncSQLiteSession, SQLAlchemySession (Postgres/MySQL), RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, plus EncryptedSession wrapper with Fernet/HKDF per-session keys and TTL. Most of any framework in the comparison.

Only `MemorySession`, `OpenAIConversationsSession`, and `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` ship. No SQLite, no Postgres, no Redis, no S3. Example custom adapters (file, Prisma) demonstrate the BYO pattern.
No session store ships in core. Durable execution layers (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate) provide their own state stores under the agent loop — the closest first-party persistence story.

Only `InMemoryConversationMemory` ships in core (an `Arc<Mutex<HashMap>>`). The `rig-memory` companion crate ships history-shaping policies, not new backends. `rig-postgres`/`rig-sqlite`/`rig-mongodb` are vector-store crates, not memory stores.
Ships `FileSessionManager` (JSON files on local disk) and `S3SessionManager` (same hierarchy on S3). Postgres/Redis/Mongo are BYO via `SessionRepository` abstract base. No native SQL store.
Two implementations of `SnapshotStorage`: `FileStorage` (filesystem tree) and `S3Storage` (same layout as S3 keys). Postgres/Redis/DynamoDB are BYO.
No JSONL, no SQLite, no Postgres, no Redis, no Blob. The SDK has zero opinion on storage — host owns everything via `onStepFinish`/`onFinish` callbacks.
`session.Service` is a 5-method interface (`Create/Get/List/Delete/AppendEvent`) returning a `Session` interface so concrete struct is caller-controlled. Trivial to BYO a Redis/S3/Cassandra adapter.

`BaseDb` and `AsyncBaseDb` are the abstract bases; about 50 abstract methods per adapter spanning sessions, memories, evals, traces, knowledge, components, schedules, approvals. Well-typed but a heavy contract to implement from scratch.

`MemoryProvider` async trait with `remember/recall/clear/clone_box/preload/export` plus optional `id`/`needs_summary`/`replace_with_summary`. Async-friendly, serializable messages — clean BYO contract, but you're implementing memory only since there's no session abstraction.

`SessionStore` Protocol with 2 required methods (`append`, `load`) and 4 optional. Crucially ships a 13-contract conformance harness `run_session_store_conformance` that third-party adapter authors can run — uniquely strong validation story in the benchmark.

`SessionStore` interface (alpha) with 2 required + 4 optional methods. Conformance suite at `examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts` (13 tests) vendored into the example adapters. Same dual-write mirror model as Python.

Three distinct pluggable interfaces: `BaseProvider` ABC for checkpoints (discriminated union on `CheckpointConfig.provider`), `StorageBackend` Protocol for memory storage, and `FlowPersistence` ABC for flow `@persist` decorator. Each has its own contract.

`CheckPointStore` is just `Get(id) -> ([]byte, bool, error)` and `Set(id, []byte)`. Trivial to implement against any backend. Trade-off: framework hands you raw gob-encoded bytes so you don't get typed access to the state.
`Store[S any]` is `Get(ctx, id) -> *Data[S]` and `Save(ctx, id, *Data[S])`. Generic over user state type. Firestore impl is the canonical reference. Very low friction to BYO.

`BaseCheckpointSaver` ABC with `get_tuple/list/put/put_writes` plus async siblings. Conformance harness lives in `libs/checkpoint-conformance/`. The interface plus the per-task `put_writes` semantics make this the gold-standard pluggable checkpointer.

`BaseMemory` is the high-level memory interface; `BaseChatStore` is the persistence interface used by `SQLAlchemyChatStore`. Community impls include `RedisChatStore`, `PostgresChatStore`, `AzureChatStore`.

`MastraStorage` is the umbrella interface, with sub-interfaces for each storage domain (memory, workflows, observability, scores, etc.). Adding a custom adapter means implementing the domain interfaces and passing the instance to `new Mastra({ storage })`.

Python: `HistoryProvider` ABC (`get_messages/save_messages`) extending `ContextProvider`. .NET: `AgentSessionStore` abstract (`SaveSessionAsync/GetSessionAsync`) plus a separate `ChatHistoryProvider`. Dual stack means two implementations to keep in sync.

`Session` Protocol with just 4 methods (`get_items/add_items/pop_item/clear_session`) plus parallel `SessionABC` for type-checker friendliness. The minimal surface area is uniquely easy to BYO — Datadog/BigQuery/custom Postgres adapters are tiny.

`Session` interface with 7 methods plus optional extension interfaces (`SessionHistoryRewriteAwareSession`, `OpenAIResponsesCompactionAwareSession`). Reference impl in `examples/memory/sessions/file.ts` is ~119 lines.
No `SessionStore` / `BaseCheckpointer` abstraction. UI adapters demonstrate the pattern only conceptually — caller persists `message_history` keyed by session id and passes it back to `run()`.

Three-method trait `ConversationMemory` (`load/append/clear`) keyed by `conversation_id`. Sits behind `Arc<dyn ConversationMemory>` on `Agent::memory`. Easy BYO contract; lacks list/delete/cross-session ops.

`SessionRepository` ABC defines CRUD over `session/agent/message` plus `list_messages(limit, offset)` and optional multi-agent methods. `RepositorySessionManager` ties any repository into the standard hook-based persistence flow.
`SnapshotStorage` interface with 6 methods (save/load snapshot, list ids, delete session, load/save manifest). File and S3 impls are the reference. Cleanly typed but BYO Postgres/Redis.
No `SessionStore` / `Checkpointer` abstraction at all. Persistence is whatever the host does inside `onStepFinish` / `onFinish` callbacks.

Every non-partial event is persisted inside a sync DB transaction (refetch, stale-check, merge state, insert event). Crash mid-tool-call loses the in-flight tool but previous events are durable. Coarser than LangGraph's per-task `put_writes` — tool-response is one merged event after all parallel tools finish.

No per-tool checkpointing during a normal run. Only durable interrupt point is `RunStatus.paused` for HITL approvals — `handle_agent_run_paused` writes the paused state via `cleanup_and_store`. Non-paused crashes lose the in-flight run.
No checkpointer, no durability. A crash mid-tool-call loses all in-memory state since `SlidingWindowMemory` is in-process only.

Local JSONL is updated by the CLI on every entry so transcript-up-to-now is durable. External store mirror is batched (~100 ms) — `session_store_flush="eager"` for near-real-time. No transactional per-tool commit; in-flight LLM call can be lost. Recovery via `--resume <id>`.

Same model as Python SDK: subprocess writes JSONL line-by-line, external store is post-local batched mirror with 3-retry backoff. Mid-tool-call crash resumes from last flushed line but loses the partial tool call. Not a true durable checkpoint primitive.

With `on_events=["*"]` or tool-usage events, a checkpoint fires per tool call. `Crew.from_checkpoint` plus `_restore_runtime` walks the event record, finds tasks that started but did not complete, sets `_resuming=True`, and continues from where it left off. Comparable to LangGraph for mid-tool-call resume but default is per-task only.

Persistence fires only when `Interrupt()`/`StatefulInterrupt()` is called explicitly. `saveCheckPoint` is synchronous before the interrupt event is forwarded. A crash without a deliberate interrupt loses everything since the last interrupt. LangGraph-style per-task durability is not provided.

No checkpointer that snapshots mid-tool-call. Closest is `StreamManager` which persists output chunks for disconnect/replay — not server-crash recovery. True mid-run resumption requires custom `WrapTool` middleware plus resume code.

Gold standard. Per-task `_runner.commit()` calls `put_writes` BEFORE super-step reduction; if 4 parallel tool calls are running and the process crashes after 3 finish, on resume the 3 completed results are in `checkpoint_pending_writes` and will NOT re-execute. `durability="sync"|"async"|"exit"` knob. Only mid-tool-call HTTP failure isn't covered.

Not automatic. Workflow can be paused at `ctx.wait_for_event(...)` for HITL, after which `ctx.to_dict(...)` can be persisted and resumed. Crash mid-tool-call loses in-flight tool result — weaker than LangGraph's per-task commit.

HITL tool suspension serializes `__streamState` via `flushMessagesBeforeSuspension()` and resumes via `agent.approveToolCall`. Survives process restarts if storage is durable. Per-tool crash recovery (non-HITL) is not first-class — debounced save means the last ~100 ms can be lost.

`PerServiceCallChatHistoryPersistingChatClient` persists chat history between every LLM round-trip in a function-invocation loop (opt-in via `RequirePerServiceCallChatHistoryPersistence`). Workflow `CheckpointStorage` with `CosmosCheckpointStorage` production impl. .NET `DurableAIAgent` makes every step a durable orchestration step, replayable from any failure.

`RunState.to_json()` is the durable checkpoint primitive (3,305-line file with `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION`) capturing original input, current agent/turn/step, generated items, session items, model responses, guardrail results, interrupt state, sandbox resume state. Automatic checkpoint is per-turn; per-tool-call requires manual `result.to_state().to_json()` in your HITL endpoint.

No automatic mid-tool-call durability. Closest is HITL: when a tool needs approval the run halts and `RunResult.state` can be serialized via `state.toString()` and resumed with `run(agent, state)`. Process crash during `tool.execute` cannot resume.

`Agent` itself has no checkpointer. Mid-run durability is only available through durable-execution integrations (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate). Inside Temporal the agent loop is a workflow and tool calls are activities — workflow replays up to the last committed activity.

`ConversationMemory.append` is called only at end-of-turn after a successful response (both streaming and non-streaming). If the loop errors mid-tool-call, `append` is not called (`memory_unchanged_on_provider_error` test verifies this). Partial trajectory is lost on crash.

`experimental/checkpoint/checkpoint.py` ships an experimental checkpoint with `position ∈ {after_model, after_tools}`; stop via `stop_reason="checkpoint"`, resume via `checkpointResume` content block. Per-tool granularity within a cycle requires a custom ToolExecutor (e.g. TemporalToolExecutor) — not first-party.

Snapshot persistence fires on `AfterInvocationEvent`/`MessageAddedEvent`/`AfterModelCallEvent`. No per-task commit inside `executeTool`. HITL interrupts persist `pendingToolExecution` and resume works after restart, but a crashed run mid-tool-call cannot resume.

SDK does not resume from a checkpoint after mid-tool-call crash. Closest is the resumable-stream recipe (Redis-backed UIMessage stream chunks) but it's resumable stream, not durable runtime — crashed tool dies and the next request starts fresh.

The `Branch` field on events is NOT a fork — it's a dotted-path label (`agent_1.agent_2.agent_3`) used by parallel sub-agents to scope which conversation history they see. Horizontal slice filter, not vertical fork. No first-class branching primitive.
No first-class branching. You read a session, copy the `runs` you want, and write under a new `session_id`. No helper API, no parent_session_id tracking.
No session, no branching. The closest workaround is `clone_box()` the memory provider and start a fresh agent.

`fork_session=True` combined with `resume=<id>` creates a new session-id branching from a prior session. `fork_session()` helper does this from outside an active client. Forked sessions get a fresh UUID with the prior transcript replayed.

`forkSession(sessionId, { upToMessageId?, title?, sessionStore? })` branches at a specific message UUID with full UUID remapping and `parentUuid` chain preservation. New sessionId minted on fork. Forked sessions start without file-checkpoint history.

`Crew.fork(config, branch=)` restores from a checkpoint then forks the `RuntimeState` to a new branch label. Same exists for `Flow.fork` and `Agent.fork`. Conceptually similar to LangGraph forks though less granular than per-step state history.
Linear thread of execution per `Runner.Run`. Only parallel sub-agents inside one run get lanes. A new `checkPointID` is a new session, but there is no session fork primitive.
No native fork/branch. You encode it in your state struct (e.g. `parent_session_id` field) and persist accordingly. No helper, no parent-child relationship tracking.

Gold standard. `graph.get_state_history(config)` returns every step; `graph.update_state(config_at_step_N, values)` creates a new branch from step N. Multiple branches per thread are first-class via the Pregel checkpointer. `CheckpointMetadata.source` literally includes `"fork"`.
No fork/branch primitive in the OSS framework. Workflow `Context` resume after pause is the closest mechanic but it is single-thread resume, not branch.
`cloneThread` exists (`packages/memory/src/clone-thread-om.test.ts`) but fork/branch is not first-class. Branching is treated as "copy thread to new id" rather than a parent-child relationship.

No fork on `AgentSession` itself. Workflow-layer `CheckpointStorage` (`_workflows/_checkpoint.py`) supports resuming from any checkpoint, which can serve as a branch point. DurableTask provides replay-from-checkpoint.

No native fork or `fork()` semantics. If you need parallel branches you create separate `session_id`s and copy the prefix items yourself. `RunState` supports interruption-resume but that is not a fork.
No fork or branch model. No `parent_session_id`. If you need branching you implement a graph layer on top.
Caller-driven: pass an explicit `conversation_id='new'` to fork while reusing the prior `message_history`. No checkpoint tree, no parent_session_id, no helper API.
No fork or branch model. Linear conversation per `conversation_id` only.
Single linear conversation per `(session_id, agent_id)` pair. No branching/forking helper. Multi-agent sessions are supported but each agent has its own message log.
Forking is "take a snapshot, hand it to another Agent instance, load it" — `Snapshot` is a JSON blob that can be branched by copying. No first-class fork API, no parent chain.
No checkpoint graph, no branch model. If you want branching you implement N sessions in your DB yourself.

Internal `replayplugin` (`internal/configurable/conformance/replayplugin/`) intercepts BeforeRun/BeforeModel/BeforeTool to return recorded responses from `generated-recordings.yaml`. Powerful but internal package — must fork/copy. Export is straightforward via `session.Service.Get` and the REST API.

`AgentSession.to_dict()` + `db.get_session(session_id)` returns a fully-serializable dict. Replay is not a first-party concept — you read `runs` and walk it manually. No `replay_session(...)` helper, no deterministic record/replay against frozen LLM responses.
`MemoryProvider::export()` returns `Vec<ChatMessage>` and `preload()` rehydrates. Replay (deterministic re-execution of past events) is not provided — events are emitted but not stored.

`list_sessions`, `get_session_messages`, `list_subagents`, `get_subagent_messages` plus `_from_store` variants. The on-disk JSONL is transparent append-only and replayable via `resume=<id>`. `import_session_to_store` migrates a local JSONL into any adapter.

`getSessionMessages`, `getSessionInfo`, `listSessions`, `listSubagents` ship. Deterministic replay via `query({ options: { resume, sessionStore } })` plus `resumeSessionAt: messageUuid` to replay up to a specific point. `importSessionToStore` for migrations.

`crewai replay -t <task_id>` CLI lets you re-run from a saved task output. `RuntimeState.event_record` is fully serializable JSON capturing emission sequence, restored on `from_checkpoint`. `crewai_event_bus._replaying` contextvar signals listeners to suppress side effects. Deterministic enough to reconstruct UI state.

note: export via Get, resume via Resume
details: Export is `r.store.Get(ctx, checkPointID)` returning the gob blob. Replay is `Runner.Resume(ctx, checkPointID)` re-entering from the saved point. No first-party deterministic replay-from-start with frozen LLM responses; you'd build that yourself by mocking the chat model.

No first-party export/replay tooling for sessions. Generation events emit OTel spans you can export. The Dev UI replays individual actions but not full session sequences. Replay is reconstruct-messages-from-DB-and-call-Generate-again.

Export: `graph.get_state(config)` returns the current `StateSnapshot`; `graph.get_state_history(config)` returns every step. Replay: pass `config["configurable"]["checkpoint_id"]` to `graph.stream(None, config)` and the loop replays from that point. `is_replaying = True` is observable on the loop.

Canonical export/import pattern: `Context.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer())` and `Context.from_dict(workflow, ctx_dict, serializer=...)`. Deterministic replay against recorded LLM responses is not built-in — you re-feed `chat_history` to a new run with mocked LLMs.
Export via `storage.getMessages({ threadId })` and resumable-stream/observe-stream endpoints. `packages/_llm-recorder` is used for test fixture replay. No first-party replay-from-event-stream engine.

`AgentSession.to_dict()` returns a typed envelope (`{"type": "session", ...}`). Workflow `CheckpointStorage` exports checkpoints. .NET `DurableAIAgent` provides replay-from-checkpoint with deterministic orchestration semantics. No first-party LLM-response replay.

`RunResult.to_input_list(mode="preserve_all"|"normalized")` exports the run for replay-as-input. `RunState.to_json()`/`from_json()` enables full state replay across processes with explicit `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` compatibility contract. `raw_responses` is the unmodified per-call log. No first-party replay viewer.

`RunResult.history` and `RunResult.state` are JSON-serializable; `RunState.fromString(agent, json)` rebuilds for replay. Hosted Traces dashboard at platform.openai.com/traces provides replay viewer. No deterministic re-execution against recorded provider responses.

`AgentRunResult.all_messages_json()` exports the full conversation as JSON bytes. Replay is constructing a new `Agent.run(..., message_history=...)`. No record/replay harness, no deterministic LLM stub built-in.

`PromptResponse.messages: Option<Vec<Message>>` gives new messages added during the turn. Replay is constructing a `PromptRequest::with_history(...)`. Deterministic replay against recorded provider responses is not built-in; tests use `MockCompletionModel` but no record/replay against real providers.

`Agent.take_snapshot(preset="session", include=[...], exclude=[...], app_data={...})` returns a Snapshot dataclass capturing messages, state, conversation_manager_state, interrupt_state, system_prompt. `Agent.load_snapshot(snapshot)` restores. Experimental checkpoint wraps this for durable pause/resume.

`agent.takeSnapshot({ preset: 'session' })` returns a `Snapshot` for JSON.stringify export. `agent.loadSnapshot(snapshot)` restores. Replay-from-event-stream is not first-class — you can re-issue `agent.invoke(initialPrompt)` against a restored snapshot but no deterministic event-by-event engine.

You already have the messages so exporting is `JSON.stringify(messages)`. Replay is passing the same messages and pinning model + seed. Determinism is not a first-party feature; no record/replay harness in the SDK.

ChatModelAgent ships the ReAct loop as the default via llminternal.Flow (preprocess → LLM call → postprocess → tool dispatch → repeat-until-final). Loop is fully owned by the framework — consumer only configures agents and tools. Termination via IsFinalResponse() and per-event session persistence.

Tool-calling loop is encapsulated inside each Model adapter's response() method rather than at the harness level, so the harness sees a single "turn" per _run invocation. ReAct mode is opt-in via reasoning=True for explicit thought-action-observation. Fully framework-owned, but the loop boundary is deeper than peers.

ReActAgent<T> is a built-in executor (max_turns default 10) driven by TurnEngine::run_turn. Also ships BasicAgent and CodeActAgent variants. Custom executors are supported via the AgentExecutor trait.

ReAct loop runs entirely inside the Claude Code CLI subprocess; the Python SDK only iterates resulting wire frames. You cannot intercept tool_call→tool_result transitions in Python — only observe. First-class for the use case but opaque to host modification.

CLI runs the ReAct loop end-to-end including PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks, tool dispatch (built-in/MCP/SDK-MCP), and result folding. TS SDK consumes the AsyncGenerator. You hook the loop, you do not own it.

Default AgentExecutor is a Flow[AgentExecutorState] with generate_plan → execute_todo_sequential/parallel → execute_tool_action. Built-in but opinionated: only the first tool call per turn is executed even if the LLM emits parallel tool_calls. Legacy ReAct text-parser still in-tree for non-function-calling LLMs.

Default loop compiled as a compose.Graph[*reactInput, Message] with Init → ChatModel → ToolNode → repeat, bounded by MaxIterations (default 20). Legacy flow/agent/react also exists. Custom loops by implementing the Agent interface or hand-building compose.Graph.

Tool-calling loop in ai.GenerateWithRequest auto-runs until LLM stops calling tools (MaxTurns default 5). No explicit Reason/Act/Observe scaffold — relies on the model's native tool-calling. No string-parsed ReAct prompt, but loop is first-class.

create_react_agent ships a prebuilt ReAct (agent node + tools node) but is @deprecated in favor of langchain.agents.create_agent. You can roll your own ReAct as a plain StateGraph — there is no special-casing. Loop discipline emerges from Pregel super-steps.

AgentWorkflow ships built-in via @step methods (init_run → setup_agent → run_agent_step → parse_agent_output → call_tool × N → aggregate_tool_results), max_iterations default 20. ReActAgent overrides take_step for Thought/Action/Observation parsing; FunctionAgent uses native function-calling.

Built-in ReAct-style 6-step workflow (llmExecutionStep → map tool-calls → foreach toolCallStep → llmMappingStep → backgroundTaskCheckStep → signalDrainStep → isTaskCompleteStep). Supervisor early-stop via completion scorers (isTaskComplete) is bolted in. Fully framework-owned.

Function-invocation loop is automatic when tools are present — no explicit ReAct wiring. Python delegates to BaseChatClient.get_response with _try_execute_function_calls; .NET delegates to FunctionInvokingChatClient from Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Both rely on the model's native tool-calling.

Runner.run drives the canonical ReAct loop (invoke → final-output? → handoff? → tool calls → re-loop), max_turns default 10. Agent.tool_use_behavior tunes termination ("run_llm_again", "stop_on_first_tool", StopAtTools, ToolsToFinalOutputFunction). Handoffs are first-class.

Built-in ReAct via run() with prepareTurn → model call → processModelResponseAsync → resolveTurnAfterModelResponse, nextStep in {final_output, handoff, interruption, run_again}. maxTurns default 10, nullable since 0.10.0.

Built-in graph-based ReAct: UserPromptNode → ModelRequestNode → CallToolsNode → loop, terminated by end_strategy (early/graceful/exhaustive) and UsageLimits. The graph is first-class and node-by-node observable via Agent.iter().

PromptRequest builder + .send() runs a multi-turn loop (max_turns configurable, tools dispatched via buffer_unordered concurrency). Effectively ReAct via LLM-driven tool calls. Ships a ThinkTool for explicit reasoning recording but no dedicated thought channel.

event_loop_cycle in event_loop.py is the canonical ReAct loop; tool execution recurses via recurse_event_loop. Model-driven approach handles tools, agent-as-tool sub-agents, and conversation-manager compaction in one loop.

_stream() contains the canonical ReAct while(true). Deferred message-append guarantees no dangling toolUse without matching toolResult on interrupt. Configured via tools, hooks, conversationManager, and toolExecutor: 'concurrent' | 'sequential'.

The do { … } while(…) in generateText/streamText is the canonical ReAct loop. Stop discipline via stopWhen (isStepCount, hasToolCall, custom StopCondition). ToolLoopAgent class is a thin OO wrapper. Default stopWhen=isStepCount(20) for the agent, 1 for raw generateText.

Flow.handleFunctionCalls spawns one goroutine per FunctionCall via sync.WaitGroup; results are merged into a single *session.Event with multiple Part.FunctionResponse entries, linked by FunctionCall.ID. BeforeToolCallback → tool.Run → AfterToolCallback / OnToolErrorCallback chain. Long-running tools and HITL gating are first-class.

Tool dispatch via FunctionCall.execute() inside the model adapter; entrypoint receives injected agent/team/run_context/fc/media plus tool_hooks chain. Result becomes a ToolExecution record. Lives inside the model adapter rather than the harness, but is robust.

ToolProcessor::process_single_tool_call_with_hooks runs on_tool_call → on_tool_start → tool.execute → on_tool_result / on_tool_error and emits Event::ToolCallRequested then ToolCallCompleted / ToolCallFailed. Tools matched by name from a Vec<Box<dyn ToolT>> (linear scan). Sequential per call inside one turn.

Inside the CLI: built-in tools execute in subprocess, external MCP via stdio/SSE/HTTP, in-process SDK MCP via control_request: mcp_message round-trips. Results matched by tool_use_id as ToolResultBlock. Dispatch is opaque to host Python; can_use_tool and PreToolUse hooks gate execution.

Three dispatch paths inside CLI (built-in, MCP-process, SDK-MCP via createSdkMcpServer). PreToolUse fires per tool, PostToolUse per tool, PostToolBatch once per batch. canUseTool callback round-trips can mutate inputs or deny. Results folded as tool_result on a synthetic user turn.

note: first tool call only per turn
details: Both legacy and new executors execute only the first tool call per turn even when the LLM emits multiple parallel tool_calls. before_tool_call → tool.run → after_tool_call hook chain via execute_tool_and_check_finality. Parallelism only exists between independent plan todos, not within a turn — a hard opinionation gap.

ToolsNode runs tool calls in parallel by default (ExecuteSequentially: false), spawning a goroutine per call; results matched by ToolCallID = ToolCall.ID, returned as []*schema.Message in input order. Rich middleware stack (InvokableToolMiddleware, StreamableToolMiddleware, EnhancedInvokableToolMiddleware, EnhancedStreamableToolMiddleware). UnknownToolsHandler covers hallucinated names.

handleToolRequests fans out one goroutine per tool call, folds results into a single tool-role message appended to the prompt. WrapTool middleware can wrap each call. Concurrency safety is explicitly documented. Tool interrupts surface as toolInterruptError with FinishReason=interrupted.

ToolNode.invoke takes the last AIMessage, splits tool_calls into separate executions (parallel via Send in create_react_agent v2), and appends one ToolMessage(tool_call_id=...) per call. Linkage is always explicit via tool_call_id. Custom routing requires user code.

parse_agent_output emits one ToolCall event per tool call; the workflow runtime fans these out to parallel call_tool invocations. aggregate_tool_results fans in via ctx.collect_events. FunctionTool gets the workflow Context injected when declared. Clean separation of dispatch and aggregation.

toolCallStep validates tool existence, runs tool.execute(input, ctx) with full ToolExecutionContext, gates via requireApproval/needsApprovalFn (emits tool-call-approval chunk and calls suspend). Results pass through llmMappingStep into the next prompt. Foreach over toolCalls inside the agentic-execution workflow.

Python _try_execute_function_calls iterates FunctionCallContent items, resolves from tool_map, invokes with FunctionInvocationContext (function, arguments, session, metadata, kwargs). approval_mode=always_require emits function_approval_request and pauses via UserInputRequiredException. .NET uses FunctionInvokingChatClient from Microsoft.Extensions.AI plus ToolApprovalAgent.

Tool calls routed through five execution paths (execute_function_tool_calls, execute_computer_actions, execute_shell_calls/local, execute_apply_patch_calls, execute_mcp_approval_requests). Each invocation receives a ToolContext (tool_name, tool_call_id, tool_arguments, parent RunContextWrapper). Results threaded back as FunctionToolResult via run_items_to_input_items.

Tool calls dispatched concurrently up to toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency. Per-tool input/output guardrails wrap tool.invoke(). Path: model → FunctionCallItem → FunctionTool.invoke(runContext, input, details) → parser → options.execute → RunToolCallOutputItem.

ToolManager.handle_call resolves the tool, validates JSON args via args_validator (SchemaValidator), fires before_tool_validate → wrap_tool_validate → before_tool_execute → wrap_tool_execute → after_tool_execute, then wraps the return as ToolReturnPart (or RetryPromptPart on ModelRetry). Robust validation-retry loop is first-class.

Tools dispatched concurrently via futures::stream::iter(...).buffer_unordered(self.concurrency). on_tool_call hook can Skip or Terminate; on_tool_result can Terminate. Tool lookup brief read-lock on ToolSet; result becomes UserContent::ToolResult linked by call_id.

ToolExecutor._stream looks up in dynamic_tools then registry, fires BeforeToolCallEvent (hook can swap tool, mutate input, cancel), runs selected_tool.stream() yielding intermediate events ending with ToolResultEvent, then AfterToolCallEvent (with retry=True support). Tool results collapsed into a single user-role message.

executeTool runs BeforeToolCallEvent (mutate input/name/toolUseId, swap selectedTool, or cancel) → effectiveTool.stream(toolContext) wrapping ToolStreamEvents → ToolResultBlock → AfterToolCallEvent (with retry support). Concurrent or sequential toolExecutor strategy is configurable.

executeTools runs all approved client tool calls in parallel via Promise.all. onToolExecutionStart → tool.execute(input, options) → onToolExecutionEnd. tool.toModelOutput? hook can reshape raw output. parseToolCall fires experimental_refineToolInput and experimental_repairToolCall for malformed calls. Approval gating (approved/denied/user-approval) is first-class.

Streaming surfaced as Partial bool on LLMResponse — partial events stream tokens but are not persisted, while non-partial events are persisted via sessionService.AppendEvent. Delivered through the same iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error] iterator. SSE wire format adds partial:true frames.

Stream mode yields RunOutputEvent dataclasses; per-token deltas surface as RunContent / RunIntermediateContent and reasoning as ReasoningContentDelta. ModelRequestCompleted carries time_to_first_token and token breakdowns. 39 event types via plain Python yield.

StreamChunk enum (Text, ReasoningContent, ToolUseStart, ToolUseInputDelta, ToolUseComplete, Done, Usage) is wrapped inside Event::StreamChunk { sub_id, chunk } and emitted through tokio mpsc. TurnEngine::stream_with_tools accumulates chunks and emits Event::StreamToolCall per complete tool call.

Partial assistant streaming events surface as StreamEvent (type='stream_event') when include_partial_messages=True, carrying the raw Anthropic SSE event. Default iterator only emits full UserMessage/AssistantMessage frames. anyio memory channel with max_buffer_size=100 backpressure.

SDKPartialAssistantMessage (type='stream_event') emits per-API-event stream payload when includePartialMessages: true, carrying raw BetaRawMessageStreamEvent. Plus SDKToolProgressMessage heartbeats for long-running tools tied to tool_use_id. Default iterator emits full messages only.

Crew(stream=True) wires LLMStreamChunkEvent into a queue and yields StreamChunk objects via CrewStreamingOutput. ToolCallChunk arguments stream incrementally. Token streaming is opt-in and only delivered via the bridge — the underlying taxonomy lives on the BaseEvent bus.

Streaming via *schema.StreamReader[*schema.Message] chunks accumulated via reducer concatenation. Each AgentEvent carries a MessageVariant with IsStreaming=true and a MessageStream you iterate to receive token chunks. One AgentEvent per assistant message; the message body is itself a pull-based stream.

Streaming via ModelStreamCallback (per ModelResponseChunk) or GenerateStream returning iter.Seq2. Chunk.Role and Part type discriminate text-delta vs tool-call (with ToolRequest.Partial=true for partial-args chunks) vs tool-result. No async EventEmitter; either callback or iterator.

stream_mode='messages' yields (AIMessageChunk, metadata) per token via StreamMessagesHandler.on_llm_new_token (LangChain callback). Plus values/updates/custom/checkpoints/tasks/debug modes for richer streaming. stream_mode list returns mode-tagged tuples and subgraphs propagation.

_get_llm_response writes AgentStream events as tokens arrive (event.delta). Consumer iterates handler.stream_events() and filters AgentStream instances. ctx.write_event_to_stream is the general primitive. AgentStreamStructuredOutput for streaming structured output.

ReadableStream<ChunkType> exposes text-start / text-delta / text-end, reasoning-start/-delta/-end, tool-call-input-streaming-start/-delta/-end, etc. (~40 variants). MastraModelOutput wraps it and exposes fullStream + per-property promises (text, usage, toolCalls, toolResults). transient:true data-* chunks supported.

RunStreaming returns AsyncIterable[AgentResponseUpdate] in Python and IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate> in .NET. Each update is a partial Message. ResponseStream.get_final_response() aggregates updates into a complete response. DevUI mapper splits these into OpenAI Responses-shaped wire frames.

run_streamed returns RunResultStreaming.stream_events() iterating RawResponsesStreamEvent (raw OpenAI Responses API events: text-delta, function-call-arg-delta, refusal-delta, reasoning-delta, response.created/completed) plus RunItemStreamEvent and AgentUpdatedStreamEvent. asyncio.Queue with sequence numbers.

StreamedRunResult exposes async-iterable RunStreamEvent with RunRawModelStreamEvent (output_text_delta and other raw chunks) plus RunItemStreamEvent and RunAgentUpdatedStreamEvent. Sub-agent stream events can be forwarded via Agent.asTool({ onStream }).

run_stream_events yields AgentStreamEvent with PartStartEvent/PartDeltaEvent/PartEndEvent (per text/thinking/tool-call), plus FinalResultEvent and AgentRunResultEvent. Distinct deltas per part with index, content_delta, and previous_part_kind for resumption-friendly streaming. Tool-call args can stream too.

Streaming Stream<MultiTurnStreamItem<R>> yields StreamedAssistantContent::{Text, ToolCall, ToolCallDelta, Reasoning, ReasoningDelta, Final} and StreamedUserContent::ToolResult. Non-streaming path returns no events. RawStreamingToolCall accumulator handles streamed tool-arg JSON.

Streaming via dict-payload async iterator. ModelStreamChunkEvent for raw provider chunks; TextStreamEvent per text delta; ToolUseStreamEvent streams partial tool-arg JSON; ReasoningTextStreamEvent / CitationStreamEvent / ReasoningRedactedContentStreamEvent for the long tail. ModelStopReason marks model-call end.

Native AsyncGenerator<AgentStreamEvent> yields ModelStreamUpdateEvent wrapping ModelStreamEvent (textDelta, toolInputDelta, citations) plus ContentBlockEvent for assembled blocks. ToolStreamUpdateEvent surfaces tool intermediate progress. ContentBlockEvent assembles toolUseBlocks with streamed input.

streamText().fullStream is an AsyncIterableStream<TextStreamPart<TOOLS>> with text-start/-delta/-end, reasoning-start/-delta/-end, tool-input-start/-delta/-end, etc. (~24 variants). UIMessageChunk wire format (~28 variants) for SSE. .textStream for text-only stream. Best-in-class stream taxonomy and conversion.

No Turn type, but the loop owns explicit "invocation" and "step" notions via invocationID and event.IsFinalResponse(). Flow.Run loops until the last event from runOneStep is final; agent/context.go documents the invocation → llm_agent_call → step hierarchy. Observable through per-event session persistence.

Uses "run" rather than "turn". One run() call = one turn = one LLM invocation cycle that may include N tool calls. RunOutput.run_id (UUID) is the turn-level identifier; AgentSession.runs is a list of RunOutputs. RunStarted/RunCompleted events demarcate boundaries.

First-class Turn concept: TurnEngine::run_turn yields Event::TurnStarted{turn_number, max_turns} and Event::TurnCompleted{turn_number, final_turn}. TurnResult enum (Continue/Complete) is the executor-level termination signal. Explicit and observable boundaries.

A turn is defined by ResultMessage emitted exactly once per user prompt; ResultMessage.num_turns reports the CLI's internal assistant↔tool exchange count. max_turns caps and triggers error_max_turns. ResultMessage.stop_reason (0.1.46+) clarifies termination.

A turn = one assistant message + synthetic user message with matching tool_result blocks. SDKResultMessage emitted once per request loop terminator (no more tool_use, or maxTurns/maxBudgetUsd/hook-stop). num_turns counts model API round-trips for this query().

A "turn" is one LLM call + one tool execution + appended tool result; self.iterations increments per LLM call. No max_turns exposed separately — only max_iter (default 25). New AgentExecutor enforces turn budget per-todo via _get_max_step_iterations. Not surfaced as an explicit event class.

No first-class Turn type. A turn boundary is implicit — defined by the loop branch from ChatModel to either ToolNode or END. AgentEvent is the smallest emitted unit; turn discipline emerges from MaxIterations (default 20) and the graph topology.

A turn is one trip through runGenerate (one model.Generate call + optional tool dispatch). MaxTurns counts these but there is no Turn type — the count is just an int carried through the recursion. Lifecycle observable only via tracing spans, not stream events.

No explicit "turn" object. Closest first-class boundary is the super-step (one Pregel tick). A ReAct "turn" is super-step agent (one LLM call → one AIMessage) → super-step tools (ToolMessage results) → repeat. stream_mode='tasks' surfaces per-node start/finish lifecycle.

A turn is one LLM call → N parallel tool calls → fan-in → next LLM call. max_iterations defaults 20 with early_stopping_method choice of force/generate (final LLM call with stopping prompt). AgentInput / AgentSetup / AgentOutput events demarcate per-step boundaries on the stream.

A turn is one full pass through the 6-step workflow chain (LLM call + tool dispatches + completion check). step-start / step-finish stream chunks demarcate boundaries; finish marks loop termination. Background-task lifecycle adds extra observable boundaries.

Implicit: a turn ends when the LLM returns a non-tool-call response (finish_reason in {stop, length, content_filter}) or when MiddlewareTermination is raised. No explicit Turn type; the run accumulates updates until terminal. Not surfaced as a discrete event class.

Documented explicitly: "A turn is defined as one AI invocation (including any tool calls that might occur)." max_turns (default 10, None=unlimited as of 0.16.0). Resumed runs from RunState do not increment the turn counter; only actual model calls advance turns. Per-turn structure is auditable.

A turn is bounded by prepareTurn → model call → resolveTurnAfterModelResponse → applyTurnResult. state._currentTurn increments at the start of each turn. Loop terminates only on next_step_final_output or next_step_interruption. maxTurns default 10, nullable since 0.10.0.

A turn is one trip around the graph until another ModelRequestNode is queued or End fires. RunContext.run_step is incremented per iteration. Node-by-node observability via Agent.iter() returning an AgentRun makes turn boundaries traversable.

A turn = one LLM call + zero-to-many tool dispatches that follow. The loop increments current_max_turns once per iteration. Multi-turn terminates when LLM returns no tool calls or max_turns + 1 is exceeded. No explicit Turn event type.

One event_loop_cycle ≈ one model call + zero-or-more tool calls. Loop continues until stop_reason in {end_turn, max_tokens, cancelled, interrupt, stop_sequence} and no further tool use, then EventLoopStopEvent. Each tool batch recurses into a fresh cycle. Boundaries observable on the event stream.

A cycle is the unit (Meter.startCycle / _meter.endCycle): one model call + tools it triggered. A full invocation may span many cycles. StopReason enum (endTurn, toolUse, maxTokens, stopSequence, guardrailIntervened, cancelled, interrupt) is explicit. ModelMessageEvent carries stopReason.

A step = one LLM call + zero-or-more parallel tool executions. stopWhen defines termination (isStepCount, hasToolCall, custom StopCondition). start-step / finish-step / start / finish chunks in TextStreamPart demarcate boundaries. StepResult exposed as steps[] on the final result. Best-in-class observability.

Go 1.23 iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error] everywhere — no EventEmitter, no channel, no callback hell. Every layer (agent, runner, flow, sub-agents) returns the same type, composable via for ev, err := range agent.Run(ctx). RunLive uses channels wrapped back into iter.Seq2.

Plain Python yield for sync stream and AsyncIterator for arun_stream. 39 distinct RunEvent enum members produced via helpers in agno.utils.events and routed through handle_event which honors agent.events_to_skip / store_events. TeamRunEvent mirrors for Team. Rich and easy to consume.

Events emitted via tokio mpsc::Sender<Event> on Context.tx; EventHelper wraps Sender::send. Two consumption modes: DirectAgent fans out via EventFanout, ActorAgent flows through runtime with Environment::take_event_receiver or subscribe_events broadcast. 17 protocol Event variants.

anyio memory-object stream with max_buffer_size=100 (asyncio.Queue equivalent). Transport read loop pushes; receive_messages() pops. Single async generator iteration is the public API; opt-in include_hook_events / include_partial_messages add hook and stream-event frames. No multi-mode streams.

Query extends AsyncGenerator<SDKMessage, void>. Same iterator everywhere — no parallel event-emitter, no on('toolStart') listener, no event bus. ~30 variants of SDKMessage discriminated by type/subtype. Control frames are peeled off internally.

Singleton CrewAIEventsBus with sync ThreadPoolExecutor + async daemon loop. 151 BaseEvent subclasses across 19 event-type files; @on decorator + BaseEventListener subclass for typed listeners. Crew(stream=True) wires bus into a queue and yields StreamChunk. Rich taxonomy and parallel dispatch.

*AsyncIterator[*AgentEvent] backed by an unbounded Go channel. AsyncGenerator.Send(v) / Close(). Consumer side uses Next() in a for loop. Hook/callback events flow through a separate callbacks.Handler subsystem (not multiplexed onto the agent stream).

Streaming via ModelStreamCallback (per ModelResponseChunk) or GenerateStream returning iter.Seq2. No async EventEmitter or topic bus. No separate lifecycle event taxonomy (no start/step-start/finish/error events). Tracing spans are the only lifecycle observability.

Per-call SyncQueue / asyncio.Queue. Pregel loop holds StreamProtocol(stream.put, stream_modes). 7 concrete StreamPart TypedDicts (values, updates, messages, custom, checkpoints, tasks, debug). stream_mode can be a list returning mode-tagged tuples. Plus GraphCallbackHandler for lifecycle events. Best-in-class multi-mode streaming.

Two mechanisms: @step return / ctx.send_event for step-routing fan-out, plus ctx.write_event_to_stream + handler.stream_events() for consumer-facing events. ctx.collect_events handles fan-in. Workflow runtime delivers events to whatever step matches type signature.

Loop returns a web-standard ReadableStream<ChunkType>. MastraModelOutput wraps it exposing fullStream + per-property promises. Processors push custom data-* chunks via ProcessorStreamWriter.custom (transient:true skips persistence). ~40 ChunkType variants. Standards-based and rich.

AsyncIterable[AgentResponseUpdate] in Python, IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate> in .NET. Middleware can wrap the stream with with_transform_hook / with_result_hook. No in-process event bus or observer pattern — composition is via middleware and ContextProvider lifecycle hooks.

Internal asyncio.Queue[StreamEvent | QueueCompleteSentinel]. Background run-loop task writes events; RunResultStreaming.stream_events() reads. Separate _input_guardrail_queue for streaming guardrail trips. StreamEvent union: RawResponsesStreamEvent / RunItemStreamEvent / AgentUpdatedStreamEvent. RunHooks + Agent.hooks add separate sync callbacks.

Two mechanisms: RuntimeEventEmitter for lifecycle (agent_start, agent_end, agent_handoff, agent_tool_start, agent_tool_end) via AgentHooks, plus StreamedRunResult exposing async-iterable RunStreamEvent (RunRawModelStreamEvent / RunItemStreamEvent / RunAgentUpdatedStreamEvent). Sub-agents can forward via Agent.asTool({ onStream }).

Agent.run_stream_events() returns an AgentEventStream async context manager yielding AgentStreamEvent | AgentRunResultEvent. Each graph node implements async def stream(ctx) yielding events. event capability hook (hooks.on.event) and run_event_stream (wrap_run_event_stream) intercept the stream. Multi-category taxonomy.

Non-streaming returns PromptResponse only — no event stream. Streaming returns futures::Stream<MultiTurnStreamItem<R>>. PromptHook trait fires at 7 known points (on_completion_call, on_completion_response, on_tool_call, on_tool_result, etc.) regardless of streaming mode. Tracing spans for GenAI semconv. No event bus.

Agent._run_loop yields TypedEvent instances; stream_async routes through event.prepare() + callback_handler. Rich taxonomy across Lifecycle / Model stream / Tool / Structured output / Throttle / Multi-agent / Hook categories. Hook event registry separate from stream allows subscribers.

Native AsyncGenerator<AgentStreamEvent, AgentResult, undefined>. Hooks invoked synchronously in-line via _invokeCallbacks() before each yield, so a hook can mutate the event before it leaves the generator. Lifecycle / Update / Completion / State-change event categories. Rich and ergonomic.

Two parallel mechanisms driven by notify({ event, callbacks }): push callbacks (experimental_onStart, onStepStart, onLanguageModelCallStart/End, onToolExecutionStart/End, onStepFinish, onFinish) plus pull async iterator (streamText().fullStream: AsyncIterableStream<TextStreamPart>). Best-in-class flexibility.

Only Gemini (`model/gemini/gemini.go`) and Apigee Vertex proxy are first-party. No first-party adapters for OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure OpenAI or LiteLLM; community adapters exist but none are vendored. Implementing `model.LLM` is doable but requires marshalling between Gemini's content model and the target API.

Under `libs/agno/agno/models/` Agno ships ~49 native provider adapters: Anthropic, OpenAI (Chat + Responses), Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, Cohere, Mistral, Ollama, Groq, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Cerebras, HuggingFace, LiteLLM, NVIDIA, xAI, OpenRouter, Together, Portkey, IBM, Moonshot, Nebius, vLLM, etc. Among the broadest first-party catalogs in the benchmark.

`crates/autoagents-llm/src/backends/` ships openai, anthropic, azure_openai, openrouter, deepseek, xai, phind, groq, google, minimax, ollama, plus local crates `autoagents-llamacpp`, `autoagents-mistral-rs`, and experimental Burn/Onnx backends. Each implements `LLMProvider`. Strong native coverage; no LiteLLM-style aggregator.
SDK is Anthropic-only (Sonnet/Opus/Haiku). Bedrock and Vertex routing are supported by the underlying CLI but the SDK is opaque to it, so no OpenAI/Gemini/etc. native paths from Python.

`AccountInfo.apiProvider` covers `firstParty | bedrock | vertex | foundry | anthropicAws | mantle | gateway` and selection is via env vars, not a config knob. No native OpenAI/Gemini direct support — those require a LiteLLM-style gateway you operate yourself. One of the largest deltas vs. peers.

`lib/crewai/src/crewai/llms/providers/` ships native SDKs for openai, anthropic, azure, bedrock, gemini, and `openai_compatible` (DeepSeek/OpenRouter/Ollama/vLLM/Cerebras/Dashscope/...). Anything else falls through to LiteLLM (100+ models). Routing logic in `LLM.__new__` (`llm.py:350-443`) handles `provider/model` strings.

`components/model/` in eino-ext provides openai (Azure-compatible), claude, gemini (Vertex + AI Studio), ollama, deepseek, qwen, qianfan, ark, arkbot, openrouter. Any `model.BaseChatModel` plugs in. No LiteLLM-style gateway bundled.

`plugins/googlegenai/` (Gemini, Vertex), `plugins/anthropic/`, `plugins/compat_oai/` (OpenAI/Azure/Anyscale/vLLM), `plugins/ollama/`. Vertex Model Garden via sample, not plugin. No LiteLLM aggregator; each provider gets a dedicated ~500-LOC plugin.

`init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4")` / `openai:...` / `google:...` / `bedrock:...` / Azure / Vertex / LiteLLM-as-OpenAI-proxy. Inherits the full `langchain-*` ecosystem natively, not as third-party glue.

`llama-index-integrations/llms/` ships 104 integration packages — Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock (+ Converse), Vertex, Google GenAI, Cohere, Mistral, Groq, Together, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Cerebras, Databricks, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Heroku, HuggingFace, IBM, Ollama, vLLM, and more. The largest catalog in the benchmark.

Inherits Vercel AI SDK's 40+ providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, Cerebras, Groq, Cohere, Mistral, ...) through one standard interface. Native across the entire AI SDK ecosystem.

Separate packages per provider: OpenAI, Azure Foundry (+ Foundry Local), Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini (alpha), Ollama, Claude (Code-style), GitHub Copilot SDK, Copilot Studio, Hyperlight Wasm sandbox. Broad coverage, parallel .NET packages for most.

`MultiProvider` (`src/agents/models/multi_provider.py:61`) ships native OpenAI plus optional `LitellmProvider` and `AnyLLMProvider` extensions; prefix routing (`litellm/anthropic/claude-...`) dispatches the call. Custom `MultiProviderMap` lets you register any provider you want.

note: OpenAI native + Vercel AI SDK adapter
details: OpenAI is first-party (Responses + Chat Completions). All other providers (Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral, LiteLLM-compatible) come via the `@openai/agents-extensions/ai-sdk` adapter wrapping a Vercel AI SDK `LanguageModelV2`. Strong but indirect for non-OpenAI.

`pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/models/` ships anthropic, bedrock, cerebras, cohere, gemini, google, groq, huggingface, mistral, ollama, openai, openrouter, outlines, xai, plus FallbackModel/InstrumentedModel/wrapper/mcp_sampling helpers. Custom models by subclassing `Model`.

`crates/rig-core/src/providers/` ships anthropic, azure, chatgpt, cohere, copilot, deepseek, galadriel, gemini, groq, huggingface, hyperbolic, llamafile, minimax, mira, mistral, moonshot, ollama, openai, openrouter, perplexity, together, voyageai, xai, xiaomimimo, zai. Companion crates add Bedrock, Vertex, Gemini gRPC, FastEmbed.

`src/strands/models/` ships Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI Responses, Gemini, LiteLLM (100+ providers), Llama API, Llama.cpp, Mistral, Ollama, SageMaker, Writer. LiteLLM transitively covers the rest.

`strands-ts/src/models/` provides BedrockModel, AnthropicModel, OpenAIModel (Chat + Responses), GoogleModel, and `VercelModel` wrapping any `@ai-sdk/provider` provider. Subclass `Model` for custom. Native list is smaller than Python but the Vercel adapter unlocks the AI SDK catalog.

50+ provider packages implementing `LanguageModelV4`: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral, Cohere, DeepInfra, DeepSeek, Fireworks, Groq, Together, Replicate, xAI, Perplexity, Alibaba, ByteDance, Moonshot, Cerebras, Baseten, HuggingFace, OpenAI-compatible generic, plus Vercel AI Gateway as a meta-provider. Native first-party, no LiteLLM dependency.
`retryandreflect` plugin retries on tool errors only, not on model errors. No first-party fallback chain — you'd write an `OnModelErrorCallback` that retries on a different model. Pure BYO.

`FallbackConfig` (`libs/agno/agno/models/fallback.py:20-40`) ships first-class: separate `on_error`, `on_rate_limit`, `on_context_overflow` lists of fallback models plus an instrumentation callback. Shortcut `Agent(fallback_models=[...])` available. Most expressive fallback API in the benchmark.

`FallbackLayer` (`crates/autoagents-llm/src/optim/fallback.rs:64`) composes with `RetryLayer` in a `PipelineBuilder`. `default_is_fallbackable` falls back on HttpError, ProviderError, Generic, ResponseFormatError, NoToolSupport; auth/InvalidRequest propagate. Streaming only falls back on initial async call, not mid-stream.

`fallback_model: str | None` on `ClaudeAgentOptions` (`types.py:1679-1680`) gives a single-step fallback (no N-rung chain). The CLI fires fallback on overage/outage; `ResultMessage.model_usage` reports the split. Good ergonomics but limited expressivity.

`Options.fallbackModel` (sdk.d.ts:1301) provides a single-step fallback on API errors and rate limits; `modelUsage` reflects which model served the turn. No chain of N models. Open issue #313 tracks exposing retry policy/max retry controls.

No first-party 'if provider A fails, retry on provider B' config. `Agent.max_retry_limit = 2` retries the task on error but doesn't switch models. Workarounds: rely on LiteLLM's per-provider retries or AMP's connection management.

`ModelRetryConfig` (`adk/chatmodel.go:307`) retries the same model with backoff. To fall back to a different model on outage you write a `WrapModel` that catches `next.Generate(...)` errors and dispatches to a backup — pure BYO at the model layer.

`Fallback` middleware (`plugins/middleware/fallback.go:59-70`) takes a list of `ModelRef` and switches on UNAVAILABLE/DEADLINE_EXCEEDED/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED/ABORTED/INTERNAL/NOT_FOUND/UNIMPLEMENTED (configurable). Separate `Retry` middleware composes outside (`Retry { Fallback { model } }`). First-class chain support.

`langchain-core` ships `Runnable.with_fallbacks([fallback_model, ...])`, usable on the model passed to `create_react_agent`. Fires on `Exception` by configured policy. No built-in retry-on-rate-limit-with-different-provider semantic — you encode the policy yourself.
No built-in cross-provider fallback in core. `llama-index-llms-cloudflare-ai-gateway` outsources it to Cloudflare's AI Gateway; otherwise you wrap an `LLM` with retry/fallback logic yourself.

`loop()` accepts a models array (`packages/core/src/loop/loop.ts:13`); if the first model fails, Mastra retries on the next. `MODEL_GENERATION` spans are re-stamped when a fallback served the request (`llm-execution-step.ts:650-660`). No separate categories like agno's rate-limit vs context overflow.

No fallback or routing primitive ships in MAF. `Microsoft.Extensions.AI` has some decorators (DistributedCachingChatClient, LoggingChatClient) and community fallback decorators exist, but MAF itself ships nothing for this.

`RetryPolicy` (`src/agents/retry.py`) wraps model calls with structured `ModelRetryAdvice`/`ModelRetryBackoffSettings`, with LiteLLM example in `examples/basic/retry_litellm.py`. Cross-provider fallback (OpenAI down → Anthropic) is BYO via try/except + re-run with different `RunConfig.model`. No `with_fallbacks` builder.

`getResponseWithRetry`/`getStreamedResponseWithRetry` (`packages/agents-core/src/runner/modelRetry.ts`) retry within a single provider. No automatic provider-fallback chain — you'd implement it inside a custom `ModelProvider` wrapping multiple `Model` instances.

`FallbackModel` (`models/fallback.py:69`) wraps an ordered list of `Model` instances and falls through to the next on `ResponseRejected` or configured exception types. Pydantic AI Gateway adds load-balanced routing groups on top. First-class, composable, and combinable with custom error policies.
No retry-on-fallback-model mechanism in core. You'd write your own wrapper around the `CompletionModel` trait.

`ModelRetryStrategy` (`event_loop/_retry.py`) is registered as a default hook with `max_attempts=6, initial_delay=4s, max_delay=240s` for throttling/transient errors. Cross-provider fallback is BYO via a custom `Model` wrapper or a hook that swaps `agent.model` on `AfterModelCallEvent.exception`.

`DefaultModelRetryStrategy` (`strands-ts/src/retry/default-model-retry-strategy.ts`) retries the same model on throttling/transient errors with exponential backoff. Provider swap requires a custom `ModelRetryStrategy` or reacting to `AfterModelCallEvent.error` by mutating `event.agent.model = backupModel` and setting `event.retry = true`.

`customProvider({ fallbackProvider })` (`packages/ai/src/registry/custom-provider.ts`) falls back to another provider when the model id is missing, and `LanguageModelMiddleware.wrapGenerate/wrapStream` lets you implement retry/fallback/circuit-breaker yourself. There is no out-of-the-box 'if Anthropic errors, retry on Bedrock' policy primitive — the hosted AI Gateway has it internally but it's not configurable from the SDK.

Each `llmagent.Config.Model` is independent (`llmagent.go`), so supervisor vs workers can use different models. Within one agent the model is fixed; you architect 'cheap-for-triage, expensive-for-hard' as a triage `llmagent` delegating to a hard-work `llmagent` via `agenttool` or `transfer_to_agent`.

Model is set per `Agent`, not per `run()`. But Agno carves out dedicated extra-model slots: `parser_model` (`agent.py:293`), `output_model` (`agent.py:297`), and `reasoning_model` (`agent.py:192`) — so you do get per-step model swaps for those specific phases. No generic per-call swap on `run()`.

`AgentBuilder::llm(Arc<dyn LLMProvider>)` lets each agent take its own LLM. No built-in 'router' that picks a model per task, but `FallbackLayer`/`RetryLayer` give the composable primitives if you want to build one.

`AgentDefinition.model` (`types.py:92`) supports Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers. `ClaudeSDKClient.set_model(model)` (`client.py:346-368`) switches at turn boundaries. No per-tool/per-step within a single agent, but the sub-agent + mid-session controls cover the common cases.

`Options.model` (sdk.d.ts:1502) per session, `AgentDefinition.model` (sdk.d.ts:56) per sub-agent, and `Query.setModel(model?)` (sdk.d.ts:2076) mid-session. Aliases like 'sonnet'/'opus'/'haiku' supported. Cheap-supervisor + expensive-worker is straightforward.

Each `Agent(llm=...)` chooses its model. On `Crew`, separately configurable `manager_llm`, `function_calling_llm`, `planning_llm`, `chat_llm` (`crew.py:241-335`) give multiple model slots per crew. No per-tool/per-step override within one agent.

Per-agent via `ChatModelAgentConfig.Model`. The `skill` middleware can specify `model: <name>` per skill, fetched from `ModelHub` (`adk/middlewares/skill/skill.go:79-88`), and inside one agent `WrapModel` swaps models per turn. No central router/cost selector.

`ai.WithModelName("name")` or `ai.WithModel(modelRef)` (`go/ai/option.go:233-244`) selects the model on every `genkit.Generate(...)` call. You write dispatch logic in code (e.g. switch on task type). No registry/gateway needed — model selection is a first-class per-call option.

`create_react_agent` accepts a callable `model=(state, runtime) -> BaseChatModel` evaluated on every turn (`chat_agent_executor.py:325-356`, `598-618`). Lets you route on tenant tier, task class, or arbitrary state — first-class dynamic per-step model selection.

Each agent has its own `llm:` (`base_agent.py:111-113`). Different sub-agents in an `AgentWorkflow` can use different models, but no first-party `Router` (cheap-for-triage / expensive-for-hard); you build it as a routing tool or a custom step.

`model: DynamicArgument<MastraModelConfig>` on `Agent` plus per-call `streamOptions.model` plus `processInputStep` returning `{ model: ... }` mid-loop. Route by `requestContext` (`model: ({ requestContext }) => requestContext.get('tier') === 'premium' ? opus : sonnet`) or per-call. Highly expressive.
No first-party gateway or router. You instantiate a different `ChatClient` per agent and select at construction time. Dynamic routing is BYO via a custom `IChatClient` decorator.

`Agent.model` (`src/agents/agent.py:311`) per agent and `RunConfig.model` (`src/agents/run_config.py:206`) per run, the latter forcing every agent in the run to use a specific model. No dynamic per-turn callable; you achieve per-task routing via handoffs/as_tool with different agents.

Per-agent via `new Agent({ model })`, per-run via `new Runner({ model })` or `RunConfig.model`, and per-`asTool` override `Agent.asTool({ runConfig: { model } })`. No first-party registry that auto-routes by task class; selection wired in code or via a custom `ModelProvider`.

`model=` kwarg on every `run*()` overrides the agent default, and `model_settings`/`AgentModelSettings` (`agent/__init__.py:177`) accept a callable receiving `RunContext` and returning settings — enabling cheap-for-triage / expensive-for-hard per-step routing inside one agent.

You build a different `Agent` per model (`client.agent(openai::GPT_4O_MINI).build()` vs `client.agent(openai::GPT_5_2).build()`) and pick at the call site yourself. OpenRouter provider gives a single endpoint with per-call model selection but that's vendor-specific.
Each `Agent` has one `model: Model`. To route by task: build multiple agents and dispatch manually, or use `agent-as-tool` so each sub-agent uses a different model. No first-party gateway/registry.

`model: Model | string` per `Agent` (`agent.ts:140`); for per-task routing you instantiate multiple agents or use `Graph`/`Swarm` with a different model per node. No first-party gateway / router-model.

Per-call `model` on `agent.generate(...)` / `streamText(...)`, `prepareStep` returning `{ model: anotherModel }` to swap mid-loop, and `customProvider({ languageModels })` (`packages/ai/src/registry/custom-provider.ts`) creating aliases like `myProvider('chat-cheap') → gpt-4o-mini` and `myProvider('chat-strong') → gpt-5`.

Each `llmagent.New` gets its own `Model` (`llmagent.Config.Model`). A supervisor on Gemini Pro + workers on Gemini Flash is the natural pattern — no special 'override' API, just construct each agent with the model you want.
Each `Team.members[i]` is itself an `Agent` with its own model. Supervisor Claude / worker Haiku is straightforward and idiomatic.
Every `AgentBuilder` takes its own `llm`, so wiring Sonnet to a supervisor and Haiku to worker agents on the same runtime is natural. No special override API; per-agent llm is the only knob.
`AgentDefinition.model` (`types.py:92`) is exactly the override knob — Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers is the canonical pattern. First-class, single-attribute setting.
`AgentDefinition.model` (sdk.d.ts:56) overrides the parent model. Set to 'haiku' for cheap workers, leave the parent on 'opus' — the API explicitly targets tenant cost control.
Each sub-agent has its own `llm`. A Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers crew is trivial with `process=Process.hierarchical` and `manager_agent=supervisor`. First-class.

Each `ChatModelAgentConfig.Model` is independent. Supervisor with `claudeOpus` and workers with `claudeHaiku` is the canonical wiring via `adk.SetSubAgents` or the `supervisor` prebuilt (`adk/prebuilt/supervisor/supervisor.go`).

Sub-agents are tools that internally call `Generate`; each can specify a different `WithModelName(...)`. Supervisor on `gemini-2.5-pro`, persona workers on `gemini-2.5-flash` is fully supported, but there's no explicit 'sub-agent.model' attribute — you set it on each Generate call.
Each subgraph (sub-agent) is built with its own `model` argument — including the dynamic callable form. Sonnet-supervisor + Haiku-worker is the standard idiom across documentation.

Each sub-agent in `AgentWorkflow` has its own `llm` (`multi_agent_workflow.py:140` builds `self.agents = {cfg.name: cfg for cfg in agents}`; each `cfg.llm` is independent). Orchestrator on Sonnet, workers on Haiku is supported.

Every sub-agent declares its own `model`. Supervisor on Opus while workers run on Sonnet/Haiku is the canonical pattern, and the model can itself be a `DynamicArgument` callable, allowing per-sub-agent dynamic selection.
Each sub-agent can be constructed with its own `ChatClient`, so Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers via `agent_as_tool` composition is straightforward. Implicit but first-class.
Each `Agent` has its own `model` field, so a supervisor on `gpt-5.1` dispatching to a worker on `gpt-5-mini` via `as_tool()` or handoff is direct. First-class.

`Agent.asTool({ runConfig: { model: 'gpt-5.4-mini' } })` lets each tool-ified sub-agent override the model (`examples/agent-patterns/agents-as-tools.ts:33-39`). Handoff-target agents can each pin their own `model`.

Each `Agent` instance carries its own model; agent delegation can mix any models. The multi-agent docs warn USD cost computation may be limited if you mix providers (`docs/multi-agent-applications.md:22-23`), but functional override is first-class.

Each sub-agent is a separate `Agent<M>` and can be on a different model than the parent (the parent wraps the sub-agent via `agent/tool.rs:16-50`). No explicit override API; you construct the sub-agent with the model you want.

Each sub-agent (whether `as_tool()`, `Graph` node, or `Swarm` node) carries its own `model`, so Sonnet supervisor with Haiku workers is straightforward. Per-agent attribute, not a dedicated sub-agent override knob.
Each sub-agent has its own `model` config (e.g. `new Agent({ model: sonnet, tools: [haikuWorker] })` with `haikuWorker = new Agent({ model: haiku })`). Per-agent attribute, no dedicated override API.

Sub-agents are BYO — you instantiate each `ToolLoopAgent` with whatever `model` you want. No dedicated sub-agent override knob because the SDK doesn't impose a sub-agent abstraction; you compose your own.

No built-in summarizer or rolling-window. IncludeContents is either 'default' (full history) or 'none'; you implement a BeforeModelCallback that summarizes when message count exceeds a threshold. BYO.
