CompressionManager compresses tool results when compress_tool_results=True. There is no automatic message-history compaction; only hard caps via num_history_messages / num_history_runs and optional enable_session_summaries that you inject yourself. Reactive at best.

SlidingWindowMemory with TrimStrategy::Summarize only flips a needs_summary flag on overflow; it does not actually summarize. The caller must invoke MemoryProvider::replace_with_summary externally. No built-in summarizer agent.

The CLI implements automatic context-window compaction when approaching the limit. SDK exposes PreCompact hook with trigger='manual'|'auto' and custom_instructions, plus get_context_usage() for live inspection and ContextUsageResponse.isAutoCompactEnabled / autoCompactThreshold. First-class default-on behaviour.

The CLI auto-compacts when context approaches the model window, emitting SDKCompactBoundaryMessage with preserved_segment / preserved_messages for clean resume. PreCompact.custom_instructions steers the summarization prompt and PostCompact has compact_summary. Default-on, no SDK option needed to enable.

Agent.respect_context_window=True triggers handle_context_length() that summarizes/truncates the message list only when the LLM raises a context-length-exceeded exception. Reactive, not proactive — there is no compaction before the limit is hit and no PreCompact hook.

adk/middlewares/summarization/ ships a built-in middleware with configurable trigger (default 190k tokens), pluggable TokenCounter, customizable summary prompt, and optional transcript-file pointer so the model can re-read full history on demand. Fires inside BeforeModelRewriteState. Plus a separate reduction middleware for tool-result reduction.
No built-in summarization or truncation. You'd BYO via a WrapGenerate middleware that watches len(messages) or token count and rewrites earlier messages into a summary.

Not built into the OSS runtime. pre_model_hook is the documented place to wire summarization / trimming. langchain-core ships trim_messages; community message-summarizer patterns and the third-party langgraph-deepagents compress tool exist, but nothing first-party.

Memory has a token-budget-driven FIFO flush (chat_history_token_ratio * token_limit) and ChatSummaryMemoryBuffer (deprecated) does explicit summarization. New Memory.memory_blocks lets you plug FactExtractionMemoryBlock to summarize ejected messages. Decent but not the most sophisticated.

Built-in via TokenLimiterProcessor and BatchPartsProcessor — triggers when token budget exceeded; strategy is 'drop oldest user/assistant pairs until under limit'. For LLM-summarized compaction you compose your own; no first-party summarizer ships.

Built-in: CompactionProvider plus five strategies (ContextWindowCompactionStrategy, SummarizationCompactionStrategy, ToolResultCompactionStrategy, ChatReducerCompactionStrategy, PipelineCompactionStrategy). HarnessAgent (.NET) wires this by default with maxContextWindowTokens / maxOutputTokens; triggers on context-window pressure before each chat call. ADR-backed design.

OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession (521 lines) implements run_compaction with three modes ('auto', 'previous_response_id', 'input') and coordinates with server-side compaction on OpenAI. For non-OpenAI providers (LiteLLM, Any-LLM) there is no auto-compaction — you implement truncation/summarization yourself.

OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession wrapper calls responses.compact server-side, triggered after each completed turn with configurable thresholds (force, compactionMode, responseId). Not built into MemorySession or generic stores — OpenAI-specific.

OpenAICompaction and AnthropicCompaction capabilities provide provider-native compaction for the two main providers. No provider-agnostic compaction in core; ProcessHistory capability lets you plug in a custom summarizer for other providers.

Not in core. rig-memory ships sliding-window and token-budget policies that filter history during memory load; InMemoryConversationMemory::with_filter takes a closure that shapes history each load. No LLM-summarization built-in.

Built-in SlidingWindowConversationManager (default, window_size=40) with optional should_truncate_results=True and per_turn proactive trigger, plus SummarizingConversationManager that calls a Model to summarize older history with a configurable prompt. Applied at end of each cycle and on ContextWindowOverflowException.

ConversationManager abstract base with reduce() runs reactively on ContextWindowOverflowError or proactively before BeforeModelCallEvent. Ships SlidingWindowConversationManager (default windowSize=40), SummarizingConversationManager (LLM-summarized), and NullConversationManager. Proactive trigger fires when projectedInputTokens / contextWindowLimit > 0.7.

No built-in summarize-and-truncate. You either use prepareStep to truncate messages before each call, LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams at the provider level, or compose with @ai-sdk/langchain. Pure BYO.

Two registration scopes — plugin.Config (cross-agent) and llmagent.Config (per-agent) — wire 12 callbacks: OnUserMessageCallback, BeforeRun, AfterRun, OnEvent, BeforeAgent, AfterAgent, BeforeModel, AfterModel, OnModelError, BeforeTool, AfterTool, OnToolError. Covers user-msg, run, agent, model, tool with pre/post pairs.

pre_hooks (after session load, before LLM) and post_hooks (after LLM, before return) on Agent/Team, plus tool_hooks middleware-chain at agent level, plus Function.pre_hook / post_hook / tool_hooks per-tool, plus @hook(run_in_background=True) for FastAPI background tasks. No separate session-start or per-LLM-call hook though.

AgentHooks trait has 9 methods: on_agent_create, on_run_start/complete, on_turn_start/complete, on_tool_call/start/result/error, on_agent_shutdown. All cover the right fire-points but they are observe-and-abort with no mutation power.

HookEvent literal covers PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, Notification, SubagentStart, PermissionRequest, plus SessionStart. Each registered as HookMatcher with optional tool-name pattern, timeout, parallel dispatch.

HOOK_EVENTS exposes 29 named events including PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, SessionStart, SessionEnd, Stop, SubagentStart/Stop, PreCompact, PostCompact, PermissionRequest/Denied, Setup, TaskCreated/Completed, Elicitation, WorktreeCreate/Remove, InstructionsLoaded, CwdChanged, FileChanged, ConfigChange. Broadest hook surface in the comparison.

Four registrable hook types (before/after × LLM/tool) plus crew-level before_kickoff_callbacks / after_kickoff_callbacks, step_callback, task_callback, plus event-bus listeners (151 event classes) and LLM transport BaseInterceptor. No SessionStart, PreCompact, or PostMessage.

Three layers: callbacks.Handler (graph-level with 5 timings), legacy AgentMiddleware struct, and modern ChatModelAgentMiddleware interface with 8 methods (BeforeAgent, BeforeModelRewriteState, AfterModelRewriteState, four WrapToolCall variants, WrapModel). BaseChatModelAgentMiddleware provides default no-op impls.

Middleware contract returns Hooks per Generate call with three Wrap points: WrapGenerate (per tool-loop iteration), WrapModel (per model API call), WrapTool (per tool execution). No traditional SessionStart / BeforeMessage / AfterMessage lifecycle hooks; the three Wrap points are the entire surface.

At create_react_agent: pre_model_hook (before each LLM call) and post_model_hook (after each LLM call, before tool dispatch). At ToolNode: wrap_tool_call / awrap_tool_call around each tool execution. Plus GraphCallbackHandler for interrupts/resume and LangChain BaseCallbackHandler for observation. Covers the main fire-points but is sparser than dedicated hook frameworks.

No dedicated hook system. You subclass BaseWorkflowAgent and override @step methods (init_run, setup_agent, run_agent_step, parse_agent_output, call_tool, aggregate_tool_results) for lifecycle override, plus FunctionTool(callback=..., async_callback=...) and partial_params for tool-level mutation. Dispatcher event/span handlers are observe-only.

Eight Processor methods (processInput, processInputStep, processLLMRequest, processLLMResponse, processOutputStream, processOutputStep, processOutputResult, processAPIError) plus top-level callbacks (onChunk, onStepFinish, onFinish, onError, onAbort, onIterationComplete, delegation.*). Comprehensive coverage of every pipeline stage.

AgentMiddleware (around run), ChatMiddleware (around each LLM round-trip), FunctionMiddleware (around tool invocation) with decorator shorthand. Plus ContextProvider lifecycle (before_run / after_run / before_chat_call / after_chat_call) and HistoryProvider get/save. .NET pipeline-builder hooks (UseFunctionInvocation, UseMessageInjection, etc.) compose the same.

RunHooks and per-agent AgentHooks with 7 methods (on_llm_start/end, on_agent_start/end, on_handoff, on_tool_start/end). Plus four guardrail decorators that can block, RunConfig.call_model_input_filter that mutates the pre-LLM input, session_input_callback, and tool_error_formatter.

RunHooks and AgentHooks as EventEmitters (agent_start, agent_end, agent_handoff, agent_tool_start, agent_tool_end), plus Input/Output/ToolInput/ToolOutput guardrails (can mutate or block), RunConfig.callModelInputFilter, sessionInputCallback, toolErrorFormatter, errorHandlers. Comprehensive surface.

Hooks capability with decorator sugar exposes before_run / after_run / wrap_run / run_error, before_node_run / after_node_run / wrap_node_run / node_run_error, before_model_request / after_model_request / wrap / error, prepare_tools / prepare_output_tools, before_tool_validate / after_tool_validate / wrap / error, before_tool_execute / after_tool_execute / wrap / error, before_output_validate / after_output_validate / wrap / error, plus deferred_tool_calls, run_event_stream, event. Tool-name filter and timeout per hook.

PromptHook<M> trait exposes on_completion_call, on_completion_response, on_tool_call, on_tool_result, on_text_delta, on_tool_call_delta, on_stream_completion_response_finish. Default impl for () makes all no-op. Covers the main fire-points but stream-flavoured.

hooks/events.py exposes AgentInitializedEvent, BeforeInvocationEvent, AfterInvocationEvent, MessageAddedEvent, BeforeModelCallEvent, AfterModelCallEvent, BeforeToolCallEvent, AfterToolCallEvent. Multi-agent flavours: BeforeMulti/AfterMulti/Before/AfterNodeCall. Experimental bidi events. Sync and async callbacks supported.

Hookable events include InitializedEvent, Before/AfterInvocationEvent, MessageAddedEvent, Before/AfterModelCallEvent, Before/AfterToolsEvent, Before/AfterToolCallEvent, ContentBlockEvent, ModelStreamUpdateEvent, ModelMessageEvent, ToolStreamUpdateEvent, ToolResultEvent, AgentResultEvent, InterruptEvent. Multi-agent flavours plus HookOrder constants (SDK_FIRST, INTERVENTION_INPUT/OUTPUT, SDK_LAST).

Multiple stages: prepareCall (once pre-loop), prepareStep (per step), experimental_onStart/onStepStart/onLanguageModelCallStart/End, LanguageModelMiddleware (transformParams/wrapGenerate/wrapStream), experimental_repairToolCall, experimental_refineToolInput[name], resolveToolApproval, onToolExecutionStart/End, tool.onInputStart/Delta/Available, onStepFinish, onFinish, Telemetry hooks. Many of the post hooks are read-only.

BeforeModelCallback mutates *model.LLMRequest, AfterModelCallback can replace response, OnModelErrorCallback can convert error to response, BeforeToolCallback mutates args in place or short-circuits with a result, AfterToolCallback mutates result. BeforeAgent/AfterAgent can short-circuit by returning content. Sequential first-non-nil-wins.

pre_hooks mutate run_input and session_state, post_hooks mutate run_output, guardrails raise InputCheckError / OutputCheckError to block, tool_hooks form a nested chain that mutates args and return values. compression_manager can compress results. No additional_messages-from-PostToolUse pattern.

All AgentHooks are observe-and-abort: on_run_start and on_tool_call return HookOutcome::Continue | Abort but cannot mutate task.prompt, tool args, or results. on_tool_result and on_run_complete are pure observation. The classic patterns (force tenant_id, summarize tool output) require subclassing the executor.

PreToolUse returns updatedInput (replaces LLM args), permissionDecision (allow/deny/ask/defer), additionalContext; PostToolUse returns updatedToolOutput (replaces tool result for any tool since 0.1.74); UserPromptSubmit injects additionalContext or blocks via decision: 'block'; SessionStart injects additionalContext; Stop can force-continue by blocking. Plus continue_=False stops the loop with stopReason.

PreToolUse: allow/deny, updatedInput, additionalContext, permissionDecisionReason. PostToolUse: updatedToolOutput (any tool) or updatedMCPToolOutput, additionalContext. Many event-specific overrides (sessionTitle, suppressOriginalPrompt, initialUserMessage, watchPaths, worktreePath). Stop returns decision: 'block' to keep going. Async hooks supported via asyncTimeout.

before_llm_call mutates messages in place and returns False to block. after_llm_call returns str to replace the response. before_tool_call mutates tool_input dict in place or returns False to block. after_tool_call returns str to replace the result. step_callback / task_callback are observe-only. No additional_messages-from-PostToolUse equivalent.

BeforeModelRewriteState mutates the message list, AfterModelRewriteState mutates post-call state, WrapModel can replace the model entirely (routing, retry, mid-stream tool filtering), WrapInvokableToolCall wraps endpoints with custom pre/post, BeforeAgent can change Instruction/Tools/ReturnDirectly. SendEvent emits custom events but no direct additional_messages mechanism.

WrapGenerate mutates messages and tools on each iteration, can short-circuit, can emit extra stream chunks via params.Callback. WrapModel can retry/fallback/cache and mutate request. WrapTool mutates Input before next(), then mutates MultipartToolResponse after. Tools[] field contributes additional tools the model sees (used by Skills/Filesystem). All Wraps fully delegate to next which is replaceable.

pre_model_hook emits {messages | llm_input_messages} (full mutation power). post_model_hook can mutate state, block (no tool_calls → END), or branch (emit additional tool_calls or route). wrap_tool_call uses ToolCallRequest.override(), can return synthetic ToolMessage without execute(), or return Command(goto=Send('tools', ...)) to fan out new dispatches mid-wrap. Strongest branching power of any framework here.

FunctionTool callback / async_callback returns ToolOutput or str to replace tool result. partial_params provides default kwargs (LLM-provided values win). For messages mutation you subclass setup_agent / run_agent_step. No first-class mutate-args hook; no block-and-return at the hook layer.

processInput / processInputStep can replace model, tools, messages, systemMessages, toolChoice, activeTools, messageList, providerOptions, modelSettings, structuredOutput, messageId. processLLMRequest can return {response: cached chunks} to skip the LLM call. processOutputStream can drop or rewrite chunks. processOutputStep can ctx.abort({retry: true}) to trigger a self-correcting retry. processAPIError can append messages and return {retry: true}.

FunctionMiddleware mutates ctx.arguments before call_next() and ctx.result after; can raise MiddlewareTermination. ChatMiddleware mutates context.messages around LLM call. AgentMiddleware can set/override result for the whole run. ContextProvider.before_chat_call injects context_messages. CompactionProvider uses these. No first-class additional_messages.

Lifecycle hooks (on_llm_start/end, on_tool_start/end, etc.) are read-only — they can only raise to abort. RunConfig.call_model_input_filter is the only true mutation hook for messages/instructions. Tool guardrails can reject_content(message=...) to replace the result with a synthetic message; this is the mutation channel. No first-class force-args or PostToolUse mutate path.

RunHooks listeners are read-only EventEmitter callbacks (await isn't honoured by the loop). callModelInputFilter mutates {input, instructions}. ToolInputGuardrail can throw to block, ToolOutputGuardrail can replace the result. HandoffInputFilter edits input history. tool({needsApproval}) halts with interruption. No additional_messages.

Sequential before/after fold-style and wrap nested. before_model_request mutates messages, model, settings (incl. model swap). before_tool_validate/execute mutates raw and validated args. after_tool_execute returns replacement result. before/after_output_validate/process mutates output. SkipModelRequest / SkipToolValidation / SkipToolExecution shortcut the next stage. Error hooks recover with replacement results. tools=[...] filter and per-hook timeout.

All PromptHook callbacks receive read-only references (&Message, &CompletionResponse, args: &str). The only control is HookAction::Continue | Terminate and ToolCallHookAction::Skip{reason} (returns the reason as the tool result). No way to rewrite args, mutate the message list, or replace a tool result; all such patterns must be baked into the tool's own implementation.

BeforeInvocationEvent.messages writable; BeforeToolCallEvent.tool_use, selected_tool, cancel_tool writable; AfterToolCallEvent.result and retry writable; AfterModelCallEvent.retry; AfterInvocationEvent.resume re-invokes the whole agent. Sliding-window/SummarizingConvMgr mutate agent.messages in BeforeModelCallEvent. Multi-agent BeforeNodeCallEvent.cancel_node + Interrupt support. _Interruptible events can raise InterruptException.

BeforeInvocationEvent can set cancel. BeforeModelCallEvent can set cancel + reads projectedInputTokens. BeforeToolCallEvent mutates toolUse.{name,input,toolUseId}, sets selectedTool to swap tool, can interrupt for HITL. AfterToolCallEvent mutates result, can set retry. BeforeToolsEvent / AfterToolsEvent for batch-level cancel / endTurn. AfterInvocationEvent.resume re-enters the loop with new input.

prepareCall (once pre-loop) and prepareStep (per step) mutate model, tools, instructions, messages, toolChoice, activeTools, etc. experimental_refineToolInput[name] mutates tool args per-call. experimental_repairToolCall fixes parse errors. LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams mutates provider prompt. But onToolExecutionEnd is read-only (returns void); the only tool-result mutation is per-tool toModelOutput. No additional_messages.

The model.LLMRequest.Config *genai.GenerateContentConfig accepts CachedContent (a Gemini feature), but the framework does not automatically place cache breakpoints or preserve stable prefixes. You'd configure caching manually in the GenerateContentConfig. BYO.

The framework reports cache_read_tokens / cache_write_tokens in Metrics and surfaces them on ModelRequestCompletedEvent, but does not automatically place Anthropic/OpenAI cache breakpoints. For a stable prefix you arrange it yourself via instructions and add_history_to_context.

CacheLayer in the LLM pipeline is a result-cache layer (caches the LLM response for identical message+tool+schema input), not a stable-prefix breakpoint mechanism for Anthropic/OpenAI prompt caching. The framework does not insert cache_control markers — you'd manage that in your provider wrapper.

The CLI handles Anthropic prompt-caching automatically; cache_creation_input_tokens / cache_read_input_tokens surface on AssistantMessage.usage. SystemPromptPreset.exclude_dynamic_sections (added 0.1.57) strips per-user dynamic sections out of the system prompt and re-injects them into the first user message — explicit support for cross-user cache amortization, the multi-tenant killer feature.

Three mechanisms: (1) Options.systemPrompt: string[] with the SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY constant inserted as a standalone element splits the prompt into cacheable prefix and dynamic suffix; (2) excludeDynamicSections strips per-user dynamic sections so the preset is identical across users (cross-user cache hit for multi-tenant fleets); (3) automatic breakpoint placement for stable-prefix content (system prompt, tool catalog).

Ships mark_cache_breakpoint(message) helper used in _setup_messages to tag the system prompt and per-task user prompt as stable prefixes. The Anthropic provider adapter translates cache_breakpoint=True into cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}; OpenAI / Gemini cache implicitly. Good engineering but you can't easily add breakpoints from a before_llm_call hook without re-applying the marker manually.

Stable-prefix preservation is the default (BeforeModelRewriteState middlewares should append rather than prepend). PromptTokenDetails.CachedTokens on schema.TokenUsage lets you observe cache hit rate. But Eino does NOT insert cache_control breakpoints for you and there is no first-class cache_control breakpoint placement helper — you'd write it on *schema.Message.Extra.

The googlegenai plugin has explicit cache support (plugins/googlegenai/cache.go) — you can attach a cachedContents reference. There is no generic prompt cache breakpoint mechanism like Anthropic's cache_control field that would work across all providers; each plugin handles its provider's cache features in its own way.

Engineers wire Anthropic cache_control flags into specific SystemMessage or HumanMessage content blocks; the pre_model_hook ensures they're at a stable prefix. No automatic breakpoint placement — BYO via hook code.

ChatMessage supports a CachePoint content block which providers like Anthropic / OpenAI honour, but the framework does not auto-place breakpoints; the developer inserts them. No multi-tenant cache amortization helper.

The processor pipeline supports response caching via processLLMRequest returning {response: cached chunks} to skip the LLM call entirely (ResponseCacheProcessor ships). Anthropic-style cache breakpoints are not auto-managed — you place them in your system prompt yourself or write a processor to insert them.

No first-party prompt-cache breakpoint controller. Providers like agent-framework-anthropic set cache breakpoints inside their own ChatClient. MAF does not expose a generic stable-prefix knob and there is no cross-provider helper.

PromptCacheKeyResolver generates a per-run cache key (visible at RunResult._generated_prompt_cache_key) threaded through model settings via model_settings_with_prompt_cache_key. This opts into OpenAI's prompt-caching pricing tier. Anthropic-style explicit cache breakpoints are not natively wired; with LiteLLM you pass through provider-specific extras.

The SDK passes previousResponseId to OpenAI's Responses API (server-side caching benefit), but doesn't manage Anthropic-style cache_control breakpoints. The ai-sdk extension's caching is whatever the underlying Vercel AI SDK provider supports.

Cache breakpoints are first-class: CachePoint message part, cache_write_tokens / cache_read_tokens on RequestUsage, provider-specific model-settings flags (e.g. bedrock_supports_prompt_caching). InstructionPart is split into static vs dynamic so the stable prefix is cache-friendly.

The Usage struct includes cached_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens so you can observe cache hit rate per turn, but there is no automatic cache-breakpoint placement. You'd configure provider-side caching (e.g. Anthropic cache_control) via additional_params.

system_prompt accepts list[SystemContentBlock] including cachePoint blocks; agent.system_prompt_content preserves them. Message content blocks also accept cachePoint. BedrockModel and AnthropicModel wire these to the API. Placement is manual — engineers add {'cachePoint': {'type': 'default'}}. The AgentSkills plugin preserves existing cache points while injecting skills XML.

Model.CacheConfig with strategy: 'auto' | 'anthropic' — 'auto' injects cache breakpoints after tools and the last user message. CachePointBlock content blocks carry the cache markers. Bedrock and Anthropic providers wire this in; OpenAI does not need explicit markers. Closer to automatic than the Python sibling.

LanguageModelUsage exposes inputTokenDetails: {noCacheTokens, cacheReadTokens, cacheWriteTokens} (better visibility than most stacks). But the SDK does not automatically place Anthropic-style cache breakpoints — you set provider-specific cache markers via providerOptions or LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams.
AfterToolCallback can mutate large results in place (write to artifact store, replace with a pointer string), but no first-party stash + summary primitive ships. Pure BYO.

compress_tool_results + CompressionManager for in-place compression of tool outputs. store_tool_messages: bool to drop tool messages from RunOutput. The skills mechanism is itself a progressive-disclosure pattern: only skill metadata is in the system prompt, full body is fetched on demand via get_skill_instructions / get_skill_reference / get_skill_script tools.

Tool results go directly into MemoryAdapter::store_tool_interaction. The only knob is the sliding-window size — large outputs simply push older messages out the back. No progressive-disclosure mechanism.

PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput lets you replace large tool outputs with a summary before the model sees them. No first-party stash-to-filesystem-and-replace-with-token-budget-summary pattern ships, but it's straightforward to layer.

Four mechanisms: PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput replaces the tool result in-place. Built-in Write/Edit/Read tools encode the file-scratchpad pattern naturally — large outputs go to disk and the model receives a path it can Read on demand. getContextUsage() returns per-category breakdown (system prompt / tools / messages / MCP / memory / agents / skills / commands). MCP tool descriptions deferred by default (alwaysLoad: false) — definitions not in the prompt until tool-search invoked.

You can implement after_tool_call to summarize/truncate any tool result longer than a threshold. There is no filesystem-stash / on-demand-re-read pattern shipped. Skills with RESOURCES disclosure level catalogue file lists in the prompt — but the agent has to fetch contents via a separate tool you provide.

adk/middlewares/reduction/ truncates oversized tool outputs in the message list, leaving a summary. The filesystem middleware automatically stashes oversized tool results into the configured filesystem.Backend and replaces the tool message with a short reference + first-10-lines preview, suggesting the LLM use read_file with offset/limit. The closest match to Claude Code's progressive-disclosure pattern in any Go framework benchmarked.

Not provided as a built-in pattern. The Filesystem middleware has a file-state dedup that returns a 'File unchanged since last read' stub when a tool re-reads an unchanged file, but there is no generic stash large tool outputs to disk, return summary pattern. BYO.

wrap_tool_call can rewrite the ToolMessage to a summary plus a 'full result available via <resource_id>' pointer, and BaseStore is a natural stash. No first-party tool result clearing primitive ships.
BYO — you can return a summary string from a FunctionTool async_callback and stash the full payload elsewhere. No first-party stash pattern.

Two mechanisms: each tool can declare toModelOutput(output) to return a truncated/summarized version to the LLM while persisting the full result in storage (this is how the sub-agent wrapper does it). processOutputStream can drop or rewrite tool-result chunks. Plus the Workspace + Skills system encourages filesystem stash: tools write full output to a workspace file and return a short summary + path the LLM can fetch via skill_read.

ToolResultCompactionStrategy explicitly clears or summarizes tool results once they exceed a threshold. Skills follow the progressive-disclosure pattern: metadata-only in prompt, body loaded on demand via load_skill. First-class for the tool-result clearing path.

FunctionTool.defer_loading=True hides the tool definition until ToolSearchTool surfaces it (ToolSearchCallItem / ToolSearchOutputItem). For large tool outputs, the Codex/Shell tools have a tool_output_trimmer extension that truncates output before the model sees it; for ad-hoc tools you @tool_output_guardrail to summarize.

Not first-class outside of Sandbox Agents. Sandbox Agents have a filesystem workspace where tools can write large outputs to disk and reference them by path. Non-sandbox tools just return their result string to the LLM.

after_tool_execute hook returns a summary instead of the raw result. Tool Search capability defers tool *loading* — tools marked defer_loading=True are only included in the model's tool list after the agent calls search_tools (a meta-tool). Available native (Anthropic, OpenAI Responses) or local. defer_loading() on any toolset.
No filesystem-stash strategy, no auto-summarization of large tool outputs. Use a rig-memory policy or implement on-the-fly truncation in your tool's call body.

SlidingWindowConversationManager(should_truncate_results=True) truncates large tool results to first+last 200 chars and replaces images with text placeholders. Plus the Context offloader vended plugin — opt-in plugin that stashes large content out-of-context with a fetch-on-demand pattern.

ContextOffloaderPlugin registers an AfterToolCallEvent hook that stores full content in a configurable Storage keyed by mem_<id> reference and replaces the in-context content with preview + reference + a sibling retrieve_offloaded_content tool the model can call later for full content / grep / line-range. Plus sliding/summarizing conversation managers drop or summarize older turns.

tool.toModelOutput lets you summarize at tool-author time, returning a different shape to the model than the actual return value. But there is no harness-level after step N, drop the tool result from history primitive — the only mutation point is per-tool and lives inside the tool definition, not a global hook.

memory.Service interface (memory/service.go:31-39) with InMemoryService and Vertex AI RAG-backed implementation; namespaced by AppName+UserID. memory.AddSessionToMemory and loadmemorytool are first-party. No auto-extraction or consolidation; only Vertex backend ships for semantic recall.

First-class MemoryManager with Agent(enable_agentic_memory) and update_memory_on_run for automatic fact extraction. UserMemory rows with topics, feedback, timestamps keyed by user_id; add_memories_to_context auto-injects. Directly fits the benchmark use case.

No long-term memory abstraction; only autoagents-qdrant + VectorStore trait + embeddings primitives exist. Engineer must build a MemoryProvider that bridges to the vector store — large effort around the framework.

Partial via CLAUDE.md files loaded by the CLI when setting_sources includes project; AgentDefinition.memory scopes which CLAUDE.md a sub-agent sees. No vector store, no embeddings, no semantic recall — filesystem-shaped only.

First-party memory recall supervisor scans ~/.claude/agent-memory and project dirs, surfaced via SDKMemoryRecallMessage with select/synthesize modes. AgentDefinition.memory ('user'|'project'|'local') scopes files. No vector index — for true semantic search RAG, BYO via MCP.

Sophisticated first-class crewai.memory.unified_memory.Memory: LLM-driven fact extraction, scope inference, importance scoring, semantic+recency+importance blending, consolidation above similarity threshold, adaptive recall_flow with exploration_budget. Defaults to LanceDB; QdrantEdge also pluggable. Closest in class to dedicated memory products.
No Memory type, no MemoryStore, no auto-recall primitive. Long-term memory must be built by combining components/retriever (vector search) with custom system-message-injection middleware.

No memory primitive (no semantic/episodic/working memory abstraction). Closest pieces are x/session (state, not vector recall) and retrievers (17.2) — engineer encodes 'memory' as documents themselves.

BaseStore (libs/checkpoint/langgraph/store/base) is a namespaced KV with optional vector search; runtime.store.put/search are first-class. Backed by pgvector in langgraph-checkpoint-postgres or in-memory. No LLM-driven extraction or consolidation built in, but the store primitive is solid.

Memory.memory_blocks accepts StaticMemoryBlock, VectorMemoryBlock (vector search over past messages) and FactExtractionMemoryBlock (LLM-extracted facts). Blocks are priority-ordered and ejected short-term messages flow in. Directly fits the benchmark use case.

@mastra/memory ships per-thread conversation history, working memory (LLM-summarized rolling notes), semantic recall (vector retrieval of prior messages) and observational memory across threads. Vector adapters for Pinecone/Qdrant/Chroma/Astra/Lance/Elasticsearch. First-class fit.

Mem0Provider (agent-framework-mem0, beta), _harness/_memory.py MemoryFileStore/MemoryStore (experimental, 1.3.0), and Azure AI Search context provider. Real adapters exist but most are beta/experimental rather than a unified built-in memory primitive.
The 10 Session backends only persist turn-level conversation history; there is no vector-search long-term memory primitive in the SDK.

No cross-session semantic memory primitive. Sandbox Agents have a memory() capability that materializes a filesystem scratchpad inside the workspace — useful for cross-turn notes inside one sandbox run but not semantic recall across sessions.

Built-in MemoryTool is Anthropic-native with no in-tree local fallback; provider-agnostic memory requires third-party pydantic-ai-memory / pydantic-ai-backend capability packages. Limited to provider-bound surface.

ConversationMemory is in-conversation only; for cross-conversation recall the user combines ConversationMemory with dynamic_context(sample, vector_store_index). Substrate via companion crates (rig-mongodb, rig-qdrant, rig-postgres, etc.) but no first-party 'memory' primitive.

Not in SDK core. strands-agents-tools ships mem0_memory, agent_core_memory, elasticsearch_memory, mongodb_memory, memory — but these are tool-side integrations the LLM must call explicitly rather than an integrated memory subsystem.
No vector store integration, no embeddings primitive, no memories/facts object. Cross-session continuity = re-hydrating from a SessionManager snapshot.
No Memory class, no semantic-recall primitive. The SDK explicitly has no concept of cross-session memory — engineer must roll their own with a vector DB or use @ai-sdk/langchain/@ai-sdk/llamaindex.

Vertex AI RAG via memory/vertexai/ is the only first-party RAG backend; no Pinecone/Weaviate/Qdrant/pgvector adapter, no built-in chunkers or rerankers. loadmemorytool is the agent-facing entry point but adapter coverage is narrow.

Knowledge class with vector DB integrations across Chroma, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Mongo Atlas, Lance, PgVector, Singlestore, Cassandra, ClickHouse. Embedders for major providers; readers for text/md/pdf/docx/csv/json/sitemap/website/S3/GCS. Auto search_knowledge tool with knowledge_filters and write-back via update_knowledge.

autoagents-core ships VectorStore trait (in-memory + Qdrant), document.rs, readers (PDF and others), embeddings abstraction. Examples for RAG patterns exist but you assemble retrieval yourself — building blocks not a turnkey RAG pipeline.
No built-in vector store, chunker, retriever or citation primitive. Layer it as an MCP server or SDK tool.
No built-in vector store, chunker, retriever or citation primitive. Standard pattern is to expose Qdrant/Pinecone/etc as an mcp__myrag__search tool.

crewai.knowledge.Knowledge is a separate first-class subsystem from Memory. Knowledge sources: String/TextFile/CSV/JSON/PDF/Excel/Docx/CrewDoclingSource/custom; each chunked+embedded+stored. ChromaDB default, Qdrant supported; EmbedderConfig covers OpenAI/Azure/Cohere/HuggingFace/Bedrock. Configured at Agent or Crew level with auto retrieval handler.

First-class components.retriever.Retriever / components.indexer.Indexer / components.embedding.Embedder / components.document.{Loader,Parser,Transformer} interfaces. Eino-ext ships adapters for Qdrant, Milvus v1/v2, Redis, OpenSearch v2/v3, Elasticsearch v7/v8/v9, Volc VikingDB, Dify, Volc Knowledge. Wired natively through the graph composition.

Retrievers are a first-class action type (ai.Retriever). Plugins: localvec, pinecone, weaviate, postgresql (pgvector), alloydb, firebase + BigQuery sample. Built-in chunkers, per-provider embedders, and a Reranker abstraction (RerankerRequest/Response). ai.WithDocs cleanly threads retrieved docs through Generate.

No first-party retriever — relies on separately packaged langchain-* vector stores (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Postgres+pgvector). BaseStore.search covers basic semantic recall but full RAG (chunking, citations) is BYO via the broader LangChain ecosystem.

Historical core competency: 60+ vector store integrations, multiple index types (VectorStoreIndex, SummaryIndex, TreeIndex, KeywordTableIndex, KnowledgeGraphIndex, PropertyGraphIndex, ComposableIndex), retrieval primitives (BaseRetriever, RouterRetriever, FusionRetriever), and citations via CitableBlock/CitationBlock. Best-in-class.

@mastra/rag ships retrievers, chunkers (recursiveChunker etc.) and citation support, integrated with the same vector store adapters used by @mastra/memory (Pinecone/Qdrant/Chroma/Astra/Lance/Elasticsearch). End-to-end primitive.

TextSearchProvider (.NET) is the generic context-provider primitive; Azure AI Search and IVectorStore (Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Vector) provide semantic backends. Strong on Azure path but limited adapter breadth and no built-in chunker/citation primitive.
FileSearchTool integrates with OpenAI's hosted Vector Stores; for non-OpenAI RAG you must write a @function_tool that queries your own store. Hosted-only retrieval and no chunker/citation primitive.
fileSearchTool wraps OpenAI's hosted file search over vector stores; otherwise BYO retriever as a function tool. Same hosted-only constraint as the Python SDK.

Embeddings package covers OpenAI, Cohere, Google, Bedrock, sentence-transformers, voyageai. Examples in docs/examples/rag.md. Vector stores are BYO (Chroma, pgvector, Pinecone) — the framework focuses on the embeddings interface.

crates/rig-core/src/vector_store ships VectorStoreIndex / VectorStoreIndexDyn traits plus InMemoryVectorStore and EmbeddingsBuilder. Companion crates: rig-mongodb, rig-lancedb, rig-qdrant, rig-sqlite, rig-surrealdb, rig-milvus, rig-scylladb, rig-postgres, rig-s3vectors, rig-helixdb, rig-vectorize, rig-neo4j. agent.dynamic_context auto-retrieves and inlines top-N docs.

strands-agents-tools/retrieve.py wraps Bedrock Knowledge Base and the memory tools (mem0/agent_core/elasticsearch/mongodb). No first-party chunker or embedder primitives in the SDK; everything sits in tool packages.

Not a first-class subsystem — pattern is to write a tool that calls your own vector search. ContextOffloaderPlugin offloads tool results to disk/blob and exposes a retrieve_offloaded_content tool, the closest built-in retrieval-like pattern.

Ships embed/embedMany and rerank (cosineSimilarity helper) but no vector store, chunker, retriever or citation rendering. Higher-level RAG via @ai-sdk/langchain or @ai-sdk/llamaindex; otherwise BYO with Pinecone/pgvector/Turbopuffer.

SearchRequest.AppName and SearchRequest.UserID give per-user scoping naturally; tenant scoping done by reusing AppName as the tenant key (with the cost of fully-isolated memory across apps). Naturally namespaced but not deeper.
UserMemory.user_id is the scoping key. For per-tenant scoping you tenant-prefix the user_id (e.g. user_id='acme:alice') or filter at query time via metadata. Convention, not enforced.
Not provided — engineer namespaces vector-store collections per tenant. No built-in tenant scoping anywhere in the framework.

Memory is filesystem-shaped: per-tenant CLAUDE.md lives under tenants/<tid>/CLAUDE.md and the SDK loads it via cwd. Works for filesystem memory but no enforcement and not deeper than directory layout.

Memory dirs are global-per-machine (~/.claude/agent-memory/) or project-scoped under cwd. Per-tenant scoping requires using a per-tenant cwd (e.g. cwd: /tenants/${tenantId}); cross-tenant memory served by vector DB is BYO via MCP.

Memory(root_scope='/tenant/acme') hierarchically scopes remember/recall. But framework does not auto-scope by tenant; engineer must construct and route a per-tenant Memory instance per request and there is no Memory.with_tenant(id) runtime filter.
Not automatic. Retriever.Retrieve(ctx, query, opts) receives ctx so you pass tenant scope through and rely on adapter Options.SubIndexes or query filter. Framework does not enforce — adapter does.

No automatic namespacing. RetrieverRequest.Options is free-form and encodes tenant filters (e.g. Pinecone.namespace, Postgres WHERE tenant_id=$1). Each plugin implements its own pass-through; no Mastra-style auto scoping.

BaseStore namespace tuples are the standard scoping convention: runtime.store.search((runtime.context.tenant_id, 'memories'), ...). @auth.on.store (auth/__init__.py:89) lets the HTTP layer inject the tenant prefix server-side so external callers cannot escape it — enforced when wired.

Memory.session_id is the only first-class scoping key; for per-tenant separation you encode tenant:user:session in session_id or use a per-tenant SQLAlchemyChatStore (different DB, table, or db_schema). Convention rather than tenant primitive.

Memory is naturally scoped per resourceId in the memory: { thread, resource } tuple. The reserved MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY makes resource server-controlled so a client cannot read another tenant's memory — strongest tenancy story in the benchmark. Index-prefixing covers vector-level separation.
Memory adapters expose scope options (Mem0ProviderScope: User/Session/Global). Tenancy = scope-by-user with tenant ID encoded into the user value; no deeper tenant primitive.
Not provided — engineer namespaces vector indexes by tenant_id.
Not provided; you namespace yourself by setting per-tenant vector store IDs in fileSearchTool(vectorStoreIds) or by partitioning a custom Session implementation.
Per-tenant scoping is engineer responsibility — namespace by tenant_id in your vector index.
Not first-class. Engineer scopes vector-store collections per tenant (e.g. namespace by tenant_id in Postgres/Qdrant schema).
BYO. The memory tools accept user/agent IDs but tenancy must be encoded into those IDs; no framework-level scoping primitive.
BYO. Namespace your vector store / DB / S3 prefix by tenantId pulled from invocationState; pattern but no enforcement.
BYO — namespace yourself in your vector DB (prefix keys with tenantId: or use a separate index per tenant). No primitive.

First-class SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter following agentskills.io spec; validates name/description/compatibility, enforces directory-name match, supports references/assets/scripts subdirs (tool/skilltoolset/).
Dedicated libs/agno/agno/skills/ module; SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, metadata, compatibility, allowed-tools) plus validator and scripts/references subfolders.
No SKILL.md, no Skill trait, no loader; term "skill" does not appear in the codebase. Closest analog is a compiled-in Rust agent type.
SKILL.md format is owned by the Claude Code CLI; the SDK only exposes a skills filter option. Schema is not redocumented in-SDK but the format is canonical Anthropic Agent Skills.
Same CLI-side SKILL.md as Python SDK; YAML frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, trigger). SDK does not parse but surfaces filtered list via Options.skills.
Complete crewai/skills/ subsystem with Pydantic SkillFrontmatter (frozen, validated): name regex + directory match, description ≤1024 chars, license, compatibility, allowed-tools, metadata dict.
First-class SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter including a distinctive context mode field (inline/fork/fork_with_context) plus optional agent and model fields, enabling sub-agent dispatch from skills.
SKILL.md with optional YAML frontmatter but schema is minimal — only name and description are parsed; body is free-form and not validated. Looser than Mastra/CrewAI/Agno.
No SKILL.md, no Skill class, no loader anywhere in libs/. The deep-agent-template (separate repo) adds skill-shaped bundles but is not in the monorepo.
No SKILL.md analogue; LlamaPacks are pip-installable code templates, not lightweight markdown skills.
Full agentskills.io spec implementation; SkillMetadata validated (name 1-64 hyphenated, description 1-1024 chars, license, compatibility, user-invocable, metadata). Most complete in this benchmark.

SkillFrontmatter with validated name/description/compatibility/allowed_tools/metadata; aligned with agentskills.io spec per ADR-0021. Marked experimental but full schema implemented in 3269-line _skills.py.

Canonical SKILL.md with frontmatter (name, description, compatibility) plus scripts/references/assets dicts; however, skills are scoped to sandbox/shell execution only — not general workflow templates.
SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter parsed by parseSkillFrontmatter; SkillDescriptor includes scripts/references/assets. Limited to SandboxAgent capability — not available on plain Agent.

No in-tree SKILL.md loader; the in-repo file mentions only the third-party pydantic-ai-skills plugin implementing the agentskills.io standard. AgentSpec YAML is the in-tree analog but is not a SKILL.md.
No SKILL.md concept, no filesystem scanner, no skill primitive in Rig. The word "skill" does not appear as a runtime concept.

SKILL.md with validated YAML frontmatter (name 1-64 lowercase hyphenated, description, optional allowed-tools/metadata/license/compatibility) plus directory-name match check (vended_plugins/skills/skill.py).
SKILL.md with validated YAML frontmatter following Claude Code spec; same name validation and parent-directory match as the Python sibling, in vended-plugins/skills.
No local SKILL.md loader; the uploadSkill helper only relays arbitrary multipart files to Anthropic's /v1/skills endpoint. No frontmatter schema enforced by the SDK.
Exposes list_skills, load_skill, load_skill_resource tools and injects an XML-formatted skill catalog into the system prompt via ProcessRequest. Lazy fetch matches Claude Code's loading model.

Hybrid: skill metadata injected into system prompt as <skills_system> XML block; get_skill_instructions/get_skill_reference/get_skill_script tools auto-registered, with scripts optionally executable via subprocess.
No skill primitive at all — you would BYO an available_skills tool and a run_skill tool yourself.

CLI exposes a Skill tool to the model; metadata listed in system prompt, body loaded on Skill(name=...) tool_use. Observable in SDK as ToolUseBlock(name=Skill). Implementation is in the Node CLI, not the Python SDK.
Same as Python SDK: CLI surfaces skill list in system prompt; model emits tool_use name=Skill to fetch body. Filtered list visible in SDKSystemMessage.skills.

Skills are rendered into the agent's system prompt at construction time via format_skill_context, wrapped in <skill> tags for cache anchoring. There is no skill tool — the body is always in-prompt, and resource files are listed but not auto-fetched.

LLM sees a single skill tool whose description enumerates names+descriptions; calling it loads the skill content either inline, as a fork sub-agent, or as fork_with_context replaying parent history. Distinctive and powerful.
Middleware injects a <skills> block listing available skills into the system prompt and exposes a use_skill(skillName) tool that reads SKILL.md from disk on demand.
No built-in mechanism. BYO via pre_model_hook or a hand-rolled skill_read tool; neither metadata catalog nor skill tool ship out of the box.
N/A — no skill concept in LlamaIndex; closest analog tool_retriever is for dynamic tool retrieval, not markdown skills.

Cleanest tradeoff in benchmark: SkillsProcessor injects only metadata in system prompt; three tools (skill, skill_search with BM25/vector/hybrid, skill_read with line ranges) drive activation. Skill tools bake in requireApproval=false.

Surfaces load_skill, read_skill_resource, and (conditionally) run_skill_script tools to the LLM; scripts can be gated by HITL approval via require_script_approval. Names+descriptions injected in the prompt.

Skill metadata is injected as a ### Skills section in the system prompt; lazy mode adds a synthetic load_skill tool that materializes files into the sandbox. The LLM then reads SKILL.md via the ShellTool — not a per-skill tool call.

Capability.instructions injects an available-skills section into agent instructions; lazy mode adds a load_skill tool that materializes the skill into .agents/. Sandbox-only — no clean tool-call invocation per skill.
In-tree has no invocation mechanism; the third-party pydantic-ai-skills plugin reportedly exposes a skill_read-style tool with progressive disclosure.
No skill primitive; you would put SKILL.md text in the preamble or dynamic_context and let the LLM decide which listed tools to call.

Metadata injected as <available_skills> XML block in the system prompt; LLM activates a skill by calling the skills(skill_name) tool, which returns the full instructions plus a listing of bundled resources.

Hybrid: BeforeInvocationEvent injects <available_skills> block into systemPrompt; registered skills tool accepts skill_name and returns the full instructions body on demand. Activation tracked in agent.appState.

No SDK-side mechanism; uploadSkill returns a providerReference passed via providerOptions.anthropic.skills. Anthropic decides internally when to consult the skill — invisible to the SDK and not a tool call.

Only frontmatters (name+description) are appended to the system prompt; bodies fetched lazily via load_skill. Resources fetched separately via load_skill_resource. Matches Claude Code's model exactly.
Body not in system prompt — only metadata. Documented Progressive Discovery Workflow (browse → load → reference → scripts) explicitly tells the LLM to load instructions only when needed.
N/A — no skill primitive to disclose progressively.
Per ContextUsageResponse.skills showing frontmatter breakdown, only metadata is in the system prompt; body loads on Skill tool invocation. Implementation hidden inside the CLI.
Lazy by default — metadata in system prompt, body fetched on Skill tool use. Options.skills filters the listed set.

Three disclosure levels (METADATA/INSTRUCTIONS/RESOURCES) defined, but Agent.set_skills() promotes Path-discovered skills to INSTRUCTIONS eagerly — body is in the system prompt by default. You can preload at METADATA but body must still be on disk.

Tool description sent to the LLM enumerates names + 1-line descriptions via renderToolDescription; full markdown body is only fetched when the LLM invokes the skill tool. Keeps context small with hundreds of skills.

note: names in prompt, body on call
details: Same model as Claude Code: only names+descriptions are in the <skills> system block; the body is fetched only when the model calls use_skill(skillName).
No first-class concept; BYO designs can implement either eager or lazy patterns via pre_model_hook or BaseStore.
N/A — no skill primitive.

Stateless lazy disclosure: only <available_skills> metadata in system prompt; body fetched via skill tool. If context is compacted, the model calls again. Distinctive search/read tools make staged access first-class.

Skill names + descriptions go into system prompt (~100 tokens per skill); bodies fetched on demand via load_skill, resources via read_skill_resource, scripts via run_skill_script. Per ADR-0021 progressive disclosure design.

Both modes supported — eager materializes everything into sandbox, lazy shows only index and loads on load_skill. Lazy is closest to progressive disclosure but invocation still requires shell-tool to open SKILL.md.
Both eager (skills+from materializes everything) and lazy (lazyFrom uses load_skill tool) supported, matching the Python SDK behavior.
In-tree AgentSpec is eager config, not a runtime catalog. Lazy progressive disclosure is reportedly available only via the third-party pydantic-ai-skills plugin.
N/A — no skill primitive. RAG via dynamic_context is the closest non-skill analog.
Only descriptions + names appear in the system prompt up-front; bodies loaded on demand via the skills tool. Activated skills tracked in agent.state and survive across turns within a session.
Lazy: only metadata in <available_skills> block; body fetched on tool call. Activation tracked in agent.appState[stateKey].activatedSkills.
Anthropic handles loading internally; from the SDK's perspective the skill is an opaque skillId. No SDK-level disclosure control.

No built-in scoping primitive — you compose a Source per tenant (NewMergedSource) or write a tenant-aware Source wrapper reading ctx. Toolset Source is set at construction time, so per-request scoping requires custom code.
Skills object is constructed once at Agent construction; no Skills(filter=lambda run_context:) hook. You either build a callable factory for agent.tools or instantiate per-tenant agents.
N/A — no skill primitive.

No programmatic per-tenant API. options.skills is a context filter, not a sandbox — files remain readable via Read/Bash. Per-tenant requires materializing tenants/<tid>/.claude/skills/ with cwd swap, plus filesystem hygiene work.
Same gap as Python SDK. Either materialize per-tenant .claude/skills/ trees or pass a whitelist via Options.skills. No tenantId → skills mapping API.
Scoping is by agent construction time + filesystem path. No Agent.set_active_skills mid-run. Per-tenant agents with different Path arguments are the standard pattern.

Backend interface gets ctx on every List/Get, so tenant filtering from ctx values is straightforward — you implement a tenantBackend wrapper. No first-class scope field in FrontMatter; metadata is BYO.
SkillPaths can be passed per Generate() call, so each request can use tenant-specific paths via fmt.Sprintf-style composition. Practical but requires the host to assemble paths from tenant context.
BYO via BaseStore namespace tuples — practical but no built-in skill scope primitive.
N/A — no skill primitive.
First-class: SkillsResolver is a function (ctx) => string[] reading requestContext to return tenant-specific paths. Cleanest scoping primitive in the benchmark.

Not first-class per-request, but composable: AggregatingSkillsSource + FilteringSkillsSource + predicate over frontmatter metadata gives tenant filtering. You build a SkillsProvider per tenant or compose via predicate.
Per-agent at construction time only — no dynamic is_enabled callable for skills like there is for tools. You build per-tenant Agent instances or use agent.clone(tools=[...]).
Different defaultManifest per SandboxAgent or override via options.sandbox.manifestPatch. No built-in tenant-aware skill catalog — you assemble the manifest from runContext yourself.

Dynamic capabilities allow a function ctx → AbstractCapability | None that runs once per run, returning a tenant-resolved capability. First-class scoping primitive, though caveats around durable execution apply.
N/A — no skill primitive.
Not first-class. Either build one AgentSkills instance per tenant, or mutate plugin.set_available_skills([...]) — but mutation affects all agents sharing the plugin instance.
Per-Agent: the plugin is attached to one agent and all invocations see the same catalog. setAvailableSkills exists for runtime swap but no built-in invocationState-driven filtering.
BYO entirely — track skillId ↔ tenant in your DB and conditionally pass different providerOptions.anthropic.skills per runtimeContext.

SKILL.md body can reference resources fetched via load_skill_resource (references/, assets/, scripts/). No @include other-skill directive; composition with other skills is whatever the LLM decides in prose.

Scripts and references bundled in the folder are first-class and accessible via get_skill_reference / get_skill_script (the latter can execute scripts via subprocess). No imports: [other-skill] directive in frontmatter.
N/A.

Cross-skill references via skill bodies, plugins that bundle multiple skills (SdkPluginConfig), and AgentDefinition.skills scoping which skills a sub-agent sees. Programmatic composition primitives are BYO at SDK level.

Can reference other skills via plugin-qualified names (<plugin>:skill-name), call sub-agents from skill markdown (LLM invokes Agent tool), and pull bundled assets via Read/Bash on relative paths inside the skill directory.

Skills bundle scripts/references/assets alongside SKILL.md; the catalog of resource files is injected at RESOURCES disclosure level. Skills cannot reference each other (no include:) and cannot call sub-agents directly. allowed-tools is documentation-only, not enforced.

Most powerful composition in benchmark: fork-mode skills spawn sub-agents that themselves have tools/sub-agents/skills (full recursion). Skill BaseDirectory is passed to the sub-agent so scripts/templates can be bundled. Skills can call other skills if the sub-agent has the skill middleware.
Skill body can reference other skills by name in prose; the model decides whether to follow. No includes: directive, no bundled references/scripts/assets — only the SKILL.md is read.
BYO entirely.
N/A.

Bundled references/scripts/assets read on demand via skill_read with line-range support and binary detection. Tool surface (skill, skill_search, skill_read) makes resource access lazy and ergonomic. Skills don't directly invoke sub-agents — delegation is via prose.

Resources (references/, assets/) fetched lazily via read_skill_resource; scripts (scripts/*.py) executed through pluggable SkillScriptRunner with optional HITL approval gating via require_script_approval. No extends: cross-skill mechanism.

Skill model has first-class scripts/references/assets fields with progressive-disclosure prompts telling the LLM to open scripts/ rather than retype code and reuse assets/. Skills do not cross-reference; chaining is text-driven.

SkillDescriptor includes scripts/references/assets bundles; injected instructions explicitly direct the model to load specific files only when needed. Lazy loader allows requesting another skill at runtime but no first-class skill-to-skill link.

Capabilities compose via CombinedCapability with ordering and overlap; a capability ships its own toolset/hooks/instructions. Skill-to-skill includes and bundled-asset directories are not first-class; AgentSpec references filesystem paths without enforcing layout.
N/A — no skill primitive.

Bundled resources in scripts/, references/, assets/ subdirs are listed in the activation response (max 20 files by default). Skills don't directly reference other skills, but activated instructions can tell the LLM to call the skills tool again — text-driven chaining.

Ancillary files in scripts/, references/, assets/ bundled alongside SKILL.md; activation response includes a listing capped at maxResourceFiles (default 20). Skills cannot directly reference other skills or call sub-agents.
N/A — Anthropic bundles arbitrary multipart files but the SDK has no composition rules or knowledge of bundle contents.

Agents-as-tools (`tool/agenttool`), workflow agents (parallel/sequential/loop), and LLM-emitted `transfer_to_agent` handoff are all first-class. Static `SubAgents []Agent` registration plus a YAML config path via `internal/configurable`. Covers both LLM-driven and deterministic orchestration.

`Team` is itself an agent-like object with `members` and auto-generated `delegate_task_to_member(s)` / `forward_task_to_member` tools selected by mode. Four modes (coordinate/route/broadcast/tasks). Sub-agents are agents-as-tools but the harness handles plumbing.

No `SubAgent`, `handoff`, or `delegate`. You publish a `Task` to a `Topic` on the shared runtime and listen for `TaskComplete` events. No agent-as-tool wrapper exists; you would write your own `ToolRuntime` impl. Multi-agent coordination is implicit only.

CLI ships a built-in `Task` tool the parent LLM calls to delegate to a registered sub-agent. Sub-agent runs its own loop in the CLI subprocess. Configured via `AgentDefinition` inline or `.claude/agents/<name>.md` markdown. First-class with rich telemetry.

CLI's built-in `Agent` tool (renamed from `Task` in 0.3.142) dispatches sub-agents with their own model context. Registered programmatically via `Options.agents` or markdown files at `~/.claude/agents/{name}.md`. First-class with rich `AgentOutput` schema.

Two awkward mechanisms: hierarchical `Crew` with `DelegateWorkTool` lets a manager LLM pick coworkers, or `Flow` with `@start/@listen/@router` decorators for explicit invocation. Plus A2A protocol for cross-org. No first-class agent-as-tool primitive; you assemble fan-out yourself.

Three first-class mechanisms: `SetSubAgents` for transfer handoffs with `transfer_to_agent` tool, `NewAgentTool` for agents-as-tools, and `NewSequentialAgent`/`NewParallelAgent`/`NewLoopAgent` workflows. Plus prebuilt patterns (supervisor, deep, planexecute). Comprehensive.

No `SubAgent`, `handoff`, or `delegate` primitive. Idiomatic pattern is to define a tool whose `execute` calls `genkit.Generate(...)` with a different prompt. No agent registry, no markdown file format. BYO.

Two patterns built on subgraphs: subgraph as node (`parent.add_node("research", compiled_subgraph)`) or subgraph wrapped as tool. No first-class `SubAgent` primitive. `langgraph-supervisor` (third-party) packages the agent-as-tool variant. Sub-agents are static at graph compile time.

First-class `AgentWorkflow` with `can_handoff_to` and auto-generated `handoff(to_agent, reason)` tool, plus the explicit agents-as-tools pattern via `FunctionTool` wrapping. Two complementary first-class invocation paths.

Sub-agents are a first-class config field on `Agent` (`agents?: DynamicArgument<Record<string, SubAgent>>`) and at runtime are exposed to the parent LLM as synthesized `agent-<name>` tools via `listAgentTools()`. Three forms: full `Agent` instances, `SubAgent` interface, network mode.

Two mechanisms: Python `agent.as_tool()` wraps any agent as a `FunctionTool`, and .NET `SubAgentsProvider` exposes six tools (`StartTask`, `WaitForFirstCompletion`, etc.) for concurrent sub-task management. Cross-runtime feature parity is uneven (provider is .NET-only).

Two first-class mechanisms: `Agent.as_tool(tool_name, tool_description, ...)` for agents-as-tools and `Handoff[TContext, TAgent]` for control transfer. Both first-class with `HandoffInputFilter` for context redaction. Clean dual model.

Both `Agent.handoffs: (Agent | Handoff)[]` for synthesized `transfer_to_<agent>` transfer and `Agent.asTool({...})` for agents-as-tools. Symmetric with Python SDK. Linked back via `RunAgentUpdatedStreamEvent` or `tool_use_id`.

'Agent delegation' = the parent agent has a `@tool` whose body calls `await child_agent.run(...)`. No `Task` or `Swarm` analog in core. Sub-agents are ordinary `Agent` instances constructed at module scope; tools call them at runtime.

`Agent<M>` implements `Tool` directly; `parent_agent.tool(child_agent)` registers the sub-agent under its name. The LLM invokes it via a normal tool call. Single mechanism, but it is built into the type system and works cleanly.

`agent.as_tool()` for agents-as-tools, plus first-class orchestrators in `multiagent/`: `Graph` for deterministic DAGs, `Swarm` for collaborative teams with shared context and handoffs, and `A2AServer` for cross-process. Comprehensive.

Three patterns all first-class: `agent.asTool()` (passing `Agent` in `tools:[]` auto-wraps), `Graph` (deterministic DAG with `maxConcurrency`), `Swarm` (model-driven handoff via `HandoffResult`). Mirrors Python SDK.

No `subAgent`, `handoff`, `delegate`, `Crew`, or `Swarm` primitive in `packages/ai/src/`. The SDK examples implicitly endorse agents-as-tools: wrap a child `ToolLoopAgent.generate(...)` inside a `tool({...execute})`. No registry, no automatic linkage.

`parallelagent` uses `errgroup` with one goroutine per sub-agent. `Flow.handleFunctionCalls` runs agent-tools in parallel goroutines when the LLM emits multiple tool calls. Two complementary parallel paths.

`delegate_task_to_members` iterates members sequentially in sync. `adelegate_task_to_members` uses `asyncio.gather` to fan-out in async. Concurrent execution requires `await team.arun(...)` and async-capable model.

Each actor processes a published message in its own tokio task, so subscribers run in parallel after the publish loop. `SingleThreadedRuntime::handle_publish_message` iterates subscribers sequentially for ordering, but each subscriber runs concurrently. Parallelism is structural, not opt-in.

CLI's `Task` tool supports parallel sub-agent fan-out natively. `_SubagentContextMixin` provides `agent_id`/`agent_type` so hooks can attribute interleaved tool-lifecycle events. `background: bool` and `stop_task(task_id)` give explicit fire-and-forget control.

Multiple `Agent` tool_use blocks in one assistant turn run concurrently; `PostToolBatch` fires once after all resolve. Background sub-agents via `AgentDefinition.background: true` or `AgentInput.run_in_background: true`; polling via `TaskOutputInput.block`. Best-in-class.

Sequential by default (`Process.sequential`); hierarchical manager picks one delegate at a time. `Task.async_execution=True` allows parallel tasks via `Future`. Crucially, native tool calls in the executor execute **first tool only per turn** — framework opinionates against parallel tool execution. Fan-out requires hand-rolled Flow + `asyncio.gather`.

`runParallel` uses `sync.WaitGroup` with one goroutine per sub-agent. Plus `ToolsNode` runs tool calls in parallel goroutines by default, so an LLM emitting N agent-tool calls in one assistant message gets N parallel sub-agent runs. Two parallel paths.

Tool dispatch fans out via goroutines by default (`go/ai/generate.go:957-999`); if the parent LLM emits N tool calls, each sub-agent invocation runs concurrently. Each goroutine inherits parent's ctx. No parent-level rate limit or pool.

`Send` API enables parallel fan-out: `add_conditional_edges(START, lambda s: [Send("persona", {...}) for p in ...])`. `create_react_agent v2` tools node uses this pattern. Each `Send` task submits to the executor and futures await. Add_edge graphs serial by default.

`AgentWorkflow` is serial (one agent active). Parallel sub-agents via agents-as-tools: parent LLM emits multiple tool calls, `parse_agent_output` fans them out via `ctx.send_event(ToolCall(...))`, runtime executes in parallel, `ctx.collect_events(...)` fans them back in.

Sub-agent invocations are tool calls, going through `foreach(toolCallStep, { concurrency })`. Default `toolCallConcurrency = 10`. Drops to 1 if any tool/sub-agent in the active set has `requireApproval` or `suspendSchema` (deterministic suspension).

`SubAgentsProvider` is fully concurrent: `StartTask` is non-blocking, `WaitForFirstCompletion` blocks until any of a list completes; parallelism via `Task.Run` in `SubAgents_StartTask`. For Python `as_tool()`, parallelism depends on LLM emitting multiple tool calls in one turn — `_execute_function_calls` is sequential in code.

Serial by default for programmatic fan-out (you write `asyncio.gather(Runner.run(...))` yourself). When LLM emits multiple parallel tool calls in one turn, `execute_function_tool_calls` dispatches them concurrently, bounded by `RunConfig.tool_execution.max_function_tool_concurrency`. No `swarm()` or `fan_out()` helper.

`Agent.asTool` invocations issued in a single turn dispatch in parallel up to `toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency` (`Promise.all` across the tool-call array in `runner/toolExecution.ts`). Handoffs are sequential by design.

Whatever you write. Parallelism = `asyncio.gather(child_a.run(...), child_b.run(...))` inside the parent tool. No built-in `Promise.all` wrapper, no `WaitGroup` analog inside the framework. Manual fan-out only.

Parent loop uses `buffer_unordered(self.concurrency)`, so multiple tool calls in a single turn run in parallel up to the configured concurrency. Default `concurrency = 1` (sequential); must opt in via `.with_tool_concurrency(N)`.

`ConcurrentToolExecutor` creates an `asyncio.Task` per tool call and awaits them concurrently within a single LLM cycle. `Graph` runs DAG layers concurrently with `asyncio.gather` across nodes with satisfied dependencies. Swarm is sequential by handoff.

`agent.asTool()` calls run in parallel by default since parent uses `toolExecutor: 'concurrent'` with a `Promise.race`-driven scheduler. `Graph` schedules ready nodes up to `maxConcurrency: Infinity` with AND-semantics on edges. Swarm sequential.

Serial if you `await`, parallel if you `Promise.all`. Within a single step multiple tool calls are already parallel inside the parent loop, but the fan-out point is in your tool body, not in the SDK. No built-in concurrency limits.

`agent.Config.SubAgents` is set at construction and immutable. LLM cannot author a new sub-agent on the fly. You can build an agent factory in Go code and ask LLM for parameters, but `agent.New(...)` must be called in Go, not by the LLM.

Members must be pre-registered. The parent LLM cannot author a new sub-agent on the fly. `members` can be a `Callable[..., List]` factory for per-request resolution — but this is host-controlled, not LLM-driven.

Configs are static, compile-time Rust types with `#[agent(name=..., description=..., tools=[...])]` macro. The parent LLM cannot generate a sub-agent config on the fly. No runtime registration path at all.

`AgentDefinition` is a dataclass you can build at request time per-tenant. No requirement that the dict be statically declared at boot. The parent LLM cannot itself generate a new `AgentDefinition` mid-run, but the Python harness can decide per-request which agents to register on `ClaudeAgentOptions.agents`.

Configs must be statically registered at session start (via `Options.agents` or on disk). The parent LLM cannot generate a new sub-agent config on the fly — it can only choose `subagent_type` from registered agents. Deliberate Claude Code design.

Sub-agents must be statically registered (in code, YAML, or AMP). The closest is `DelegateWorkTool` letting the LLM pick among pre-registered coworkers and supply a task + context — but it doesn't create new agents. AMP allows fetching JSON configs from `app.crewai.com` at boot, not from LLM.

Configs are static at the Go struct level. The closest workaround is the `taskTool` pattern in `prebuilt/deep` where the LLM picks a `subagent_type` from a fixed registry and supplies free-text `description`, but the sub-agent itself is pre-registered.

Configurations are inlined per call in Go code (you write Go that calls `genkit.Generate` with the persona's system prompt). The parent LLM cannot generate a sub-agent config; it can only call a tool that accepts a free-form prompt and forwards it to a `Generate` call you wrote.

Parent LLM cannot dynamically construct a 'new sub-agent with this system prompt and these tools' mid-run. Closest workaround is dynamic-model selection inside an existing sub-agent (`chat_agent_executor.py:325-356`). Sub-agents are statically registered at parent graph compile time.
Not first-class. You can build a `FunctionAgent` dynamically inside a tool, but there's no markdown-loader analogue to Claude's `Task` tool. Host code, not LLM, owns construction.

Configs are statically registered or returned by the `DynamicArgument` resolver at the start of the run. The LLM picks an existing `agent-<name>` tool but CAN pass additional `instructions`, `maxSteps`, `threadId`, `resourceId` to it; the wrapper merges those onto the sub-agent's defaults — partial runtime customization.

Parent LLM cannot create a brand-new sub-agent with custom system prompt at runtime. Sub-agents must be registered ahead of time. Workaround: implement a custom tool that constructs an `Agent` from a dict and invokes it (BYO).

Sub-agent configs are static Python objects. The parent LLM cannot synthesize a `system_prompt` for a fresh sub-agent at runtime. You could implement it yourself by giving the parent a tool that constructs an `Agent` from arguments and runs it, but that's BYO.

Sub-agents are statically declared TypeScript at module load. You cannot have the parent LLM generate a fresh `system prompt + tools` and spawn a child at runtime. Closest: parameterize via `Agent.asTool({ parameters, inputBuilder })` so the parent passes structured input that influences sub-agent behavior, but the sub-agent code itself is fixed.

Not directly. A capability factory can synthesize an agent at run time from `ctx`, but there is no built-in 'let the parent LLM author a sub-agent spec' primitive. Parent's tools can call `Agent.from_spec(dict)` if you wire it that way.
Sub-agents are statically registered Rust structs built via `AgentBuilder`. The parent LLM cannot dynamically generate a sub-agent's preamble or toolset. No runtime registration path.

Not natively. The parent LLM can call a tool that itself constructs a new `Agent` (`strands-agents-tools` provides `use_agent.py` for this), but there is no 'generate a sub-agent description on the fly' primitive baked into the loop.
Not supported. Sub-agent configs are statically constructed in code. A `Swarm` route is dynamic at runtime (LLM picks `agentId`), but the set of agents is fixed at swarm construction.

No native support. You can write a meta-tool whose `execute` body itself instantiates a `ToolLoopAgent` from arguments the LLM provides — but the SDK has no opinion on this and no telemetry/streaming integration.

Each sub-agent invocation gets a new `InvocationContext` with its own `Branch`. Shared `session.Session` but `Branch` field scopes which history each sub-agent sees when `ContentsRequestProcessor` filters events. Agent-tool isolation is stronger: brand new `InMemoryService` for the sub-agent. Logically isolated, physically shared storage.

Each member call passes a copy of `run_context.session_state` so member mutations to `session_state` don't bleed back unless the leader explicitly merges. Member knowledge filters fall back to the leader's `run_context.knowledge_filters` if member has no knowledge. All members share the same `session_id`.

Each agent has its own `BaseAgent` with its own `memory`, `tools`, and `Context`. Parent's memory is not shared. Data passed via `Task::prompt` you publish; the parent's chat history is not. Isolation enforced by `BaseAgent` ownership of `Arc<Mutex<Box<dyn MemoryProvider>>>` and absence of shared mutable state.

Each sub-agent has its own transcript at `<projects_dir>/<project_key>/<session_id>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl`. Parent does not see sub-agent's internal turns; only the final summary string returned by `Task`. Sub-agent's system prompt is its own (`AgentDefinition.prompt`); parent context not inherited.

Sub-agent starts fresh. It does NOT see the parent's context — only its own system prompt, its own `initialPrompt`, and its own tool catalog. Sub-agent transcripts persist separately under `<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl`. Parent receives only final result or, with `forwardSubagentText: true`, intermediate text.

Each `Agent` has its own `executor.messages` list — agents inside the same `Crew` do not share message history unless wired through `context` in `Task.execute_sync(agent, context, tools)`. A delegated coworker via `DelegateWorkTool` receives only the `task` and `context` strings the manager LLM provided.

Parallel branches fork `runContext` via `forkRunCtx`, creating per-lane `runSession` that shares Values + valuesMtx with the parent but has its own `LaneEvents`. AgentTool keeps session Values shared via `withSharedParentSession`. Transfer destinations inherit the same `runContext`. `ClearRunCtx(ctx)` available for explicit isolation.

Sub-agent's `Generate(...)` has its own `Messages` (whatever the parent's tool function passes in); parent's message history is NOT automatically inherited. The `context.Context` is inherited so `ActionContext` flows through.

Not enforced — depends on state schema design. Same `state_schema` → subgraph sees parent's full messages (shared scratchpad). Own `state_schema` → parent state invisible except via explicit channel mapping at the node boundary. `Command(graph=Command.PARENT, ...)` lets subgraph write back to parent.
Each sub-agent invocation via `.run(...)` gets its own `Context` (default) — fresh memory, fresh state. You can pass `ctx=parent_ctx` to share state explicitly.

Sub-agent gets a sanitized copy of parent's message history via `stripParentToolParts` (removes parent's `tool-call` and `tool` messages because the sub-agent doesn't have those tools registered). Parent's `MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY`/`MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY` are cleared so it writes to its own isolated thread. If sub-agent has no own memory, parent's is injected.

`as_tool(propagate_session=False)`: sub-agent gets a fresh session — context isolated. `as_tool(propagate_session=True)`: parent's session is forwarded; they share state. `SubAgentsProvider`: each sub-task runs in its own session by default. Explicit, configurable isolation.

Sub-agent gets a fresh `ToolContext` derived from the parent's `RunContextWrapper`. Sub-agent does NOT see the parent's conversation history; it only sees the input string the parent generated (or structured `parameters` Pydantic model). Approvals propagate (parent and sub-agent share `_approvals`). Handoffs are the opposite: full history flows by default, redacted via `HandoffInputFilter`.

Nested `Agent.asTool` runs **share** parent's `RunContext.context`, approvals, and usage via `_cloneSharedState`. The `toolInput` on the fork is the structured input that triggered the nested run. No isolation by default — useful if children should write back to a shared todo list, dangerous if you want strict separation.
By default each `agent.run(...)` gets a fresh `RunContext` and an empty `message_history` — full isolation. To share, pass `message_history=ctx.messages` or pass shared `deps`/`usage` explicitly.

Sub-agent starts with its own `Vec<Message>` (just `args.prompt`) — the parent's history is not passed through. Enforced at `agent/tool.rs:43-45` (`self.prompt(args.prompt).await` builds a fresh `PromptRequest`). Strict, by construction.

`as_tool(preserve_context=False)` (default) snapshots child's initial `messages` and `state` at construction and `_reset_agent_state()` resets them before every invocation. `preserve_context=True` keeps the child's conversation across calls (incompatible with child `session_manager`). `GraphNode.reset_executor_state()` follows the same pattern.

`AgentAsTool.preserveContext: false` (default): sub-agent reloads its initial snapshot before each call — fresh conversation every time. `true`: sub-agent retains messages across calls. The sub-agent does NOT see the parent's `agent.messages` either way; only the tool's `input` string crosses the boundary.
Each child `ToolLoopAgent.generate({ messages })` starts with whatever messages you give it. No automatic parent-context inheritance, no automatic redaction. You own isolation entirely.

Agents-as-tools: sub-agent runs in new in-memory session, last text-bearing event's text returned as `{"result": outputText}`, parsed against `OutputSchema` if set, linked via tool name. Workflow agents: events stream into parent's event stream. Agent transfer: new agent's events stream directly into the original `runner.Run` stream.
