Each member run produces a `RunOutput` (or `TeamRunOutput`) that gets re-injected as a tool result into the leader's loop. Member runs are linked to the parent via `parent_run_id`. Four modes (coordinate/route/broadcast/tasks) shape how output flows back.

Sub-agent output reaches the parent only via `Event::TaskComplete{sub_id, actor_name, result}` broadcast through runtime's event stream. Parent must track submission_ids, filter incoming events, and assemble results manually. No linkage back to a parent `tool_use_id` because sub-agents are not modelled as tool calls.

Parent LLM calls `Task` tool; sub-agent runs to completion; result returns as `ToolResultBlock` (text summary) on the next user message. Parent sees a single result string per sub-agent call. Harness gets per-task progress/usage telemetry via `TaskStartedMessage`/`TaskProgressMessage`/`TaskNotificationMessage`.

Parent sees sub-agent result as a regular `tool_result` block linked by `tool_use_id`. Default emits only `tool_use`/`tool_result`; `forwardSubagentText: true` forwards sub-agent assistant text and thinking as nested `SDKAssistantMessage` with `parent_tool_use_id`. `AgentOutput` schema includes `agentId`, `content`, `totalToolUseCount`, `totalDurationMs`, `usage`, `toolStats`.

For `Crew` delegation: delegating LLM gets a single string back ('the coworker's task output'), wrapped in the standard tool-result message. For `Flow`: each `@listen` method returns a Python value; downstream methods receive it as an argument. No `parent_tool_use_id` linkage by default. A2A events carry parent IDs but only for A2A delegation.

Single result string (last assistant message content) via `agentTool.InvokableRun`. Optionally all sub-agent events streamed up to parent's iterator via `ToolsConfig.EmitInternalEvents: true` — useful for UI streaming, NOT recorded in parent's session. Linked back to parent's `tool_use.id` via the `tool_call_id`.

Parent receives a single `ToolResponse.Output` (text or structured output). Parent does not see sub-agent's intermediate tool calls or token stream by default — those are child spans in tracing but not surfaced. Linkage via `ToolRequest.Ref` ↔ `ToolResponse.Ref`.

Pattern A (subgraph as node): sub-agent's final state is the node's writes; parent's channel reducer merges them. Shared `messages` channel with `add_messages` → sub-agent's messages append; isolated channels → declare a different channel name and write only a summary. Pattern B (subgraph as tool): output is `ToolMessage.content` (string), linked back via `tool_call_id`.

For `AgentWorkflow`: handoff returns a string from the `handoff` tool, workflow switches `current_agent_name`. Final `StopEvent.result` is an `AgentOutput`. For agents-as-tools: sub-agent's `.run(...)` is awaited; result string returned to parent LLM as normal tool result. Linked via `tool_id`.

Synthesized `agent-<name>` tool returns `{text, subAgentThreadId, subAgentResourceId, subAgentToolResults}`. By default `toModelOutput` strips everything except `text`, but `delegation.includeSubAgentToolResultsInModelContext = true` opts in to richer context. Sub-agent chunks stream to parent via `fullStream` as nested `agent-execution-event-*`. Linked via synthesized tool call.

`as_tool`: parent receives a string (final response text) as `function_result` content; wrapping function awaits `stream.get_final_response()`. If `stream_callback` is set, intermediate updates observable. Linked via `FunctionCallContent.call_id`. `SubAgentsProvider`: results pulled from `SubAgents_GetTaskResults`; state lives in `SubAgentState`/`SubAgentRuntimeState`.

Agents-as-tools: nested agent's `final_output` returned as tool result string; `custom_output_extractor` callback can rewrite. `on_stream` callback re-emits nested stream events to parent stream. Handoffs: new agent receives full conversation history (possibly filtered by `HandoffInputFilter`) and continues the same `RunResult`. Linked via `call_id` (`AgentToolInvocation`).

`asTool`: nested agent's final output becomes the function tool result (string by default, customizable via `customOutputExtractor`). Linked via `tool_use_id` of the wrapping `FunctionCallItem`. Full nested `RunResult` exposed on `FunctionToolResult.agentRunResult`. Handoffs: output is new agent's final output, linked via `RunAgentUpdatedStreamEvent`.

The child returns an `AgentRunResult[OutputDataT]`; the parent tool returns its `.output` (or a string summary). Linkage to parent `tool_use_id` is implicit through the parent's `ToolCallPart`/`ToolReturnPart` pair.
Parent receives the sub-agent's final `String` (the `Tool::Output`) as a regular tool result, bound to the parent's `tool_call_id`. No streaming events bubble up — parent only sees terminal text.

`_AgentAsTool.stream` yields `AgentAsToolStreamEvent` for every intermediate event from child's `stream_async`, then a `ToolInterruptEvent` (HITL) or `ToolResultEvent` with `content=[{"text": str(result)}]` or structured `{"json": ...}`. Linkage via `tool_use_id`. Both intermediate and final visible.

`agent.asTool()` returns a `ToolResultBlock` with either the sub-agent's structured output (`JsonBlock`) or `TextBlock` of `result.toString()`. Linked via `tool_use_id`. `Graph`/`Swarm` aggregate node results into `MultiAgentResult` streamed via `MultiAgentStreamEvent` (`NodeResultEvent`, `MultiAgentHandoffEvent`).

Whatever the tool returns. To stream sub-agent results back through the parent's UI stream, use `createUIMessageStream({execute: ({writer}) => writer.merge(subAgent.stream(...).toUIMessageStream({sendStart: false}))})`. No automatic `tool_use_id` correlation between parent and child — you build that yourself.

Each sub-agent's `BeforeAgentCallback`/`AfterAgentCallback` fires, and any events the sub-agent emits are forwarded into the parent's iterator. There is no dedicated 'sub-agent started/completed' lifecycle event type — you infer it from `Author` and `Branch` changes on consecutive events.

`TeamRunEvent` enum emits `MemberDelegationStarted`, `MemberDelegationCompleted`, and propagates member `RunStarted`/`ToolCallStarted`/`RunCompleted` upward with `parent_run_id` set on each frame. Full lifecycle visibility.

Parent gets `TaskStarted`, `TurnStarted/Completed`, `ToolCallRequested/Completed`, `TaskComplete` from the child agent's event stream because all actors share the runtime's single broadcast channel. To filter, match on `actor_id` or `actor_name` and `sub_id`. Manual filtering required.

`TaskStartedMessage` / `TaskProgressMessage` / `TaskNotificationMessage` (added 0.1.46) carry per-task `task_id`, `description`, `usage`, `status`. Combined with `SubagentStart`/`SubagentStop` hooks, parent can observe sub-agent lifecycle in flight. Comprehensive.

`SubagentStart` hook, `SubagentStop` hook, `TaskCreated`/`TaskCompleted` hooks. `SDKTaskStartedMessage`, `SDKTaskProgressMessage` (with summary if `agentProgressSummaries: true`), `SDKTaskUpdatedMessage`, `SDKTaskNotificationMessage` emitted on parent's stream so UI can render sub-agent status.

`AgentExecutionStartedEvent`/`Completed`/`Error` fire per agent execution. For A2A delegation, ~30 events: `A2ADelegationStartedEvent`, `A2AStreamingChunkEvent`, etc. Good coverage but limited to in-Crew + A2A; not as integrated for Flow patterns.

`callbacks.Handler.OnStart`/`OnEnd` fire once per agent boundary (parent + each sub-agent). `RunInfo.Component = ComponentOfAgent` and `RunInfo.Type = ChatModel/Sequential/Parallel/Loop/Supervisor` distinguishes types. Sub-agent per-message/per-tool-call events are NOT in parent iterator by default — opt in via `ToolsConfig.EmitInternalEvents: true`.

Sub-agent lifecycle is observable via tracing, not via the parent's stream. OTel spans are nested: parent generate-span → tool-span → sub-agent generate-span → sub-agent's tools. Parent's SSE stream just shows one `toolResponse` chunk for sub-agent's final answer.

Yes via `stream_mode="tasks"`. Each subgraph dispatch emits a `TasksStreamPart` start frame and a `TasksResultStreamPart` finish frame. With `subgraphs=True` on `graph.stream(...)`, parent stream sees `(ns, mode, data)` triples where `ns` identifies the subgraph.
When `AgentWorkflow` hands off, `AgentInput`/`AgentOutput`/`AgentStream` events tagged with the new `current_agent_name` are emitted on the stream. Parent stream sees each sub-agent's tokens.

`delegation.onDelegationStart(ctx)` runs before sub-agent fires; returns `{proceed?, rejectionReason?, modifiedPrompt?, modifiedInstructions?, modifiedMaxSteps?}`. `delegation.onDelegationComplete(ctx)` runs after, with `bail()` to cancel sibling concurrent delegations. `delegation.messageFilter(ctx)` lets supervisor decide which parent messages to forward. Strong programmatic surface.

`as_tool`: yes if `stream_callback` is provided; otherwise parent only sees the final string. `SubAgentsProvider`: status retrievable via `SubAgents_GetAllTasks`; not a streaming lifecycle. Opt-in and uneven across the two mechanisms.

`on_stream` on `as_tool(...)` callback receives `AgentToolStreamEvent` containing the inner event, the nested `Agent`, and the originating `tool_call`. Lets the parent stream forward sub-agent progress events to its own consumer.
`Agent.asTool({ onStream })` receives every `RunStreamEvent` from the nested run, plus a reference to the `toolCall` that triggered it. Clean opt-in hook for nested stream forwarding.

Parent stream does not auto-include child events. To bubble them, parent's child-calling tool can iterate the child via `child.run_stream_events()` and yield events back (custom code; framework does not auto-merge streams).

Not provided. No 'sub_agent_started'/'sub_agent_completed' event. Parent loop sees only the eventual tool result. You can attach tracing spans inside sub-agent's `prompt()` call to follow it via OTel — but no harness-level lifecycle event.

`AgentAsToolStreamEvent` forwards each child event to the parent stream. For `Graph`/`Swarm`, dedicated events: `MultiAgentNodeStartEvent`, `MultiAgentNodeStopEvent`, `MultiAgentHandoffEvent`, `MultiAgentNodeStreamEvent`, `MultiAgentNodeCancelEvent`, `MultiAgentNodeInterruptEvent`. Comprehensive coverage.

Parent stream sees `ToolStreamUpdateEvent`s whose `event.data` carries sub-agent's `AgentStreamEvent`s (re-wrapped). For `Graph`/`Swarm`: dedicated `BeforeNodeCallEvent`, `AfterNodeCallEvent`, `NodeResultEvent`, `MultiAgentHandoffEvent`. Mirrors Python coverage.

Parent stream has no 'sub-agent started/progress/finished' event category. The child's events live in its `streamText` call and are not surfaced to the parent's stream unless you explicitly `writer.merge(...)`. Entirely BYO.

ADK Go ships `Source` as a thin loader interface plus a `MergedSource` composer; there is no registry layer, no publishing lifecycle, no versioning, no governance. The report explicitly states the abstraction is a loader, not a manager.

Agno has a `Registry` dataclass cataloguing tools/models/dbs/agents/teams in-process and a separate `Components` subsystem that versions configs in the DB with drafts/current/history and HTTP CRUD endpoints. Components are the closest first-class registry, but they only cover component configs, not skills or external resources.
No Registry, no SkillSource, no plugin marketplace, no publish workflow. The only loader is a local MCP TOML config file, which is not a general resource manager.

SDK has no registry, no source abstraction, no publish workflow. The only registry-shaped surface is the `setting_sources` flag (user/project/local) and `options.plugins=[{type:'local',path:...}]`; everything else is BYO scaffolding.

SDK exposes a `plugins: SdkPluginConfig[]` option and reads a Claude Code Settings `marketplaces.autoUpdate` concept, but the only supported plugin `type` is `local`. There is no programmatic registry API; resources are discovered from filesystem paths the CLI scans.

OSS ships only a filesystem skill loader; the closest unified registry is AMP's vendor-locked Agent Repositories accessed via `Agent(from_repository=...)`, which only stores agent configs (not skills or tools). No unified skill+agent+tool registry.

Eino provides three pluggable interfaces (`skill.Backend`, `skill.AgentHub`, `skill.ModelHub`) but only ships a filesystem `Backend`. Each interface is a seam you build a Resource Manager on top of; no registry, no versioning, no publishing.

The only registry is the in-process `*registry.Registry` holding actions for one running process — a runtime concept, not a publishing concept. The per-call `Resource` abstraction is a content-loading utility, not a marketplace.

OSS ships only `BaseStore` (rows-as-resources with namespace tuples) and no source abstraction or publish workflow. LangGraph Platform adds a versioned Assistants API, but that is closed-source and paywalled.
No registry, no source abstraction, no publishing workflow. Tools are loaded from Python imports; LlamaHub is a community directory, not a draft/publish workflow.

Skills have a real resource-manager layer (`VersionedSkillSource`, `CompositeVersionedSkillSource`, blob storage). Stored agents/skills carry `visibility` and `favoriteCount` in storage with FGA/RBAC under `ee/`. No formal draft→active workflow, but otherwise the most complete stack.

Ships `FileSkillsSource`, `InMemorySkillsSource`, `AggregatingSkillsSource`, `FilteringSkillsSource`, `DeduplicatingSkillsSource`, `CachingAgentSkillsSource`. These are loader primitives — there is no draft/active lifecycle, no publish workflow, no RBAC layer above them.

No registry. Closest pieces are `MultiProviderMap` (model routing, not skills) and `LocalDirLazySkillSource` for filesystem skill loading. Sandbox entries can pull a `GitRepo` into a session but only as sandbox content.

No registry, no marketplace; resources are scoped to a `SandboxAgent`'s `manifest.entries`. `localDir`, `localFile`, `gitRepo`, and inline `dir`/`file` entries exist, but composition is per-manifest with no cross-agent registry.
No platform-level registry. `AgentSpec.from_file()` is a single-source loader; `Agent.from_spec()` builds an Agent in memory. No source composition, no publish workflow shipped.

No registry, no source abstraction, no publishing workflow. The only `ToolSet` is an in-process `HashMap<String, ToolType>`; `ToolServerHandle` allows runtime `add_tool`/`remove_tool` but is not a resource manager.

No registry abstraction. The closest is `AgentSkills(skills=[...])` accepting filesystem paths or HTTPS URLs — a thin loader, not a registry. Tools have `ToolRegistry.process_tools` but no versioning or publishing.

`AgentSkills` carries a single in-memory `Map<string, Skill>` populated from filesystem dirs or HTTPS URLs. No marketplace, no versioning, no per-tenant scoping at registration, no draft/active machine.
`customProvider` and `createProviderRegistry` are model-routing registries, not skill/sub-agent/prompt registries. There is no skill source loader, no Git/S3 puller, no Hub.

Ships `FileSystemSource` over any `fs.FS` (so `embed.FS` works) plus a `MergedSource` composer and preload wrappers. Git, OCI, cloud blob storage, Postgres, vendor registries, and HTTP fetch are all BYO via custom `Source` implementations.

`LocalSkills(path)` for filesystem skills; sessions/memories/traces/components live in DB; knowledge content via `Knowledge(contents_db=...)`. Skills themselves do NOT come from Postgres; Git, OCI, S3, HTTP all BYO via custom `SkillLoader`.
Only loader is the local TOML config (`crates/autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/config.rs`) that registers MCP servers. No skill source of any kind; everything else is BYO.
Local filesystem via `cwd` + `.claude/`, `~/.claude/`, and `setting_sources`. `SdkPluginConfig` only supports `type:'local'`. Git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres for skills, HTTP — all BYO.

Skills load from `~/.claude/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, plugin dirs, plus agents/commands directories. Plugins only accept `type:'local'`. MCP HTTP/SSE/WS servers are the only non-filesystem dynamic source, and only for tools, not skills.

Local filesystem for skills via `Agent(skills=[Path('./skills/')])` and YAML `agents.yaml`. `Agent(from_repository=...)` pulls agent configs from AMP over HTTPS (vendor-locked). Skills cannot come from AMP; Git, S3, OCI, Postgres all BYO.
Skill middleware ships only `NewBackendFromFilesystem`. Git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, vendor hub, HTTP fetch are all BYO via custom `skill.Backend`.

Prompts: `WithPromptDir` and `WithPromptFS(embed.FS, …)`. Skills middleware: `Skills{SkillPaths: []string}` filesystem only. Git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres for skills/prompts, HTTP all BYO. Postgres exists for embeddings, not skills.
OSS supports local Python imports and Postgres rows via `BaseStore` (the closest row-as-resource abstraction). No Git/S3/OCI/HTTP loaders for resources. LangGraph Platform Hub is paywalled.
No source abstraction for skills/sub-agents/tools beyond Python imports and `tool_retriever`. No concept of loading a skill from S3/GCS/Git/HTTP.

`LocalFilesystem({basePath})` plus `VersionedSkillSource` backed by `BlobStore` (S3/GCS/R2 adapters). Stored agents/skills via `storage.getStore('agents'|'skills')` with Postgres. Mastra Cloud deployment is a managed registry. Git and HTTP fetch still BYO but coverage is the broadest.

`FileSkillsSource`/`AgentFileSkillsSource`, `InMemorySkillsSource`, `AggregatingSkillsSource`, `FilteringSkillsSource`, `DeduplicatingSkillsSource`, and a caching wrapper exist. No first-class Git, S3/GCS/Azure Blob, OCI, or vendor-managed source; all those require subclassing `SkillsSource`.

`LocalDirLazySkillSource` for filesystem skills. `agents.sandbox.entries.GitRepo` materializes a Git repo into the sandbox — but only into the sandbox, not into the SDK as a skill source. OCI/S3/Postgres/HTTP all BYO.

Manifest entries support `localDir`, `localFile`, inline `dir`/`file`, and notably `gitRepo({repo, ref, subpath})` cloned into the sandbox session. OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, vendor cloud, HTTP fetch are not provided.
`AgentSpec.from_file(path)` and `Agent.from_spec({...})` from a Python dict. MCP servers as toolsets. Git, OCI, S3/GCS/Blob, Postgres, HTTP all BYO.

File `loaders` exist for reading files into prompts but not as a resource registry. `rig-postgres` and `rig-s3vectors` are vector stores, not resource sources. No Git/OCI/managed/HTTP resource loading.
`AgentSkills(skills=['./skills/'])` for filesystem and `Skill.from_url('https://...')` for raw skill content over HTTPS (30s timeout, no caching). No Git, OCI, S3, Postgres, or vendor sources.

`AgentSkills` accepts filesystem dirs (skill dir or parent dir) and HTTPS URLs via `Skill.fromUrl` (naïve 30s `fetch()`, no ETag/cache). No Git, OCI, S3 (only sessions), Postgres, or vendor sources for skills.
SDK provides only model registries (`createProviderRegistry`, `customProvider`). No skill source loader of any kind — local, Git, OCI, S3, Postgres, vendor, HTTP all BYO.

`MergedSource` collects from sources in order; `ListFrontmatters` errors on duplicate skill names rather than override, and lookup is first-wins. Override semantics (tenant-overrides-global by same name) require BYO subtract/fallback wrapper.
`Skills(loaders=[a,b,c])` loads all loaders; on name collision the later loader wins with a warning (`agent_skills.py:42-44`). No declared priority model, no per-tenant override pattern.
No composition mechanism exists; BYO entirely.

`setting_sources` layers `user → project → local` with CLI-defined conflict resolution; SDK doesn't expose precedence configuration. Plugins add another fixed layer via `options.plugins`. Useful but inflexible.

Five-tier Settings cascade (`--settings` > local > project > user > managed), with project winning over user for resource layering. Conflict resolution is by name with later-loaded winning; no programmatic precedence diagram or override knobs.

Skills loader iterates `skills=[Path(...)]` in order and de-duplicates by name; first occurrence wins (`agent/core.py:451`). Not declared as `local > tenant > global`; you order paths yourself. No tenant-overrides-global semantic.
No composition layer ships; you'd write a `layeredBackend` that consults multiple `Backend`s and merges with your own priority rules.

Skills middleware scans `SkillPaths []string` in order and later entries with the same name overwrite earlier ones (via `map[string]skillInfo` mutation in `scanSkills`). For prompts, `WithPromptFS` and `WithPromptDir` are mutually exclusive.
No source abstraction; the BYO pattern is to call `store.search(('skills', tenant_id))` then fall back to `('skills', 'global')`. All composition is hand-rolled on top of `BaseStore`.
No source abstraction exists; composition is fully BYO.

`CompositeVersionedSkillSource` mounts multiple versioned skill trees into a virtual filesystem with declared `local > managed > external` priority (`workspace-skills.ts:207`), plus optional live filesystem fallback. The most explicit composition model in the field.

`AggregatingSkillsSource` + `DeduplicatingSkillsSource` preserves first-occurrence when names clash; `FilteringSkillsSource` applies after aggregation. No declarative `local > tenant > global`; you choose by ordering sources in the aggregator.
No source composition surface (only `LazySkillSource` per-agent). Multi-source priority requires a BYO `LazySkillSource` subclass.
A `SandboxAgent` has one `defaultManifest`; merging is `cloneManifest` plus capability `processManifest`. No `local > tenant > global` cascading across manifests.
Capabilities compose at the Agent level (`CombinedCapability`), but resource sources do not. Multi-source priority is BYO.
No source abstraction; the closest is last-`add_tool`-wins via `HashMap` insertion on `ToolServerHandle`.
`AgentSkills._resolve_skills` does last-write-wins with a logged warning on duplicate name. No priority/fallback configuration.
Sources are processed in order; duplicate name overwrites the earlier one with a warning (`agent-skills.ts:191-194`). No priority/fallback/merge configuration.
No mechanism to stack resource sources; all priority/override logic is BYO in your loader code.
`Frontmatter` has no `version` field; `Compatibility` is a free-text up-to-500-char string with no enforcement. Versioning requires baking a suffix into the directory name or using git commit SHAs.

`Components` subsystem maintains drafts + current + version history per component (`agno_components` definition + `agno_component_configs` versioned configs), with `POST /components/{id}/configs/{version}/set-current` to promote and `DELETE` to retire. Skills themselves only have a descriptive `metadata.version` field.
No versioning for skills/tools; Cargo handles crate versions but per-resource versioning is absent.
CLI version pinned via `_cli_version.py` (`2.1.143`); skill/agent versioning is the file mtime on disk.

Skills/sub-agents in plugins are versioned by whatever Git tag the plugin dir comes from — no semver enforcement by the SDK. CLI itself is pinned to npm version. No content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback API.

Skills have no version field, no content-hash, no rollback. AMP's Agent Repositories support versioning in the dashboard, but `from_repository='...'` has no documented API field for pinning to a version.
Skills are mutable files (or rows in your store); no semver, no content-hash refs, no rollback. Versioning is whatever your custom backend implements.
Skills, prompts, tools are versioned by your source-control / deployment. No semver, no content-hash, no immutable ref system.
OSS has no versioning. LangGraph Platform's Assistants API ships versioned assistants, but Platform is closed-source and paywalled.
Integration packages (PyPI) have semver and changelog; for agent resources (skills/sub-agents/tools) there is no versioning — they live in your codebase.

Per-call versions for sub-agents via `MASTRA_VERSIONS_KEY` (`packages/core/src/request-context/index.ts:44`). `VersionedSkillSource` uses `SkillVersionTree` manifest with content-hashed blob refs, backed by `storage/domains/versioned.ts`. Immutable content-hash refs rather than semver.
Skills have no version field beyond `SkillFrontmatter.compatibility` (free-form text). No semver, no content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback.
`Skill.compatibility: str | None` is an opaque marker not enforced by the SDK. No version field for sub-agents/prompts.
`gitRepo({ ref })` lets you pin a git ref (branch / tag / SHA), which provides git-level immutability. No semver registry, no content-hash addressing beyond git, no rollback primitive shipped.
Per-package via PyPI (semver) and per-spec via your VCS. No content-hash / immutable-ref system in-tree.
No versioning surface for tools or resources.
Skill `metadata.version` is a free-form field the loader does not interpret. Tools have no versioning at all.
Snapshot IDs use UUID v7 (chronological, immutable) for session checkpoints, but skills themselves have no version field that the SDK reads.
No semver, no content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback for skills/sub-agents. AI Gateway can cache model responses provider-side, unrelated.

No draft/active/deprecated/retired lifecycle states. Skills are either in the filesystem the `Source` reads or not. Multi-environment promotion via separate git branches or buckets per env is operational, not API.

Components router exposes `POST /components` to create, `POST /components/{id}/configs` to add a new config version, and `POST /components/{id}/configs/{version}/set-current` to promote (draft → current). No separate staging environment baked in, and skills are not covered.
No publishing workflow exists; BYO entirely.
No publish workflow shipped; promotion is BYO via filesystem layout (e.g., `skills/draft/` vs `skills/active/` directories).
No draft → review → publish → promote pipeline. BYO via per-tenant Git repos, CI publishing to S3, and a sync agent that pulls trees on session start.

OSS has no publishing concept — `git push` is the workflow. AMP Agent Repositories dashboard has draft → published flow; AMP Automations have dev/staging/prod separation via separate deployments + env vars. No formal approval gates documented.
No draft/review/promote/multi-environment workflow. Build with git tags and your own CI.

Variable quality. File tools include line-numbered Read/Edit semantics; code execution tools (e2b/daytona/docker) sandbox executions; knowledge search tools understand filters/citations. Most others are thin wrappers over the underlying vendor SDK.

Thin wrappers over stdlib + a few external SDKs. Useful for getting started but no anchor-matching edits, no line-numbered returns, no event streaming from tools. WASM sandbox and CodeAct executor add value but are runtime primitives rather than tool quality.

note: Claude Code patterns end to end
details: Read returns line numbers and renders images; Edit uses anchor matching; Monitor streams stdout line-by-line as events; Bash integrates with sandbox settings; WebFetch honors network allowlists. Battle-tested in Claude Code itself.

Anchor-string matching with uniqueness validation in Edit; Read prefixes line numbers for downstream Edit; Bash mandates natural-language description for audit; Grep exposes the full ripgrep flag surface (-A/-B/-C/-i/-n); Agent supports isolation: 'worktree'; Skill does lazy body fetch. Genuinely the strongest built-in catalog in the benchmark.

E2B/Daytona sandbox tools encode three lifecycle modes (persistent=False/True/sandbox_id=<existing>) and atexit cleanup hooks. Web-search and most other wrappers are thin with no built-in rate limiting/retries. No anchor-matching Edit, line-numbered Read, or Monitor-style streaming.

Filesystem middleware read_file supports offset/limit and ships a large_tool_result-stash-to-FS pattern; edit_file does single-anchor replace (simpler than Claude Code's Edit). MCP tools are thin wrappers around the underlying SDKs; search tools are thin REST wrappers.

Filesystem middleware is genuinely well-engineered: bounded reads (256 KB chunk, 10 MB max), os.Root symlink-safe sandbox, line numbers on read like Claude Code's Read, internal fileStateCache that returns a stub when the file is unchanged, mtime/size check before overwriting. Surface is tiny but depth is high.
No built-in tools to score in core LangGraph.

Web and file tools are thin wrappers around vendor APIs. No equivalent to Claude Code's Edit (anchor matching), Read (line numbers), or Monitor (line-event streaming). For agent-piloting use cases you would author your own.

skill_read does line-range slicing and binary-file detection; skill_search runs full BM25/vector/hybrid against indexed content. Workspace filesystem primitives are thin but consistent. No Bash/Edit/Read catalog to evaluate beyond skills.

LocalShellExecutor/DockerShellExecutor have ShellPolicy, environment sanitization, container-user controls, network mode, head-tail buffering — substantially more than thin wrappers. FileAccessProvider mediates through AgentFileStore (filesystem/in-memory backends). TodoProvider persists state; Skills tools mirror agentskills.io spec. Hosted tools are pass-throughs.

ShellTool is the standout — full sandbox configuration model (network policies, container references, inline skill bundles). ApplyPatchTool encodes the Codex apply-patch protocol with structured operations. ToolSearchTool is a thoughtful lazy-catalog pattern. The hosted tools (WebSearch/FileSearch/CodeInterpreter/ImageGeneration) are thin Responses API pass-throughs.

Hosted tools are thin wrappers that emit HostedTool descriptors; execution is server-side. Sandbox shell capability is more substantive: manages local/container shells, skill bundles, network policies. No Claude-Code-style anchor-matching Edit or Monitor-with-line-events.

WebSearch/WebFetch/ImageGeneration/MCP/ToolSearch capabilities automatically pick a native (provider-side) implementation when the model supports it and fall back to a local Python implementation otherwise. Constraint fields (e.g. allowed_domains) sometimes require native and raise UserError on unsupported models. No coding-agent-style Edit/Read/Monitor by design.
Only ThinkTool ships, and it is a pass-through that echoes the LLM's thought string. Effectively N/A for quality evaluation.

Mixed but generally feature-rich. editor and file_write ship intelligent diff modes; python_repl requires user confirmation; calculator has AST validation; many tools have optional extras for mem0/browser/rss/use_computer. Catalog depth is closer to Claude Code than to thin-wrapper SDKs.

Vended tools are functional but not Claude-Code-grade. file-editor supports common read/write/edit operations but no anchor-matching/uniqueness validation or line-number patterns at the studied commit.
N/A — no SDK-shipped tools to evaluate. Provider-side built-ins (Anthropic web_search/bash, OpenAI code-interpreter) are as good as the upstream provider; the SDK is a thin passthrough.

functiontool.New[TArgs, TResults] uses Go generics; JSON schema is auto-inferred from struct tags via jsonschema reflection. Config exposes InputSchema/OutputSchema overrides, RequireConfirmation, IsLongRunning. Clean enough that defining a tool is roughly 5 lines plus the handler.

The @tool decorator inspects function signature, type hints and docstring (docstring-parser) and builds a Function with JSON schema in Function.parameters. Decorator accepts name, description, strict, instructions, show_result, requires_confirmation, requires_user_input, external_execution, pre_hook/post_hook, cache options. Slightly heavier surface than minimal SDKs.

Requires deriving ToolInput on an input struct, then #[tool(name, description, input)] on a unit struct, then implementing ToolRuntime::execute manually (with serde_json::from_value). Verbose compared with single-decorator Python/TS APIs, but typed end-to-end.

@tool(name, desc, schema) decorator supports dict ({name: type}), TypedDict, raw JSON Schema, or Annotated[type, desc]. Must wrap tools in create_sdk_mcp_server and reference them by MCP namespaced name (mcp__server__tool). Clean but indirect compared with one-step decorators.

tool(name, description, zodShape, handler) factory is ergonomic; must be packaged in createSdkMcpServer and registered under mcpServers; LLM sees the tool as mcp__{server}__{name}. Minor friction from MCP namespacing but the authoring step itself is concise.

Subclass BaseTool with name/description/args_schema (Pydantic), implement _run. Args_schema is auto-derived from _run signature if not provided. Decorator-style @tool('name') is also supported. Rich knobs: result_as_answer, cache_function, max_usage_count via _claim_usage.

utils.InferTool('name', 'desc', func(ctx, *In) (*Out, error)) auto-generates schema from struct tags via eino-contrib/jsonschema. utils.InferOptionableTool, utils.NewTool, and direct InvokableTool implementations are available for more control. Clean Go ergonomic with good defaults.

genkit.DefineTool(g, name, desc, func(ctx, in) (out, error)) is essentially a one-liner. Input schema is inferred from the Go type (string, struct with jsonschema tags) via InferSchemaMap reflection; output schema inferred for multipart tools. WithInputSchema and WithStrictSchema let you override. Minimal authoring surface.

@tool from langchain_core.tools auto-generates JSON schema from function signature + docstring; Pydantic/dataclass arg classes supported; async via async def. BaseTool subclass available for richer control with name/description/_run. Standard LangChain authoring path.

Pass a typed Python function directly; framework wraps it via FunctionTool.from_defaults using create_schema_from_function. Optionally use FunctionTool.from_defaults explicitly to override name/description, set return_direct, add callbacks, or fix partial_params. Idiomatic Python — minimal boilerplate.

createTool({ id, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute }) — concise, typed end to end, JSON schema auto-derived from the Zod schemas. Supports requestContextSchema, suspend payloads, ctx.writer for streaming. First-class TypeScript developer experience.

Python @tool decorator (with optional input_model: type[BaseModel] and approval_mode) is concise. .NET uses AIFunctionFactory.Create on a [Description]-attributed method — minimal boilerplate. Both paths derive JSON schema automatically; .NET infers from C# parameter metadata.

@function_tool decorator inspects the signature and parses the docstring (Griffe-style) to build a strict-mode JSON schema by default. Context-aware tools add RunContextWrapper or ToolContext as the first parameter. Approval-gated tools add needs_approval. Concise and well thought through.

tool({ name, description, parameters: z.object(...), execute }) parses Zod or JSON schema, wires JSON parse/validate, wraps timeouts and error handling, and produces a typed FunctionTool. Concise, fully typed, and integrates with errorFunction for retry semantics.

@agent.tool_plain for context-free tools and @agent.tool for ctx-aware tools. JSON schema is auto-derived from Python type hints and docstrings via FunctionSchema; custom generators are pluggable. Among the cleanest authoring APIs in the benchmark.

Default path implements the Tool trait with NAME, Args, Output, Error associated types and manually authors a serde_json::json!({}) schema inside definition(). A #[tool_macro] proc-macro exists behind the derive feature but the example documented in the report is verbose by today's SDK standards.

@tool decorator extracts name, description, and JSON schema from the function signature, docstring, and type hints (Pydantic-backed via create_model). For framework context add tool_context: ToolContext and decorate with @tool(context=True). Class-based AgentTool subclass is also supported.

tool({ name, description, inputSchema, callback }) accepts either a Zod schema (typed + validated) or a raw JSON schema (no runtime validation). Tool subclass available for fully custom streaming behaviour. Concise but JSON-schema mode loses type safety.

tool({ description, inputSchema, execute }) is the basic shape; surface also includes contextSchema, onInputStart/onInputDelta/onInputAvailable, toModelOutput, needsApproval, outputSchema. Supports Zod 3 and Zod 4. Fully typed and the most ergonomically scoped tool API across the JS SDKs.

TArgs/TResults are Go generics; LLM's map[string]any args are converted to TArgs via typeutil.ConvertToWithJSONSchema (functiontool.go:196-199). Conversion failure returns ErrInvalidArgument which flows through OnToolErrorCallback. Tools that need richer validation must add it inline; the retryandreflect plugin is the opt-in retry primitive.

Pydantic-driven schemas from type hints. On invalid args the model adapter raises AgentRunException, which the framework captures as a ToolCallErrorEvent and feeds back to the LLM as an error message so it can retry.

Executor parses raw JSON to Value then calls tool.execute(parsed_args); the tool body must serde_json::from_value::<MyArgs>(args) to type-check. Failure yields ToolCallError::SerdeError and the executor produces a ToolCallResult{ success: false, result: 'Failed to parse arguments…' } returned to the LLM. Validation lives inside the tool rather than at the boundary.

JSON-schema-driven validation by the MCP runtime. Invalid args produce an MCP error response that the CLI surfaces to the model as a tool error so the LLM can retry. TypedDict support was fixed in 0.1.51; per-parameter Annotated descriptions added in 0.1.52.

Zod v3/v4 schemas generate the JSON schema sent to the LLM and run runtime validation on LLM tool_use args. Invalid args trigger an SDK MCP error result and the loop sees is_error: true on the tool_result, prompting model self-correction.

args_schema (Pydantic) drives validation through _validate_kwargs (base_tool.py:264). On failure it builds a schema hint via build_schema_hint and raises ValueError; the executor catches it and surfaces the message to the LLM so it can retry with corrected args.

utils.InferTool runtime-validates by unmarshalling LLM args into the typed struct via sonic. Unmarshal errors propagate to the model as tool errors. There is no Pydantic-level validation — callers must layer go-playground/validator/v10 themselves (Ray does this in pkg/conversation).

Standard Go json.Unmarshal into the input type; failure becomes the tool error returned to the LLM. There is no explicit reject-on-bad-args mechanism beyond the decode error and no built-in field-level validators. WithStrictSchema(true) asks supporting providers (e.g. OpenAI) to enforce strict tool schemas server-side.

Pydantic v2-driven validation runs on every tool call. Invalid args raise ToolException; ToolNode catches the exception and converts it to a ToolMessage with status='error' and the validation message in content so the LLM can self-correct.

create_schema_from_function builds a Pydantic BaseModel from the function signature; invalid LLM args raise a Pydantic ValidationError which _call_tool catches and wraps in ToolOutput(is_error=True, content=str(e), ...) so the model sees a structured error and can retry.

Input validation via Zod (or any standard schema — JSON Schema, Yup) at the boundary. Invalid args produce a ValidationError returned to the model (not the host) so the LLM can self-correct. requestContextSchema additionally validates the request context against the tool's expectations.

Python uses Pydantic-based validation (_validate_arguments_against_schema, _tools.py:1084); invalid args raise ValidationError. Tools can declare input_model: type[BaseModel] for strict schema. .NET infers a JSON schema from C# parameter metadata via AIFunctionFactory and validates at deserialization.

Decorator builds a Pydantic model from the signature and calls schema.params_pydantic_model(**json_data). ValidationError raises ModelBehaviorError('Invalid JSON input for tool ...') which failure_error_function can transform into a model-visible message (default: default_tool_error_function). Output side supports ToolOutputText/Image/FileContent.

Zod or JSON schema; with strict: true (default) the LLM's args are JSON.parse'd and validated. Invalid args throw InvalidToolInputError which is caught and routed through errorFunction; default returns a model-visible 'Invalid tool input' message and the run continues so the LLM can retry.

Tool.args_validator is a SchemaValidator (Pydantic). On invalid model-generated args the framework raises ModelRetry which becomes a RetryPromptPart sent back to the model; max_retries is configurable per tool. Native Pydantic-grade validation throughout.

Args: Deserialize and Output: Serialize are enforced statically. The ToolDyn::call dispatcher deserializes the LLM-supplied JSON and returns ToolError::JsonError on failure, which the loop renders to a string and surfaces back to the LLM as the tool result. No Pydantic-grade field validation.

Pydantic validation in tools/decorator.py:62-65 and tools/_validator.py. Invalid args produce a ToolResult with status='error' and a descriptive message (tools/executors/_executor.py:204-220) returned to the LLM so it can self-correct.

With Zod, the ZodTool constructor runs this._inputSchema.parse(input) at the boundary; failures throw and the agent converts them into an error ToolResultBlock returned to the model. With raw JSON-schema mode, the declared schema is sent to the model but the SDK does NOT validate the model's args — the callback receives unknown.

Zod 3 or Zod 4 schemas; runtime validation via parseToolCall against inputSchema. On invalid LLM args, experimental_repairToolCall(toolCall, error) is invoked to potentially repair; if that fails or isn't provided, a tool-input-error chunk surfaces and the loop continues so the LLM can retry.

A tool's Run returns (map[string]any, error) — single-shot. Long-running tools mark IsLongRunning: true and pause the agent loop but do not yield mid-execution progress events back to the model. LiveSession bidi streaming exists but is for the LLM, not for tool-internal progress.

Generator-tool support exists: FunctionCall.execute detects isgenerator(result) and stores the generator. The model adapter must consume it, but chunks are aggregated and the LLM only sees the assembled result — there is no first-class 'tool yields progress events to the LLM mid-execution' pattern.

ToolRuntime::execute returns a single Value, not a stream. A tool cannot yield progress events back to the model mid-execution. One could approximate by sending Event::SendMessage from inside the tool if a Sender<Event> is captured at construction time — but execute(args) has no Context access.

Not supported in the SDK MCP server path. Tool handlers must return a single {'content': [...]} dict. The Claude Code CLI itself streams output for built-in tools like Monitor, but third-party SDK MCP tools are strictly request/response.

Partial. Bash with run_in_background: true returns immediately and output is polled via TaskOutputInput.block: true. SDKToolProgressMessage emits elapsed_time_seconds heartbeats during long tool calls so the UI can render progress. Mid-execution partial results to the model are NOT supported — the model only sees the final tool_result.

_run returns a single value (string or Any cast to string). There is no mechanism for a tool to yield partial results to the model mid-execution. For long-running tools the only option is to log progress to the event bus (or stdout) and return a single final string.

First-class streaming. StreamableTool returns *schema.StreamReader[string] (components/tool/interface.go:53-57); the tool can yield chunks and the framework concatenates/forwards them. EnhancedStreamableTool does the same for multimodal results.

Tool functions return (Out, error) after fully executing. There is no yield-style API for emitting partial results to the model mid-execution. MultipartToolResponse can return multiple parts at the end, but not during. Long-running operations use a BackgroundModel pattern or return an Operation ID for polling.

A tool that takes runtime: ToolRuntime can call runtime.stream_writer({'progress': 0.5}) to emit CustomStreamPart frames mid-execution (tool_node.py:1663-1730). Visible to clients on stream_mode='custom'. First-class incremental progress.

Tools can write to the event stream via ctx.write_event_to_stream(...) inside the tool body (they receive the live Context), emitting custom events to the consumer mid-tool-execution. Tools do NOT yield partial results back to the LLM mid-call though — the tool itself returns once.

Tools can yield mid-execution progress via ctx.writer: ToolStream which produces tool-output chunks in fullStream. Tools can also suspend(payload) via ctx.agent.suspend for HITL pauses with custom payloads. Among the strongest streaming-tool stories.

Tools cannot yield partial results to the model mid-execution; the LLM expects a single function_result content. Within the agent loop a tool can update session state which the next chat call will read. .NET FunctionInvocationDelegatingAgent exposes progress events to the surrounding agent stream so a UI can render in-flight tool progress.

Not native. The function-tool API has no 'yield partial result to the model mid-execution' primitive. Hosted ShellTool streams stdout deltas and ApplyPatchTool streams patch progress, but those are special-cased hosted-tool flows. Recommended patterns are job-id polling or sub-agent streaming via on_stream.

Not first-class. The execute function returns a Promise<Result>; there is no yield-based incremental output to the model. Buffer-and-return is the only option; HITL approval pause is suggested as a poor substitute for long-running tools.

Limited. Tools return a single value (sync or async). For tool-yields-progress mid-execution the recommended pattern is to call back into the parent agent loop via additional ToolCallPart/ToolReturnPart messages, or to use deferred external execution (CallDeferred).
A tool's call returns one Output; there is no incremental yield mechanism for a tool to emit progress while running.

Tools return an AsyncGenerator; yielded values are wrapped as ToolStreamEvents (tools/executors/_executor.py:227-256) and surface to the agent stream. The final yield must be a ToolResult, which the executor extracts. First-class streaming.

Tool callbacks can be async generators that yield ToolStreamEvent or arbitrary values (strands-ts/src/tools/tool.ts:93). yield { progress, message } becomes ToolStreamUpdateEvent; the final return value becomes the ToolResultBlock. Idiomatic streaming-tool API.

Tool execute can return AsyncIterable<OUTPUT> (tool-execute-function.ts:38). Each yielded chunk becomes a tool-output-available chunk with preliminary: true, then a final non-preliminary chunk. Useful for tools that progressively reveal output (e.g. a long-running search).
`tool/mcptoolset/` wraps the official `github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.4.1` with lazy connect, tool filter predicates, and HITL confirmation hooks on the toolset config.
`agno.tools.mcp.MCPTools` is a Toolkit that connects to external MCP servers and surfaces their tools to the agent with header/header_provider auth and lifespan management.
`McpToolsManager` in `autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/client.rs` connects to one or many MCP servers via the rmcp Rust crate and wraps each tool as an `McpToolAdapter`; gated by the `mcp` feature flag.
`Options.mcp_servers` (types.py:1615) drives the underlying CLI which acts as the MCP client; stdio, SSE, HTTP, and SDK in-process configs are all first-class.
`Options.mcpServers` accepts stdio, SSE, streamable HTTP, and SDK in-process configs (sdk.d.ts:979); the bundled CLI handles handshake, auth, and tool listing transparently.
`lib/crewai/src/crewai/mcp/` ships a full MCP client; agents accept `mcps=[slug | URL | MCPServerConfig]` with stdio/HTTP/SSE config classes and tool filters.

`components/tool/mcp/` (mark3labs/mcp-go) and `components/tool/mcp/officialmcp/` (modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk) both expose MCP tools as Eino `tool.BaseTool` via `mcp.GetTools`; schema is auto-translated from MCP `InputSchema`.
`go/plugins/mcp/` provides `GenkitMCPClient` per server plus `MCPHost` to orchestrate many servers; tools register directly into Genkit's tool registry.

`AgentBuilder.rmcp_tool` / `rmcp_tools` consume `rmcp` tools and `McpClientHandler` reacts to `tools/list_changed` notifications to re-register tools on the `ToolServerHandle`.

`create_sdk_mcp_server` plus `@tool` defines an in-process MCP server bridged via the control protocol — there is no standalone stdio-publish entrypoint, so external clients need a separate `python -m mcp` wrapper.

`@CrewBase` carries an `_mcp_server_adapter` field and the enterprise dashboard ships an Export-as-MCP feature; `docs/en/learn/custom-mcp-server.mdx` walks through publishing a crew.
Eino-ext ships no `NewMCPServer` helper; users must use `mark3labs/mcp-go`'s server API themselves to expose Eino tools.

Every agent deployed via `langgraph_api` automatically exposes an `/mcp` route (CLI schema field `disable_mcp` documents the default-on behavior); the runtime context wires per-run MCP connections.
`workflow_as_mcp(workflow)` wraps any `Workflow` (including `AgentWorkflow`) as a FastMCP server exposing it as a single tool and streams workflow events as MCP log messages.
`@mastra/mcp` (packages/mcp/src/server/) lets you expose Mastra tools and skills as an MCP server for external agents/clients to consume.

`Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows.Declarative.Mcp` and Azure Functions' `McpToolTriggerOptions` provide MCP server hosting; Python `_mcp.py` references the same capability though the surface is less first-class than agno or genkit.
`HostedMCPTool` lets the agent consume an OpenAI-hosted MCP server but there is no expose-my-tools-as-MCP-server wrapper; you would use the `mcp` SDK directly.
The SDK does not ship a wrapper to expose its tools as an MCP server; you must build one with the upstream `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` directly.
`fastmcp.py` toolset and `_fastmcp_toolset.py` in durable_exec expose agent tools as an MCP server via FastMCP; less polished than Genkit/Mastra/Agno's dedicated server APIs.
`tool/server.rs` is Rig's internal `ToolServer`/`ToolServerHandle`, not an MCP server exposure; no `rmcp_serve` example surfaces in this commit.
The `strands-agents/mcp-server` companion repo exposes Strands agents as MCP servers, but the SDK itself does not directly run one.
The TS SDK ships no MCP server stack; the separate `strands-agents/mcp-server` repo handles MCP exposure.
`@ai-sdk/mcp` is client-only; to expose tools as an MCP server you build one with `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` directly.

Whatever `github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk` supports — stdio, HTTP, and SSE — wired by passing an `mcp.Transport` to the toolset config; examples in `tool/mcptoolset/set_test.go` and `examples/mcp/main.go`.
`MCPTools(transport='stdio'|'sse'|'streamable-http', ...)` with default streamable-http when `url` is set and stdio otherwise; SSE is deprecated in favor of streamable-http.
`rmcp::transport::TokioChildProcess` is the only wired transport in `autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/client.rs`; SSE/HTTP are supported by `rmcp` but not wired through the config layer.
`McpStdioServerConfig`, `McpSSEServerConfig`, `McpHttpServerConfig`, plus `McpSdkServerConfig` for in-process SDK transport (types.py:602-633).
`McpServerConfig` union covers stdio, SSE, streamable HTTP, in-process SDK; CLI internals additionally support WebSocket for IDE integrations (`ws`, `ws-ide`, `claudeai-proxy`).
`mcp/transports/` ships `stdio.py`, `http.py` (streamable HTTP), and `sse.py`; no in-process transport but all three external transports are first-class with cache_tools_list flags.

note: stdio SSE HTTP via two SDKs

Stdio for subprocess servers, SSE/HTTP for remote, and an in-process transport for SDK-defined MCP servers without a subprocess.
Python ships `MCPStdioTool`, `MCPStreamableHTTPTool`, and `MCPWebsocketTool`; .NET adds HTTP/SSE through the ModelContextProtocol SDK.
`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerSse`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` (with session_id resumption); in-process via the `mcp` library is possible but no first-party `InProcessMCPServer` ships.
`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` (recommended), `MCPServerSSE` (legacy), plus `hostedMcpTool({serverLabel, serverUrl, connectorId, ...})` for OpenAI Responses-API hosted MCP.
`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerSSE`, `MCPServerStreamableHTTP` plus a FastMCP toolset that provides in-process / SDK transport.

Inherits the `rmcp` crate's transports (stdio, SSE, HTTP) depending on how you construct the `rmcp::service::ServerSink`; no transport-specific config sugar on the Rig side beyond the `rmcp_tool` builder.
`mcp>=1.23.0` dependency gives stdio (used in examples via `stdio_client(StdioServerParameters(...))`), SSE, and streamable HTTP; `MCPClient` accepts any transport callable.
`StdioClientTransport` for subprocess and `StreamableHTTPClientTransport` first-class via `McpClientConfig.url`; SSE/other transports require BYO via the upstream MCP TS SDK's `Transport` interface.
`@ai-sdk/mcp` ships stdio (`mcp-stdio/`), SSE (`mcp-sse-transport.ts`), streamable HTTP (`mcp-http-transport.ts`), and a mock transport for tests.

Lazy connect on first `ListTools` (`set.go:31`); `connectionRefresher` in `tool/mcptoolset/client.go` reconnects on errors. Credentials flow through the transport (HTTP headers or stdio env); no built-in OAuth/JWT flow.

`MCPTools(headers={...})` plus `header_provider: Callable[..., dict]` enables dynamic per-request JWTs; AgentOS `mcp_lifespan` manages `connect()`/`close()` (os/app.py:77-86). No status/toggle API documented.
Auth limited to `env: HashMap<String, String>` for the spawned MCP server (config.rs:18) with a connection timeout (default 30s); no automatic reconnection or health surface documented.

`ClaudeSDKClient.reconnect_mcp_server`, `get_mcp_status` (returns `McpServerStatus`), `toggle_mcp_server`; `strict_mcp_config: bool` (0.1.74) isolates per-call MCP set — critical for multi-tenant; env/headers pass through configs.

`reconnectMcpServer`, `mcpServerStatus` (`connected|failed|needs-auth|pending|disabled`), `toggleMcpServer`, `setMcpServers` mid-session, background-connect with `alwaysLoad`, OAuth flow config (`clientId`, `callbackPort`, `scopes`), and `onElicitation` callback.

Headers for HTTP/SSE, env for stdio; `MCP_MAX_RETRIES = 3` with 30s timeouts for connection/discovery/execution (mcp/client.py:47); 5-minute tool-schema cache TTL; static tool filters via `create_static_tool_filter`.

`Config.CustomHeaders` lets you pass Bearer tokens on every MCP call and `Config.Meta` adds metadata; reconnection, health, and version negotiation are delegated entirely to the underlying SDK with no framework wrapper.

Headers for SSE/StreamableHTTP, env for stdio; `client.connect` supports re-establishing and `MCPHost` tracks `*GenkitMCPClient` per server name. No built-in healthcheck — failed transports surface errors at tool call time.

`MakeRuntimeContext.ert.context` initializes per-run MCP connections lifecycle-bound to the run; external MCP credentials follow `langchain-mcp-adapters` (env vars, OAuth). No first-party health/toggle API.
OAuth supported through `OAuthClientProvider` and a `TokenStorage` interface; `DefaultInMemoryTokenStorage` is the default but production deployments implement persistent token stores.

Credentials via boot-time `mcpClients` config or runtime `requestContext.get(MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY)` for per-request token forwarding (the editor reuses this); reconnection and health are delegated to the client implementation.

`MCPStreamableHTTPTool` accepts a custom HTTP transport with auth headers but the framework wraps very little — lazy init is a documented gotcha in the DevUI README; health/version negotiation defers to the underlying `mcp` SDK.

Headers/env for credentials; `MCPServerManager` pairs connect/cleanup; `_InitializedNotificationTolerantStreamableHTTPTransport` handles out-of-order init; 0.13.0 `session_id` resumes streamable-HTTP across reconnects/stateless workers. `require_approval` accepts always/never/dict/callable.

Stdio receives parent env, HTTP/SSE accept `headers`, hosted MCP accepts `authorization`/`headers`; `connectMcpServers` opens connections in parallel and closes on shutdown. Reconnection and version negotiation are basic and delegated upstream.

`_MCPSessionState` provides reconnection state; HTTP transports support headers and OAuth via `_make_httpx_client_factory`; MCP sampling (server-side LLM calls) wires back to a Pydantic AI `Model` via `mcp_sampling.py`.

Auth and lifecycle inherit entirely from `rmcp` with credentials wired via transport setup; `McpClientHandler` only reacts to `tools/list_changed` notifications. No first-class auth, health, or reconnect API on the Rig side.

`MCPClient` runs in a background thread with `cleanup()` and a finalizer; the agent's `tool_registry.cleanup()` invokes it on destruction. `_NON_FATAL_ERROR_PATTERNS` keeps transient errors from tearing down the session; tracing via `mcp_instrumentation`.

`McpClientConfig` covers `auth: {clientId, clientSecret, scopes}` (ClientCredentials), custom `authProvider: OAuthClientProvider`, `headers`, `failOpen`, `disableMcpInstrumentation`, experimental `tasksConfig` for progress polling, and `elicitationCallback`; cancel-signal is forwarded to MCP tool calls (PR #1069).

OAuth in `packages/mcp/src/tool/oauth.ts`, standard HTTP headers via HTTP/SSE transports, reconnection logic in `DefaultMCPClient` (`mcp-client.ts:226`), and version/capability negotiation during handshake.
Not provided. No PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination scoring ships in ADK Go. Engineers must implement via BeforeModelCallback / AfterModelCallback hooks.

First-class with BaseGuardrail abstraction (libs/agno/agno/guardrails/base.py:8) and three built-in detectors: PromptInjectionGuardrail, PIIDetectionGuardrail, OpenAIModerationGuardrail. Wired as pre_hooks/post_hooks. Direct fit for the benchmark.

First-party autoagents-guardrails crate with built-in prompt_injection, regex_pii_redaction, and toxicity guards plus an LLMLayer that plugs into the LLM pipeline. Block/Sanitize/Audit policies; GuardrailBlocked errors propagate through the executor. Direct fit.
No PII, prompt-injection, or hallucination detection ships. Only UserPromptSubmit/PostToolUse hook primitives are provided to BYO any detector.
No first-party guardrails. The PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook surface is the only primitive — engineers wire regex redaction or third-party detectors themselves.

Agent.guardrail and Task.guardrail (agent/core.py:302) support a callable/string output guardrail with retries. AMP-only HallucinationGuardrail and pii-trace-redactions exist. No first-party PII redaction or prompt-injection detector in OSS.
Not first-party. PII, prompt-injection, and hallucination detection all BYO via ChatModelAgentMiddleware running custom regex/classifier/LLM-judge logic.
Not provided as a first-party primitive in go/. No PII redaction, prompt-injection, or hallucination detection ships; engineers use WrapGenerate or WrapTool hooks to BYO.

Not provided in the OSS runtime. Common pattern is pre_model_hook for input scrubbing and wrap_tool_call for output scrubbing, with LangChain ecosystem detectors (Lakera/Presidio/OpenAI moderation) wired as callbacks.
Not first-party in core. The llama-index-integrations ecosystem ships llama-index-guardrails (PyPI) and bridges to Guardrails AI / NeMo Guardrails — usable but out of core.

Built-in processors under packages/core/src/processors/processors/: moderation.ts (LLM-based), pii-detector.ts, prompt-injection-detector.ts, cost-guard.ts, regex-filter.ts, plus language/unicode/system-prompt scrubbers. Each can ctx.abort with optional retry-with-feedback. Direct fit.

First-party prompt-injection defense via IntegrityLabel/ConfidentialityLabel/ContentLabel/LabeledMessage and PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware (security.py), backed by ADR 0024. Purview integration handles compliance/sensitivity labels. PII redaction remains BYO.

Four decorator types: @input_guardrail, @output_guardrail, @tool_input_guardrail, @tool_output_guardrail (src/agents/guardrail.py, tool_guardrails.py) with allow/reject_content/raise_exception tri-state and parallel input execution. No bundled PII detector but the framework integrates third-party detectors trivially.

First-class with five surfaces: InputGuardrail, OutputGuardrail, ToolInputGuardrail, ToolOutputGuardrail, HandoffEnabledPredicate (guardrail.ts, toolGuardrail.ts, handoff.ts:94-98). Tripwires halt runs cleanly. No first-party PII/prompt-injection detector — BYO with LlmGuard/Lakera.

Not provided. No PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination check ship in rig.

Not provided. PII, prompt-injection, and hallucination detection are all BYO via LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams or prepareStep for pre-call redaction.

No allow/deny list and no canUseTool-style hook. tool.FilterToolset removes tools from the LLM's view but in-toolset tools execute as raw Go function calls. RequireConfirmation gates per-call HITL but is not policy.

AgentHooks::on_tool_call returning Abort is the per-call allow/deny primitive (no per-tool allowlist data structure). WasmRuntime executes tools in a wasmtime sandbox and CodeActAgent runs TypeScript via Deno AST + rquickjs (codeact.rs:36). Sandbox primitives exist but no central ACL.

SandboxSettings (types.py:873-916) governs macOS/Linux bash sandboxing with network allow/deny domains. permission_mode {default/acceptEdits/plan/bypassPermissions/dontAsk/auto} including a model classifier and dontAsk for default-deny, with can_use_tool callback for per-call interception. Direct first-class fit.

Excellent: canUseTool callback (sdk.d.ts:155), PreToolUse hook with allow/deny/defer, PermissionMode including dontAsk and auto, PermissionUpdate rules persisted at user/project/local/session/cliArg scope, McpServerToolPolicy per-MCP ACL, Options.disallowedTools, and Options.tools:[] kill-switch. Most complete permission surface in the comparison.

Allow/deny at construction time via Agent(tools=[...]); max_usage_count caps invocations per tool; before_tool_call hook returning False blocks; MCP ToolFilter narrows server tools; AMP RBAC scopes at org-role level. No per-tool ACL with roles/groups/scopes in OSS — write your own hook.

Two real primitives: ToolApproval middleware (plugins/middleware/tool_approval.go) with AllowedTools allowlist that interrupts unknown calls until RestartWith carries toolApproved=true, and Filesystem middleware with an os.Root sandbox preventing .., absolute, or symlink escapes plus strict size caps. Strong narrow primitives but no broader ACL/permission framework.
wrap_tool_call is the per-tool ACL hook — engineers wire policy in the wrapper. No declarative allow_tools=[...] list, no built-in HITL approval primitive.

details: No canUseTool-style hook. Permission is enforced by what tools you pass in tools=[...] at agent construction. Inside a tool you can raise to refuse but there is no declarative ACL.

activeTools per-call whitelist; requireApproval boolean or needsApprovalFn(args) per tool; RBAC and FGA at the HTTP layer (agents:execute, agents:read) with requiresPermission overrides. processInputStep returning { activeTools } is the functional equivalent of canUseTool. FunctionTool/@tool decorator approval_mode (always_require/never_require, _tools.py:302,393, ADR 0006). .NET ToolApprovalAgent with ToolApprovalRule/ToolApprovalState for standing always-allow rules. Allow/deny via ContextProvider tool filtering; FunctionMiddleware raising MiddlewareTermination implements canUseTool. Hyperlight Wasm sandbox is a unique hardware-isolated execution surface.

Multi-layered: function_tool(needs_approval=True|callable) with ToolApprovalItem and RunState.approve/reject; per-MCP-server require_approval; the four guardrail decorators that gate or reshape per-tool calls; is_enabled visibility. No general allow/deny list primitive, but the building blocks compose to the same effect. Direct fit.

tool({ needsApproval: true | predicate }) (tool.ts:1408), tool({ isEnabled }) visibility filter, per-tool inputGuardrails/outputGuardrails, and agent.toolUseBehavior to cap tool loops. Composable primitives but no declarative ACL list.

on_tool_call hook can Skip { reason } or Terminate (agent/prompt_request/hooks.rs:39-47). That is the entire permission model — no per-tool ACL, no structured canUseTool verdict, no default-deny mode.
BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel_tool (hooks/events.py:147-155) can be set to True or a reason string to cancel. The Interrupt mechanism supports HITL approval. No declarative allowlist.

BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel (hooks/events.ts:255) and InterventionHandler.beforeToolCall returning deny(reason) (interventions/actions.ts:60). No declarative allowed_tools list at the agent config layer — policy is hand-written.

toolApproval (tool-approval-configuration.ts:111) per-tool or global function returning approved/denied/user-approval, activeTools allowlist filter, and per-tool needsApproval boolean/function. Denied tools surface a tool-output-denied chunk. Composable and explicit.
No E2B, Daytona, Modal, or code-interpreter integration. Gemini's native code_execution tool runs in Google's sandbox but is not controlled by the framework.
Three first-party sandbox tools: E2B (tools/e2b.py), Daytona (tools/daytona.py), and Docker (tools/docker.py) — all execute code in remote/isolated sandboxes. Direct fit.
No E2B/Daytona/Modal integrations. AutoAgents brings its own sandbox via wasmtime (WasmRuntime) and rquickjs (CodeActAgent for TypeScript).
First-party bash sandbox via OS primitives (macOS sandbox-exec, Linux seccomp). No E2B/Daytona/Modal adapters.

Built-in Linux sandbox via bubblewrap with Options.sandbox: SandboxSettings (sdk.d.ts:1645) configuring filesystem/network restrictions including allowLocalBinding and allowUnixSockets. Linux-only with failIfUnavailable safety belt. No E2B/Daytona/Modal adapters.

Both E2B and Daytona first-party in crewai-tools: E2BBaseTool, E2BExecTool (shell), E2BFileTool (file ops), E2BPythonTool (Python REPL) with three lifecycle modes plus DaytonaSandboxTool. Strong but narrower than openai-agents-python's seven-provider matrix.

These are filesystem-middleware backends rather than general code-execution sandboxes — no E2B/Daytona/Modal.

No E2B/Daytona/Modal/code-interpreter plugin. googlegenai/code_execution.go exposes Gemini's built-in code execution as a model feature but not as a Genkit-level sandbox. Filesystem middleware's os.Root sandbox is the only first-party sandbox primitive.
No sandbox provider integrations in this repo. Engineers wire E2B/Daytona/Modal as @tool-decorated wrappers around the SDKs themselves.

First-party llama-index-tools-code-interpreter (local Python, not sandboxed by default), llama-index-tools-azure-code-interpreter (Azure-hosted sandbox), and llama-index-tools-aws-bedrock-agentcore. No E2B/Daytona/Modal first-party packages.
Not first-party. Bring your own E2B/Daytona/Modal and wrap it in createTool — no provided adapters.

UnixLocalSandboxClient (@openai/agents/sandbox/local) and OpenAI-hosted shell with container_auto. Third-party Docker/Blaxel/E2B-like providers referenced in CHANGELOG (e.g. 0.11.1 align Blaxel sandbox errors). Sandbox surface is real and growing, though not yet at the seven-provider scope of the Python sibling.
Third-party pydantic-ai-backend with DockerSandbox and community packages. No E2B/Daytona/Modal integration in core.
Not provided. No E2B, Daytona, or Modal integration.

Not provided. The bash tool runs in-process; the SDK does not include sandbox-provider adapters — sandboxing is left to the OS/container level.

Concrete adapters (E2B/Daytona/Modal) are not first-party — implement the interface yourself.
Default-allow. Any tool placed on llmagent.Config.Tools or Toolsets is callable by the LLM. There is no policy layer to flip the posture.
Default-allow at tool registration (you ship the catalog), then deny via tool_hooks, guardrails, or RBAC. JWT auth is deny-by-default when os_security_key or JWT is configured.
Default-allow. AgentHooks::on_tool_call defaults to Continue and there is no central ACL or default-deny posture.

permission_mode='default' prompts on dangerous tools; permission_mode='dontAsk' is true default-deny (only pre-approved tools run). bypassPermissions explicitly opt-in to default-allow. For multi-tenant servers, default + can_use_tool callback is the natural posture. First-class spectrum.

Default-ask: permissionMode='default' prompts for dangerous operations against a CLI-defined exhaustive list. 'dontAsk' flips to default-deny. bypassPermissions requires allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true as a safety belt. Provides the cleanest spectrum across the comparison.

Layered: tools and skills are default-deny (only what you load is present), MCP is default-allow once a server is connected unless ToolFilter is set, hooks are default-allow (returning anything other than False proceeds). Mixed but lean toward deny for OSS tool catalogs.
Default-allow. All registered tools are visible to the LLM unless explicitly filtered; skill middleware enumerates all skills by default. No allowTool gate.

Default-allow for tools generally (everything registered is callable). ToolApproval middleware flips this to default-deny with an explicit allowlist or per-call approval. No global toggle — opt-in per call.
Default-allow. Whatever tools you pass to ToolNode / create_react_agent are dispatched; wrap_tool_call is opt-in for tightening.
Default-allow. Whatever you pass to tools=[...] is callable; no built-in deny-by-default mode.

Default-deny for HTTP routes when server.auth is configured (packages/server/CLAUDE.md). Default-allow for tools unless requireApproval or activeTools whitelist is set. Strong on the HTTP boundary but tool dispatch is allow-by-default.

Tools default-allow (approval_mode defaults to never_require, _tools.py:393). Shell tools default to a ShellPolicy that denies unless explicitly allowed — strong selective default-deny for dangerous surfaces.

Default-allow for tools — any tool in Agent(tools=[...]) is callable; opt-in via needs_approval=True and guardrail decorators. No global default-deny mode. Shell sandbox network policy supports ShellToolContainerNetworkPolicyAllowlist (deny + allowlist) and Disabled (deny all).
Tools default to isEnabled: true and needsApproval: false. The default is allow with no built-in deny posture.
Default-allow for declared tools, default-deny for unknown tools (the model can only call what you've registered). Approval is opt-in per tool.
Default allow-all-registered — every tool you .tool(...) is callable. Filtering is opt-in via on_tool_call hook logic. No default-deny mode.
Default-allow. python_repl and shell tools ship with confirmation prompts, but the SDK does not enforce an allow-list otherwise — caller is responsible.
Default-allow. No tool requires explicit permission; the model can call any registered tool unless interventions intercept.

Default-allow at tool dispatch — if toolApproval is not set, tools execute. Setting a global toolApproval: () => 'user-approval' flips to default-deny-pending-human approval. Composable opt-in spectrum.

Native OpenTelemetry with GenAI semantic conventions (`internal/telemetry/telemetry.go:18-58`). Spans for `invoke_agent`, `generate_content`, `execute_tool`, `execute_tool (merged)` are emitted by the framework. OTLP HTTP exporter out of the box, plus `WithOtelToCloud(true)` for GCP Cloud Trace. The REST server bundles an in-memory `DebugTelemetry` exposing last N traces via `/debug/trace/...` for live inspection.

`openinference-instrumentation-agno` (`tracing/setup.py:13-80`) wires a `TracerProvider`, `AgnoInstrumentor()` (auto-traces Agent runs, model calls, tool executions, team coordination, workflow steps), and a `DatabaseSpanExporter` writing to `agno_traces`/`agno_spans` tables. Standard OTLP exporters (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger) compose by adding a `SpanProcessor`; `weave` and `openlit` extras wire alternative backends.

`autoagents-telemetry` ships a `TelemetryProvider` trait with bundled OTLP and Langfuse implementations (`langfuse` feature flag). `Tracer::from_direct` / `Tracer::from_environment` subscribe to the agent event stream and map events to OTel spans/metrics. OTLP HTTP/gRPC and a `RedactionConfig` are first-class config knobs.

OTel context auto-propagation added 0.1.60 (`subprocess_cli.py:441-462`): the SDK injects `traceparent`/`tracestate` into the CLI subprocess env so the CLI's own spans parent under the caller's distributed trace. Install with `pip install claude-agent-sdk[otel]`. The Python SDK itself emits no spans — you depend on the CLI's OTel emission. No first-party LangSmith / LangFuse / Datadog adapters.

Mirrors the Python SDK: caller's OTel trace context is auto-propagated to the CLI subprocess (CHANGELOG.md:143). The CLI binary emits OTel spans when configured via settings; the TS SDK itself emits no spans. No first-party LangSmith / LangFuse exporter — instrumentation around `query()` and hook callbacks is on the host.

OpenTelemetry built-in (`telemetry/telemetry.py`) with an OTLP HTTP exporter (default endpoint configurable, disable via `CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true`); the doc explicitly states no prompts/responses leave unless `share_crew=True`. First-party listener integrations include Datadog, Langfuse, Langtrace, Langdb, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, Galileo, MLflow, Maxim, Neatlogs, Openlit, Opik, Patronus, Portkey, TrueFoundry, Weave, plus AMP's own Prompt Tracing dashboard. The 151-event bus is the underlying signal.

Three first-party tracing exporters in eino-ext: Langfuse (`callbacks/langfuse/`) with batched submission, redaction mask, sampling; LangSmith (`callbacks/langsmith/`) with hierarchical `dotted_order` for nested runs; APMPlus (`callbacks/apmplus/`) emitting OTel spans + metrics. Plus CozeLoop for ByteDance internal tracing. `callbacks.AppendGlobalHandlers(handler)` at boot makes every component invocation (Graph, ChatModel, Tool, Retriever, Indexer, Embedding, Lambda) automatically traced.

OTel-native (`go/core/tracing/tracing.go`). Spans include `generate`, `tool`, plus custom flow steps via `genkit.Run`; attributes cover action name/type, latency, error. Tracing is on by default; the `googlecloud` plugin ships Cloud Trace, Metrics, and Logging exporters. No first-party LangSmith plugin on the Go side — point your own OTel exporter at LangSmith's OTel endpoint.

LangSmith is the first-party (paid, hosted) tracer — LangChain auto-traces all `Runnable` invocations when `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` is set. No native OTel emission, but LangSmith ships an OTel exporter and the LangChain callback ecosystem brings Langfuse, Arize-Phoenix, W&B, Opik, etc. Score limited by LangSmith being the primary path and OTel not being native.

`llama-index-instrumentation` (extracted from core in 2025) provides a dispatcher tree with event/span handlers that are async-task and thread safe — preserves trace trees across coroutines. `llama-index-observability-otel` bridges spans to any OTel backend. ~20+ first-party callback / observability packages (Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, Opik, OpenInference, PromptLayer, UpTrain, W&B, HoneyHive, AgentOps, Literal AI, Argilla, AIM).

Three observability pipelines run inside `ObservabilityEntrypoint`: (1) stream chunks carry usage on `step-finish` / `finish`; (2) metrics bus (`observability/types/metrics.ts:26-36`) with cardinality protection (UUID-shaped values and high-card labels blocked by default); (3) spans/traces via `IModelSpanTracker` for every LLM call, tool call, and processor call. Exporters: Langfuse, OpenTelemetry, custom storage. `MODEL_GENERATION` spans are re-stamped if a fallback model serves the request so cost attribution stays correct.

`enable_instrumentation()` (`observability.py:83`) wires tracer/meter/logger using OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. Spans: `invoke_agent`, `chat`, `execute_tool`, plus Compaction's own spans (`CompactionTelemetry.cs`). Compatible with Azure Monitor / Application Insights / Jaeger / any OTel collector. Span type coverage is narrower than the strongest stacks but the OTel surface is clean and first-class.

Built-in `TraceProvider` + `BatchTraceProcessor` + default `BackendSpanExporter` to OpenAI's hosted Traces dashboard. `add_trace_processor` / `set_trace_processors` extend or replace. Span data types include `AgentSpanData`, `FunctionSpanData`, `GenerationSpanData`, `GuardrailSpanData`, `HandoffSpanData`, `MCPListToolsSpanData`, `ResponseSpanData`, `SpeechGroupSpanData`, `SpeechSpanData`, `TaskSpanData`, `TranscriptionSpanData`, `TurnSpanData`. Documented partner integrations: W&B, Arize-Phoenix, Future AGI, MLflow, Braintrust, Logfire, AgentOps, Scorecard, Respan, LangSmith, Maxim AI, Comet Opik, Langfuse, Langtrace, Okahu-Monocle, Galileo, Portkey, LangDB, Agenta.

First-party tracer with batch processor and default OpenAI Traces exporter (`packages/agents-core/src/tracing/`). Span types: `AgentSpan`, `GenerationSpan`, `FunctionSpan`, `HandoffSpan`, `GuardrailSpan`, `MCPListToolsSpan`, `TranscriptionSpan`, `SpeechSpan`. Replace via `setTraceProcessors([new BatchTraceProcessor(yourExporter)])`. Documented integrations limited to AgentOps, Respan, PromptLayer. No first-party OTel exporter ships — the OTel ecosystem requires a community adapter to the SDK's `TracingProcessor`.

The `Instrumentation` capability (`capabilities/instrumentation.py`) installs spans for the agent run, model requests, and tool calls with OTel-spec attribute names (`_otel_messages.py`). First-party Logfire integration; works with any OTel backend. Clean OTel surface but no rich partner-exporter catalog like openai-agents-python.

First-class via the `tracing` crate. `invoke_agent` and `execute_tool` spans (`agent/prompt_request/mod.rs:354-368`, `mod.rs:573-588`) carry GenAI semantic-convention fields including `gen_ai.prompt`, `gen_ai.completion`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`, `gen_ai.tool.call.result`. `crates/rig-core/src/telemetry/mod.rs` exposes `ProviderRequestExt`, `ProviderResponseExt`, `SpanCombinator` for providers to populate spans. OTel export via standard `tracing-opentelemetry`; no first-party LangSmith/Langfuse adapter shipped.

`Tracer` (`telemetry/tracer.py:77`) creates spans for the agent (root), event-loop-cycle, model-invoke, and tool-call, all using GenAI semantic conventions (`gen_ai.*`). Exports via OTLP when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set (`pyproject.toml` `otel` extra installs `opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http`). Clean OTel surface that fits the benchmark out of the box.

`setupTracer()` (`telemetry/config.ts:167`) configures a global OTel `TracerProvider`; the agent auto-emits spans for `agent.invoke`, `agent.loop.cycle.<N>`, `agent.model.invoke`, `agent.tool.<name>`. OTLP HTTP and console exporters plus anything else registered on the global OTel SDK. A lightweight in-memory `AgentTrace` tree (`telemetry/tracer.ts:73`) is always collected regardless of OTel config and exposed on `AgentResult.traces` for in-process inspection.
