`Telemetry` interface (`packages/ai/src/telemetry/telemetry.ts:80-218`) exposes 12 callbacks covering language-model calls, tool execution, embed/rerank, step lifecycle, and end/error. `executeTool` wrapping enables nested-span propagation. `@ai-sdk/otel` provides an OpenTelemetry implementation; wire it to Datadog / Honeycomb / Tempo / Signoz. No first-party LangSmith/LangFuse exporter — the OTel layer is the integration point.

The session event stream effectively IS the audit log. Every `session.Event` carries `Author` + `Timestamp` + `Content` + `Actions`. Persisted to DB and append-only by design (no `UPDATE` paths in `session/database/service.go`). Not tamper-evident (no hash chain or signatures) but suitable for forensic review. An out-of-band sink can be wired via `plugin.OnEventCallback` (`plugin/plugin.go:31, 167`) shipping every event to Datadog / BigQuery.

No first-class audit-event stream, but the persisted combination is audit-friendly: JWT auth fills `request.state.user_id`, per-resource RBAC via `require_resource_access`, `agno_traces`/`agno_spans` tables hold tracing data, runs are persisted with `user_id`/`agent_id`/timestamps, and `agno_approvals` table holds the HITL audit trail (`db/schemas/approval.py`). Not tamper-evident.
BYO via the event stream. Events carry `sub_id`, `actor_id`, `actor_name`, and timestamps (added on receive). No tamper-evident or sequence-numbered audit log built in.

Indirect. The SessionStore mirror is the audit log — every transcript line (tool calls, tool results, prompts, mode changes) flows through `SessionStore.append()`. Combined with `include_hook_events=True` (added 0.1.74), a hook-execution audit stream is available too via `HookEventMessage` (`hook_event_name`, `subtype` ∈ `{hook_started, hook_response}`, exit codes, outcomes). No tamper-evident chain.

Not first-class. The closest equivalent is the on-disk JSONL transcript (tool calls, decisions, permission denials, model responses), which is append-only on local disk. With a `SessionStore` mirror you get a tamper-resistant copy. For a true audit log, hook `PostToolUse` / `PermissionDenied` / `PermissionRequest` and push to your own sink.

note: Event bus with sequence + parent ids
details: Not first-class. The event bus emits structured events with timestamps, `emission_sequence: int`, and parent IDs; persist them via a custom listener. The `event_record` is part of every checkpoint, so post-hoc reconstruction of a run is straightforward. No tamper-evidence (no hash chain or signatures).

Not first-class as separate from tracing. Write a `callbacks.Handler` (or use the agent-level `WithCallbacks` option) that emits structured audit events to your sink. Tamper-evident logging (hash chain, signed events) is not provided.
Not provided as a distinct primitive. Tracing is the only signal; no audit-log interface you can swap to a separate, tamper-evident sink. BYO via a `WrapTool` hook that logs to a write-once store.

Not provided as a tamper-evident audit stream. Engineers BYO by hooking `on_chain_start` / `on_chain_end` / `on_tool_start` / `on_tool_end` and shipping to an immutable log sink (S3, BigQuery, ClickHouse).
Not first-class. The instrumentation event stream + your own sink (Postgres / S3) is the recommended approach. Not tamper-evident out of the box.

Spans + metrics are the primary audit signal, persisted via `storage/domains/observability/` for query. RBAC + FGA route guards log denials at the middleware layer. No first-party tamper-evident audit log; you ship spans to an append-only sink yourself.

Trace data is the audit substrate; no separate tamper-evident audit log. `security.py`'s `LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware` (`security.py:793`) records which labelled content flowed through which tools — useful for prompt-injection audit but not a general audit log.
Not first-class. Tracing serves a similar role but is not tamper-evident. For audit, hook into `RunHooks.on_tool_start` / `on_tool_end` and ship to your own append-only log.

Tracing spans (with `traceIncludeSensitiveData: true`) capture LLM inputs/outputs and tool inputs/outputs (`docs/guides/tracing.mdx:100-107`). For tamper-evident logging build your own append-only sink and call `addTraceProcessor` to mirror. No native audit primitive.
Audit is via OTel spans — Logfire treats every agent/model/tool span as an audit record. No tamper-evident store in-tree; ship spans to a write-once backend for that property.

Not provided as a distinct facility. Tracing spans contain message-level data (`gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages` — `mod.rs:451-452`); use them as your audit log by routing to your exporter of choice.
Not first-class. Tracing serves double duty; for tamper-evident audit, BYO sink subscribing to `MessageAddedEvent` + `BeforeToolCallEvent` + `AfterToolCallEvent`.

Not a separate primitive but the hook event stream is the natural audit-log source — every event has `event.toJSON()` designed for wire transport. The newer `interventions` subsystem (`interventions/registry.ts`) is closer to a tamper-evident policy log, but no signed/append-only ledger is shipped.
Not provided — BYO. Use the `Telemetry` interface + your structured logger. The SDK does not ship tamper-evident audit-log primitives; the hook callback surface is the natural sink point.

Gemini-shape UsageMetadata (prompt/candidates/total/cached/thoughts) lives on every session.Event and is persisted to the DB row as JSON and exposed on the REST wire. Per-call coverage is solid but per-turn, per-session and per-tenant rollups are all DIY — no first-party helpers.

RunMetrics aggregates MessageMetrics across the run, SessionMetrics aggregates across the session, and ModelMetrics breaks down by (provider, model_id). Per-step events also stream input/output/cache/reasoning tokens, and metrics are persisted to the agno_metrics table — easily the most complete usage-rollup story in the comparison.

Usage is surfaced only as a StreamChunk::Usage event per LLM call carrying prompt/completion/total tokens. There is no per-turn, per-session or per-tenant aggregator in the framework — the telemetry crate maps events to OTel spans where you build rollups downstream.

AssistantMessage.usage holds per-call Anthropic-shape tokens (cache create/read included), ResultMessage.usage and model_usage are per-turn, and TaskUsage rolls up sub-agent tasks. Per-session and per-tenant aggregation still have to be summed across ResultMessages by the host.

SDKAssistantMessage.usage (per call), SDKResultMessage.usage (per turn), modelUsage (per model under fallback), AgentOutput.usage (per sub-agent) and Query.getContextUsage() (categorized live state) cover every granularity except multi-turn/per-tenant. The Anthropic-API usage shape (cache_creation, cache_read, server_tool_use, service_tier) is the richest in the comparison.

UsageMetrics carries prompt/completion/cached/reasoning/cache-creation/successful_requests, surfaces on LLMCallCompletedEvent (per call), TaskOutput.token_usage (per task) and CrewOutput.token_usage / Crew.usage_metrics (per kickoff). Per-tenant rollup is BYO since the framework has no tenant primitive.

TokenUsage on message.ResponseMeta.Usage exposes prompt/completion/total plus cached and reasoning sub-token details on each generation. Per-turn / per-session / per-tenant aggregation is DIY via callbacks.Handler.OnEnd summing into your metric sink.

resp.Usage carries a very rich GenerationUsage struct (input/output/total/cached/thoughts plus multi-modal counts) per model call, but the final ModelResponse.Usage reflects only the last call of a tool loop. Per-turn aggregation requires walking trace spans or adding telemetry middleware, and per-session / per-tenant are BYO.

LangChain's UsageMetadata (input/output/total plus audio/cache/reasoning sub-details) attaches to every AIMessage and is visible on stream_mode='updates'. Per-call and per-turn fall out naturally; per-session and per-tenant require summing usage_metadata across thread state and a custom callback handler.

TokenCountingHandler accumulates prompt/completion/total tokens across the handler's lifetime; per-call counts come from ChatResponse.raw (provider-dependent). Per-tenant is BYO using instrument_tags() to stamp spans, and there is no built-in session-scoped rollup separate from the handler instance.

LanguageModelUsage (input/output/reasoning/cached/cacheCreation plus provider raw) is exposed via onStepFinish (per call), onFinish.totalUsage (per run), and MastraModelOutput.totalUsage promise. Storage persists usage on conversation messages so per-session queries work; per-tenant is BYO.

UsageDetails (input/output/total plus arbitrary extras) appears on every ChatResponse and the outer AgentResponse, with INNER_ACCUMULATED_USAGE accumulating across all inner chat-client calls in one agent run. OTel histogram gen_ai.client.token.usage and span attributes provide downstream aggregation.

result.context_wrapper.usage exposes the Usage dataclass (requests/input/output/total plus cached_tokens and reasoning_tokens sub-details), with request_usage_entries preserving per-API-call breakdown. Per-turn turn_span metadata and per-session task_span aggregation are also wired into the tracing pipeline.

RunContext.usage carries inputTokens / outputTokens / totalTokens / inputTokensDetails / outputTokensDetails plus requestUsageEntries that preserve the per-API-call breakdown after aggregation. Per-session / per-tenant rollups are BYO.

RequestUsage on ModelResponse (per request) and RunUsage on AgentRunResult / RunContext (live + final) cover input/output/cache_read/cache_write tokens with details. Per-session is summed across runs sharing a conversation_id; per-tenant is BYO via OTel attribute grouping.

Usage (input/output/total/cached_input/cache_creation/reasoning) appears on CompletionResponse and is aggregated in-place on PromptResponse via usage += resp.usage across a multi-turn prompt call. Per-conversation and per-tenant aggregation is not provided — you sum PromptResponse.usage by conversation_id yourself.

Usage TypedDict (input/output/total plus cacheRead/cacheWrite) lives on every assistant message's metadata, and agent.event_loop_metrics.accumulated_usage keeps a running session-level total. BeforeModelCallEvent.projected_input_tokens additionally projects the next call's input — unusual for the comparison.

AgentMetrics exposes cycleCount, agentInvocations[] per-invocation metrics+usage, accumulatedUsage across all invocations, per-tool toolMetrics, and projected/latest context size. Per-tenant rollup still requires tagging traces via agent.traceAttributes and aggregating in the OTel collector.

LanguageModelUsage carries unusually granular inputTokenDetails (noCache/cacheRead/cacheWrite) and outputTokenDetails (text/reasoning) per call, per StepResult.usage, and on GenerateTextResult.totalUsage — better suited to prompt-cache cost analysis than most stacks. Per-session and per-tenant rollups are aggregated via onFinish or telemetry callbacks.

ADK Go surfaces Gemini token counts but does not maintain a price table or compute USD anywhere; the report states 'Not provided — BYO' explicitly. Cost has to be derived from tokens × your own $/Mtoken table.

agno.models.defaults.py ships per-model pricing tables and BaseMetrics.cost is populated in USD on every MessageMetrics, then accumulated into RunMetrics.cost and SessionMetrics.cost via ModelMetrics.accumulate(). One of only four frameworks in the comparison with first-party USD computation.
The report explicitly states 'Not provided — BYO'. AutoAgents emits Usage on stream chunks but has no price-per-1k-tokens table, no $ conversion helper, and no cost field anywhere in the SDK.

The CLI computes ResultMessage.total_cost_usd per turn, including across mid-turn model fallback, and exposes it directly on the Python SDK's ResultMessage. The report calls this the only stack in the comparison with first-party USD cost on the result object (alongside the TypeScript twin).

SDKResultMessage.total_cost_usd is computed per turn by the CLI from bundled model pricing tables, and Options.maxBudgetUsd enforces a server-side ceiling that aborts the run with subtype 'error_max_budget_usd'. The only stack in the comparison combining first-party USD with an enforced budget cap.

LLM.completion_cost: float | None exists on the LLM class but no code path populates it from a pricing table — LiteLLM provides cost helpers that CrewAI never wires up. Effectively no first-party USD; external observability vendors compute their own.
Eino reports tokens through ResponseMeta.Usage but provides no pricing table and no cost computation. Users multiply tokens by an external price table keyed on RunInfo.Type.

The report explicitly notes 'no pricing.json, no cost_usd field, no getSpendReport(...)'. USD must be computed externally from token counts × a self-maintained price table or via an external observability platform like LangSmith / Helicone.

OSS LangGraph has no built-in pricing table, no total_cost_usd field, and no max_budget cap. Cost computation is deferred to the paid LangSmith platform whose UsageMetadata extends LangChain's with cost fields server-side.

Searching the entire core package for cost_usd / cost_in_dollars / usd returns no results — USD is computed by the host from token counts and an external pricing table. Vendor integrations (Phoenix, Langfuse, Opik) layer cost on top of OTel traces.

CostContext.estimatedCost is a field on the observability types that the caller (or an exporter) fills in — Mastra does not ship a pricing table or compute USD itself. The report estimates ~30 lines of host code to hook onStepFinish, multiply by a price table and emit a cost metric.
UsageDetails is token-only (input/output/total plus arbitrary extras); no pricing table, no cost_usd field, no spend report API. Cost has to come from a downstream OTel processor or evaluator.
The report explicitly states 'Not provided — BYO'. Only tokens are reported; USD is computed in a RunHooks.on_llm_end hook or a custom TracingProcessor using a model→$/Mtok table.

The SDK reports tokens via Usage on RunContext but does not compute USD — there is no pricing table, no cost_usd field, no spend report. Cost is computed from your own pricing table in a custom TracingProcessor.

RequestUsage.extract() integrates the Pydantic-maintained genai-prices package, so per-call and per-run USD is computable directly from RunUsage + model name + provider without leaving the SDK. One of only four stacks with first-party USD computation.
Rig's Usage struct (input/output/total/cached/cache_creation/reasoning) is token-only — no pricing table, no cost field. USD is computed externally from your own price table.

The SDK reports tokens via accumulated_usage but has no per-model price table and no cost_usd field. The light-usage example shows the user multiplying usage by their own price dictionary in an AfterModelCallEvent hook.
AgentMetrics.accumulatedUsage exposes inputTokens / outputTokens only — no pricing table, no cost field. The example multiplies tokens by hardcoded per-token rates in the host.

The ai package itself has no pricing tables or cost helper — direct OpenAI/Anthropic calls force BYO cost. The Vercel AI Gateway exposes a GatewaySpendReportRow with totalCost (USD) plus token breakdowns, but only for calls routed through the Gateway.

Per-tenant rollup is explicitly 'Not provided — BYO' — you tag OTel spans with tenant_id and aggregate in your tracing backend. No first-party tenant primitive in ADK Go means even per-conversation has to be summed from per-event usage_metadata.

RunMetrics.cost is available and SessionMetrics holds per-session cost; per-tenant aggregation is BYO via a DB query against agno_sessions / agno_metrics keyed on session.metadata['tenant_id']. The cost field is computed so the rollup math is trivial — only the tenant tagging is BYO.

The framework has no tenant field at all, so per-tenant cost is entirely BYO from Usage events you tag in your own code. The telemetry crate's TelemetryProvider can attach arbitrary attributes including tenant_id, then OTel spans aggregate downstream.
BYO aggregation, but the SessionKey.project_key is the natural tagging key and ResultMessage.total_cost_usd makes the actual cost math free — you only have to accumulate by tenant id.

total_cost_usd is per SDKResultMessage so per-conversation roll-up is straightforward by session_id, but the SDK does not aggregate for you. The maxBudgetUsd option does enforce a per-call USD ceiling, which no other stack in the comparison ships.
Not provided — BYO via metadata-tagged tracing. CrewAI has no tenant primitive, and AMP's Traces dashboard offers org-wide cost views but only at the organisation level.
Not provided — first-party rollup absent. BYO pattern is metadata-tagged tracing where callbacks.Handler.OnStart reads tenantId from ctx (via WithSessionValues) and emits tenant-tagged metrics.

Not provided — BYO via metadata-tagged tracing (add tenant_id as a resource attribute on your OTel SDK and query downstream in Cloud Trace / Datadog / Grafana). The googlecloud plugin's built-in span attributes do not include tenant_id.

OSS LangGraph offers no per-tenant or per-conversation cost rollup; BYO via a BaseCallbackHandler that joins metadata['tenant_id'] + model_name + usage_metadata and emits OTel metrics. LangSmith does it server-side if you pay for it.

BYO via metadata-tagged spans, but the dispatcher's instrument_tags context manager is a clean, first-party mechanism for stamping arbitrary tags (tenant_id, user_id) on every span inside a context. Aggregation still happens in your tracing backend.

BYO — the report estimates ~30 lines: keep a pricing table, hook onStepFinish to compute tokens × rate, emit a metric with costContext.estimatedCost. The observability metrics bus accepts the costContext shape natively so the path is well-defined even though no rollup is performed.
BYO via OTel — add a tenant_id attribute on the span (through a ChatMiddleware or enable_instrumentation configuration) and aggregate downstream. No first-party tenant primitive.
BYO via RunConfig.trace_metadata={'tenant_id': 'acme'} and RunConfig.group_id — rolled up in your tracing backend. No first-party per-tenant aggregator.

BYO via groupId (RunConfig.groupId) attached to traces so you can aggregate downstream, plus tenantId stuffed into runContext.context. Aggregation happens in your TracingProcessor / OpenAI Traces dashboard.

In-process aggregation is BYO via a before_run/after_run hook folding result.usage into your billing store keyed by metadata['tenant_id']. Pydantic AI Gateway adds first-party per-project/user/key USD caps with daily/weekly/monthly windows — the closest thing in the comparison to a real per-tenant cost service, though it requires running the Gateway.
Not provided. Per-conversation aggregation is BYO — sum PromptResponse.usage across all agent.prompt(...) calls sharing the same conversation_id. Per-tenant has no aggregator at all.
BYO — subscribe to AfterModelCallEvent, multiply event.stop_response.message['metadata']['usage'] by your price table, and aggregate by tenant from invocation_state. No first-party tenant primitive.
BYO — read result.metrics.accumulatedUsage from the host and apply your own price table. agent.traceAttributes can tag every span with tenantId, but aggregation happens in your OTel collector.

With AI Gateway, gateway.getSpendReport({ groupBy: 'user' | 'tag' | …, tags, userId, model, provider, credentialType }) provides first-party per-tenant rollups in USD — tag each call via providerOptions.gateway.tags or metadata and group by tag. Without AI Gateway it is BYO from LanguageModelUsage × your pricing table in onFinish.

`runner.Runner.Run(ctx, userID, sessionID, msg, cfg, opts...)` exposes user/session/app as first-class args but has no tenant or locale field; tenant/strategy/locale ride along in `Session.State` via `WithStateDelta` using `app:`/`user:` prefixes (`runner/runner.go:131`, `agent/run_config.go:28-35`). Untyped state-bag pattern.

`Agent.run(...)` exposes `user_id`, `session_id`, `session_state`, `dependencies: Dict[str, Any]`, `metadata: Dict[str, Any]` (`agent.py:1336-1361`); both `dependencies` and `metadata` land on `RunContext` and flow through the whole run. No first-class `tenant_id` field but dependencies is the documented carrier.

`Task` carries only `prompt`, `image`, `system_prompt`, `submission_id` (`autoagents-protocol/src/task.rs:9`). No tenant, user, locale, metadata fields anywhere on the public surface — you cannot pass per-call context without stuffing it into the prompt.

`ClaudeAgentOptions` (~50 fields) exposes `session_id`, `user`, `cwd`, `env`, `setting_sources` but no first-class `tenant_id` (`types.py:1578-1939`). `SessionKey.project_key` is documented for multi-tenant deployments but only scopes session storage. Closure capture is the recommended carrier.

`Options` (~80 fields) exposes `sessionId`, `cwd`, `env`, `settingSources` but no first-class `tenantId` (sdk.d.ts:1158-1836). `SessionKey.projectKey` documented for multi-tenant scoping. Tenant identity must be modeled via cwd + env + sessionStore.

No `tenant_id`/`user_id`/`org_id` field on any entrypoint; only `kickoff(inputs: dict)` for template interpolation plus `Crew.config`/`Agent.config` as free-form dicts and OTel baggage carrying `crew.id`/`crew.key` for tracing only (`crew.py:948`). No way to thread typed context through the run.

`Runner.Run(ctx, messages, opts...)` accepts `WithSessionValues(map[string]any)` plus the standard Go `context.Context` (`adk/runner.go:75-99`, `adk/call_option.go:21-77`). No typed `Spec T` / `Context T` field — everything goes through the untyped map or `context.WithValue`.

No native `tenantId`/`userId`/`sessionId`/`locale` on `GenerateActionOptions`; the designed-for pattern is `ContextProvider(ctx, req) -> ActionContext` reading HTTP headers into `core.ActionContext = map[string]any` (`go/core/context.go:29-55`, `go/genkit/servers.go:66-72`). Untyped map but framework-recognized carrier.

`StateGraph(context_schema=Context)` accepts a typed dataclass/TypedDict (`graph/state.py:215-269`); `context: ContextT` is the documented run-dependencies channel for `tenant_id`, `db_conn`, `user_id`, `feature_flags`, frozen in `Runtime.context` for the run (`runtime.py:198-201`). Strongest typed solution.

`AgentWorkflowStartEvent` has no `tenant_id`/`user_id`/`metadata` — only `user_msg`, `chat_history`, `memory`, `max_iterations`, `**kwargs` (`workflow_events.py:116-147`). Tenant flows via `initial_state` → `ctx.store` (untyped KV) or via `**kwargs`.

`AgentExecutionOptionsBase.requestContext: RequestContext` is a typed `Map<string, unknown>` with four reserved keys (`MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY`, `MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY`, `MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY`, `MASTRA_VERSIONS_KEY`) explicitly designed to prevent hijacking (`request-context/index.ts:17-51`). The HTTP layer merges body/server contexts with reserved-key precedence.

Python `agent.run()` exposes `function_invocation_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any]` (`_agents.py:271`) as the per-call carrier; .NET uses `AgentRunOptions.AdditionalProperties` plus the `AgentRunContext.CurrentRunContext` async-local. No typed tenant/user/locale fields — callers stuff arbitrary dict.

`Runner.run(starting_agent, input, *, context: TContext | None = None, ...)` exposes a fully typed `TContext` generic (`src/agents/run.py:197-211`); `Agent[TContext]` and `RunContext[TContext]` thread it everywhere. `RunConfig.trace_metadata` adds free-form tagging on top.

`run(agent, input, { context: TContext, ... })` exposes a fully typed `TContext` generic, wrapped in `RunContext<TContext>` at run start (`run.ts:318-339`, `run.ts:771-774`). First-class typed carrier paralleling the Python SDK.

`Agent.run(..., deps: AgentDepsT, metadata: AgentMetadata)` exposes both a typed dependencies channel and a free-form metadata channel (`agent/abstract.py:276-297`); `deps` is the canonical place for `tenant_id`/`user_id` and flows to every tool, hook, and instruction function.

`PromptRequest` has no `tenant_id`/`user_id`/metadata field beyond prompt, history, preamble, static_context (`agent/prompt_request/mod.rs:46-93`). Tenant must be smuggled via prompt/preamble (LLM-visible) or `conversation_id` string encoding or per-tool closures.

`Agent.stream_async(prompt, *, invocation_state=None, **kwargs)` accepts a free-form `dict[str, Any]` as the only per-call context channel (`agent/agent.py:772-779`). No first-class `tenant_id`/`user_id`/`locale` typing.

`stream(args, { invocationState: Record<string, unknown> })` exposes a free-form record as the only per-call context (`agent/agent.ts:608`). No typed tenant/user/locale fields; same shape as the Python SDK.

`ToolLoopAgent<CALL_OPTIONS, TOOLS, RUNTIME_CONTEXT, OUTPUT>` carries a compile-time generic `runtimeContext` plus per-tool `toolsContext` validated against each tool's `contextSchema` (`tool-loop-agent-settings.ts:42-306`). Cleanest separation between agent-wide and per-tool context typing.

Tools receive `tool.Context` with `UserID()`, `AppName()`, `SessionID()`, `State()`, `UserContent()`, `Artifacts()`, `SearchMemory()` (`tool/tool.go:53-102`). Tenant is fetched via `ctx.State().Get("app:tenant_id")` — no first-class tenant field but rich context object.

If the tool signature declares `run_context: RunContext`, the framework injects it with `dependencies`, `user_id`, `session_state`, `metadata` (`tools/function.py:890-939`). The canonical pattern; `session_state` is mutable from the tool.

`ToolRuntime::execute(&self, args: serde_json::Value)` has no context parameter (`crates/autoagents-core/src/tool/runtime/mod.rs:15`). Tool sees only its `&self` (captured at construction) and the LLM-generated args. No way for harness to inject runtime context.

note: closure capture only; no ctx param
details: SDK MCP tool handler is `Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Awaitable[dict[str, Any]]]` — args in, dict out, no context object (`__init__.py:196-220`). Tenant context only reaches the handler via Python closure capture at server-construction time. External MCP tools see only LLM args.

note: closure capture or extra; no ctx
details: SDK MCP tool handler is `(args, extra) => Promise<CallToolResult>` where `extra` is MCP request meta, not a harness-injected RunContext (sdk.d.ts:5592). Tenant context flows only via closure capture or `PreToolUse.updatedInput` injection. No first-class ctx param.

Tool `_run(self, **kwargs)` receives only LLM-generated arguments validated against `args_schema` (`tools/base_tool.py:288`). No `context: ToolContext` parameter. Only workarounds are global hook (`ToolCallHookContext`), closure on a BaseTool subclass with `__init__(tenant_id)`, or fragile reads of `self.agent.execution_context`.

Standard `context.Context` is plumbed through to `tool.InvokableRun(ctx, argumentsInJSON, opts...)` (`components/tool/interface.go:42-47`); tools call `getRunCtx(ctx)` or their own context-key lookup. Session values via `WithSessionValues` map are also reachable. Untyped pattern but standard Go idiom.

Tool signature `func(ctx *ai.ToolContext, input In) (Out, error)` embeds `context.Context` (`go/ai/tools.go:38, 194-202`); inside the tool, `core.FromContext(ctx.Context)` returns the `ActionContext` populated by the `ContextProvider`. Schema for `In` is auto-generated and excludes context.

Typed `runtime: ToolRuntime[ContextT, StateT]` parameter exposes `state`, `context`, `config`, `store`, `tools`, `execution_info` (`tool_node.py:1663-1730`); also `Annotated[..., InjectedState/InjectedStore]`. Both forms are stripped from the JSON schema sent to the LLM. Cleanest typed injection.

If the tool's signature declares `ctx: Context`, the workflow injects the live `Context` via `_call_tool` (`base_agent.py:346-363`); `ctx.store` is a KV the host populates. Context params are stripped from the LLM-facing schema (`function_tool.py:204-247`). Convention-based but effective.

Every tool's `execute(args, ctx)` receives `ToolExecutionContext.requestContext: RequestContext<TRequestContext>` typed against the tool's `requestContextSchema` (`tools/types.ts:385-426`, `:448`). Reserved keys (`mastra__authToken`, `mastra__resourceId`, etc.) flow automatically through the HTTP merge layer.

Python `FunctionInvocationContext` is auto-injected to tools that declare it as a parameter (`_tools.py:_discover_injected_parameters` line 406); it exposes `function`, `arguments`, `session`, `metadata`, `kwargs`, `result` (`_middleware.py:204-262`). .NET reads `FunctionInvokingChatClient.CurrentContext`.

`ToolContext[TContext]` is passed to every `on_invoke_tool(ctx, input)`; it extends `RunContextWrapper[TContext]` adding `tool_name`, `tool_call_id`, `tool_arguments`, `agent`, `run_config` (`tool_context.py:36`). The decorator auto-detects the optional ctx parameter via `schema.takes_context`.

`execute(parsedInput, runContext, details)` is the standard signature; `RunContext<TContext>` exposes `context: TContext` typed at compile time (`tool.ts:1397, 1806-1845`). Every tool, lifecycle hook, guardrail, and handoff in a run shares the same `RunContext` instance.

`RunContext[DepsT]` is passed to every tool, system-prompt function, hook, and toolset (`_run_context.py:33`) carrying `deps`, `metadata`, `usage`, `tool_call_id`, `tool_name`, `retry`, `model`, `messages`, etc. Tools declare it as first arg via `@agent.tool`.

`Tool::call(&self, args: Self::Args)` has no context parameter (`crates/rig-core/src/tool/mod.rs:112-143`). The tool sees only the LLM-generated JSON args; per-tenant state must be captured as struct fields at construction time. No harness-injected context anywhere.

`invocation_state` is forwarded to every tool's `stream(tool_use, invocation_state, **kwargs)` (`tools/executors/_executor.py:138-149`); decorated tools that opt in via `@tool(context=True)` get a typed `ToolContext` with `agent`, `model`, `messages`, `invocation_state` (`tools/decorator.py:404-412`).

Every tool callback receives `ToolContext` exposing `toolUse`, `agent`, `invocationState` (`strands-ts/src/tools/tool.ts:13`); `invocationState` is the per-call bag, threaded by reference through every hook and tool callback. Mutations are visible across the invocation.

Every tool's `execute(input, options)` receives `ToolExecutionOptions<CONTEXT>` whose `context: CONTEXT` is validated against the tool's `contextSchema` (`tool-execute-function.ts:8-44`). Per-tool typing prevents tenant info from leaking into tools that don't need it.

`BeforeToolCallback(ctx, tool, args map[string]any)` lets you mutate `args` in place; returning `(nil, nil)` continues with the mutated args (`agent/llmagent/llmagent.go:303-313`). Caveats: it is per-call (you check `tool.Name()` yourself) and the LLM still sees the tenant field in the tool schema — no LangGraph-style InjectedToolArg stripping.

`tool_hooks=[hook]` wraps every tool call as middleware with signature `hook(function_name, next_func, args)`; the hook mutates `args` before `next_func(**args)` (`tools/function.py:971-1017`). `run_context` is auto-injected if requested. The LLM still sees any tenant field in the schema; no declarative "hidden arg" primitive.

`AgentHooks::on_tool_call(&ToolCall, &Context) -> HookOutcome::Continue|Abort` takes `&ToolCall` immutable; cannot modify args (`hooks.rs:34`). The only workaround is capturing tenant on the tool struct at construction time, but the LLM still sees the tenant field in the schema and may try to lie.

Two first-class mechanisms: `PreToolUse` hook returns `hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput` which the CLI dispatches instead of the original args (`types.py:412-419`), and `can_use_tool` returns `PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=...)` (`types.py:233-239`). Both are out-of-band Python callbacks via control protocol — LLM cannot bypass.

Same two first-class mechanisms as the Python SDK: `PreToolUse` hook with `hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput` (sdk.d.ts:2028) and `canUseTool` returning `{ behavior: 'allow', updatedInput: { ...input, tenantId } }` (sdk.d.ts:1887). The CLI dispatches with `updatedInput`, not the LLM's original args.

`register_before_tool_call_hook(fn)` lets a hook mutate `ctx.tool_input` in place (`hooks/tool_hooks.py:35`). But the hook is **process-global** — same hook fires for every crew/agent. Tenant id must come from a `ContextVar` you set in the HTTP handler. The LLM still sees the tenant field in the schema.

`ToolsNodeConfig.ToolArgumentsHandler` runs once per tool call to rewrite the raw JSON before dispatch (`compose/tool_node.go:176-185`); alternatively `compose.ToolMiddleware.Invokable` wrapper or ADK `WrapInvokableToolCall` middleware. All work but are hand-rolled; LLM still sees the field in the schema unless you scrub it manually.

`WrapTool` middleware in `ai.Hooks` mutates `params.Request.Input` (a `map[string]any` after JSON parsing) before calling `next(ctx, params)` (`go/ai/middleware.go:75-81`). Effective but BYO — no built-in middleware ships and you must remember to wire it for every tenant-aware tool. No schema stripping.

`ToolNode._inject_tool_args` explicitly strips caller-supplied values for injected arg keys, then re-injects trusted values from runtime (`tool_node.py:1315-1430`): `tool_call_copy['args'] = {**stripped_args, **injected_args}`. Schema fields marked `InjectedToolArg` are hidden from the LLM. `wrap_tool_call` is a second mechanism. Cleanest in the benchmark.

`FunctionTool(partial_params={...})` exists but merge order is `{**_field_defaults, **partial_params, **kwargs}` so LLM-provided kwargs WIN over `partial_params` (`function_tool.py:374-376`). Forcing requires either a closure-wrapping factory or reading from `ctx.store` inside the tool — both conventions, not enforcement.

No dedicated `PreToolUse → updatedInput` hook. Canonical pattern is to keep tenant out of `inputSchema` entirely and read it from `ctx.requestContext.get('tenantId')` inside `execute`, leveraging the typed `requestContextSchema` (`tools/types.ts:448`). `processInputStep`/`prepareStep` lets you rebuild tools with closures per step. Effective but not an arg-mutation hook.

`FunctionMiddleware.process(context, call_next)` lets you mutate `context.arguments` before `call_next()` (`_middleware.py`); registered as `middleware=[...]` on the agent. Effective but BYO — no `pinned_args` / `forced_args` decorator-level support and no schema stripping.

No `PreToolUse → updatedInput` hook exists. `RunHooks.on_tool_start` fires before invocation but cannot mutate (`lifecycle.py:70`). `tool_input_guardrail` can block but not rewrite. The recommended pattern is to keep tenant out of the LLM-visible schema and read it from `ctx.context` inside `@function_tool`.

`callModelInputFilter` operates on messages, not on already-emitted tool args (`runner/conversation.ts:31-33`). No `PreToolUse.updatedInput` equivalent. The standard pattern is to ignore any LLM-passed tenantId inside `execute` and pull the trusted value from `runContext.context`, optionally paired with `isEnabled` to hide the tool.

`@hooks.on.before_tool_validate(tools=['topic_search'])` returns a new `RawToolArgs` dict that takes precedence over LLM-generated args (`capabilities/hooks.py:162, 259`). Two more mechanisms: `args_validator` on the `Tool` and the idiomatic "tenant only on ctx.deps, never in schema" pattern. Multiple first-class options.

note: hook is read-only; struct capture only
details: `on_tool_call(&self, _name, _id, _internal_id, _args: &str)` receives `&str` by reference and returns only `Continue|Skip|Terminate` (`hooks.rs:39-47`). Cannot mutate args. The only workaround is to capture tenant on the tool struct at construction time and ignore the LLM-supplied field in the tool body.

`BeforeToolCallEvent.tool_use` is explicitly writable (`hooks/events.py:157`: `_can_write(name)` allows `tool_use`); the executor re-reads `tool_use` after the hook (`tools/executors/_executor.py:186-189`). Canonical mechanism to rewrite `event.tool_use['input']['tenantId']` regardless of what the LLM produced — equivalent to Claude SDK's `PreToolUse → updatedInput`.

`BeforeToolCallEvent.toolUse` is a mutable object (`strands-ts/src/hooks/events.ts:237-248`); docstring explicitly states hooks may "mutate toolUse to rewrite the tool input, id, or name before execution". The new `interventions.transform({ apply })` API provides a typed equivalent.

`experimental_refineToolInput` is a declarative per-tool input refiner applied inside `parseToolCall` before dispatch (`generate-text.ts:807-815`): `refineToolInput: { weather: input => ({ city: input.city.trim() }) }`. Combined with `toolsContext` (where tenant lives outside the LLM-visible schema) and `contextSchema` validation, the pattern is first-class.

`FilterToolset(toolset, predicate)` with `AllowedToolsPredicate` (`tool/tool.go:116-173`); `Toolset.Tools(ctx)` is called per request so the predicate can read `ctx.ReadonlyState().Get("app:tenant_id")`. But static `agent.Tools` slice is NOT filtered per request — only `Toolsets` are dynamically resolved.

`tools` can be a `Callable[..., List]` (`agent.py:166`) receiving `agent`, `run_context`, `session_state` and returning the filtered list (`utils/callables.py:79-89`). Set `cache_callables=False` to re-run per request; `callable_tools_cache_key` keys cache on tenant id. Same factory pattern works for knowledge, members, instructions.

`AgentDeriveT::tools()` returns `Vec<Box<dyn ToolT>>` at agent build time (`base.rs:46`); typically the `#[agent]` derive macro emits a fixed list. Runtime filtering requires constructing a different agent per tenant. No `activeTools`/`allowed_tools`/`prepareStep` exists.

`tools`, `allowed_tools`, `disallowed_tools` form a three-layer whitelist/blocklist on `ClaudeAgentOptions`; per-sub-agent `AgentDefinition.tools` adds another layer. `disallowed_tools` removes from model context entirely. Per-session at construction; mid-session changes require `set_permission_mode` or `toggle_mcp_server`.

Same `tools`, `allowedTools`, `disallowedTools`, `toolAliases`, per-`AgentDefinition` scoping, plus `Query.setMcpServers(servers)` for mid-session replacement (sdk.d.ts:2230). Skills filter via `skills: string[] | 'all'`. Per-session strong, per-turn via setMcpServers.

`Agent(tools=[...])` at construction is the only filter — there is no `activeTools`/`prepareStep` mid-run mechanism. `BaseTool.max_usage_count` is a crude per-tool cap. MCP-source tools support `tool_filter`/`ToolFilter` at connection setup. Per-request tenant filtering effectively requires building a fresh Crew per request.

`ChatModelAgentMiddleware.BeforeAgent` gets a mutable `ChatModelAgentContext.Tools []tool.BaseTool` slice you can replace once per run (`adk/handler.go:117`, `adk/chatmodel.go:294-303`). For per-turn filtering, wrap the chat model via `WrapModel` and apply `model.WithTools(filtered)` — example in `adk/middlewares/dynamictool/toolsearch`.

Tool set declared per `Generate(...)` call via `ai.WithTools(tools...)` (`go/ai/option.go:227-231`); the host code branches before the call to add/remove tools per tenant. No per-turn `activeTools`/`prepareStep` mechanism — once Generate is in flight the tool set is fixed. `Middleware.Tools` can only add.

Three mechanisms: `bind_tools` on the model upstream, dynamic model selection where `select_model(state, runtime)` returns a model with different tools bound per turn (`chat_agent_executor.py:325-356`), and `wrap_tool_call` short-circuit to return a synthetic ToolMessage without execution. Per-turn filtering driven by `runtime.context` is first-class.

`FunctionAgent(tools=[...])` static at construction; for per-turn dynamic resolution, `tool_retriever: ObjectRetriever` is called each turn with the current `user_msg_str` (`base_agent.py:104-107, 272-281`). Effective but cache/retrieve semantics differ from a simple predicate.

Two first-class mechanisms: dynamic `tools: ({ requestContext }) => ...` factory at construction, and `activeTools` whitelist on `AgentExecutionOptions` per call; `prepareStep` returns `{ activeTools }` per step. The `toolCallStep` enforces by rejecting non-active tool calls (`tool-call-step.ts:316-348`).

Per-agent `tools=[...]`, per-run `agent.run(..., options={'tools': [...]})` via `_merge_options` (`_agents.py:92-126`), and `ContextProvider.SessionContext.tools` (`_sessions.py:151-200`) lets a provider inject/filter tools (used by `SkillsProvider`). OpenAI/Gemini `allowed_tools` via tool_choice in 1.3.0.

Per-tool `is_enabled: bool | (RunContextWrapper, AgentBase) -> bool | Awaitable[bool]` (`agent.py:250-263`, `tool.py:314`); evaluated inside `Agent.get_all_tools` (`agent.py:246`) which the runner calls per turn. Handoffs have the same `is_enabled`. Tenant-driven hide/show without restarting the agent.

`isEnabled: boolean | ((args: { runContext, agent }) => boolean | Promise<boolean>)` per tool (`tool.ts:1411-1414`), evaluated at turn-prep in `Agent.getAllTools(runContext)` (`agent.ts:1038-1064`). Handoffs also support `isEnabled`. MCP tools filtered via `MCPServer.toolFilter`.

Multiple first-class options: `@agent.toolset` decorator building a toolset from `RunContext`, `prepare_tools=` kwarg returning a filtered `list[ToolDefinition]` per step, `.filtered(predicate)`/`.prepared(prepare_func)` wrappers on any `AbstractToolset`, and per-run `toolsets=[...]` kwarg. All runtime-aware via `RunContext`.

Tools visible to the LLM are read once via `tool_server_handle.get_tool_defs(...)` (`tool/server.rs:167-263`). Per-request filtering requires either building a fresh `Agent` per tenant or mutating a shared `ToolServerHandle` via `add_tool`/`remove_tool` which affects all concurrent users. No `activeTools`/`allowedTools`/`prepareStep`.

Filtering at construction via `Agent(tools=[...])`. No first-class per-turn `activeTools`/`prepareStep`. Workarounds: build one Agent per tenant, mutate `agent.tool_registry.registry` between turns, or use `BeforeToolCallEvent.selected_tool = None` to veto a call (model still sees the tool though).

`ToolRegistry` is set at construction (`new Agent({ tools: [...] })`); the visible tools are read once per model call (`agent.ts:1272`). No `prepareStep` mid-cycle filter. Workarounds: per-tenant agent, mutate registry between invocations, or `BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel = 'unauthorized'` to block (model still sees the tool).

Three layers: `activeTools` at construction (`tool-loop-agent-settings.ts:96`), `prepareStep(...) -> { activeTools }` per step (`prepare-step.ts:118`), and `prepareCall(...) -> { tools }` per call. All driven by `runtimeContext` / `CALL_OPTIONS`.

No `Session.TenantID` field. `AppName` is the closest first-class identifier and is sometimes used as the tenant boundary; otherwise tenant lives in `State["app:tenant_id"]` by convention. Real gap noted by the report — every Toolset.Tools, BeforeToolCallback, InstructionProvider must check it.

`AgentSession` has first-class `user_id`, `agent_id`, `team_id`, `workflow_id` but no `tenant_id` column. Tenant is stuffed in `session.metadata` or `dependencies` per request. AgentOS JWT scopes recognize tenant separation at the HTTP layer via `user_id` and resource-id scoping rather than a tenant field.
Neither `Task` nor `Context` nor `AgentConfig` carries a tenant field, and there is no first-class session concept. Per-tenant separation requires per-tenant agent instances.

`SessionKey.project_key` is explicitly documented as the multi-tenant primitive for the session store: "Multi-tenant deployments should set this to a tenant ID or project name." (`types.py:1276-1295`). Scopes session storage only — not toolset/skills/agents. No first-class `tenant_id` on Options.

Same `SessionKey.projectKey` recommendation for multi-tenant scoping (sdk.d.ts:3669). Scopes the session store; no `tenantId` field on Options or `SDKSessionInfo`. Tenant must be modeled as cwd + projectKey + env var.

note: no tenant field; config dicts only
details: No `tenant_id` field on Crew/Agent/Task/Flow. Only carriers: `Crew.config`/`Agent.config` (free-form dicts), `execution_context: ExecutionContext`, or OTel baggage (`crew.id`/`crew.key` for tracing). None validated; none flow to tools as a trusted field.

Tenancy lives in `context.Context` or `runSession.Values` via `WithSessionValues(map[string]any{"tenantId": "acme"})`. Read back via `adk.GetSessionValue(ctx, "tenantId")`. No type safety, no validation, no `session.tenant_id` property.
No `Tenant string` field on `Session`; you add it to your typed state `S` struct and key your session store by `tenant:userId:sessionId` yourself. Convention only.

No first-class `Session.tenant_id` column. Documented practice is to stamp `metadata["owner"] = tenant_id` on thread creation via `@auth.on.threads.create` (server side) and/or store tenant in `Runtime.context`. Convention enforced by `@auth.on` decorators in LangGraph Server.
No first-class `tenant_id` field on session or context; stuffed in `ctx.store` (generic KV) or `Memory.session_id` (single string you can encode `tenant:user:conversation` into).

Tenant identity is not a first-class top-level field. Conventionally lives in `requestContext` (typed key) and/or `resourceId` (reserved key) which is the tenant scope. RBAC + FGA layers consume `requestContext` for permission checks.
Not first-class. Stuff tenant id in `session.state["tenant_id"]` or `AgentSessionStateBag["tenant_id"]`. No reserved key, no validation.

`Session.session_id: str` is the only identity field. Conventions are encoding in the id (`acme:user-123:conv-abc`), carrying in `TContext`, or per-tenant `SQLAlchemySession`/`RedisSession` instances. No tenant column at the store layer.
`Session.sessionId: string` is the only identity. Encode tenant in the id (`acme:user-123:thread-...`) or use a custom Session impl that scopes reads by tenant.
No first-class tenant field. Idiomatic pattern is a typed `deps` dataclass containing `tenant_id` plus `metadata={'tenant_id': ...}` for OTel/Logfire tagging. Convention only.
Not a first-class field. Tenants are encoded in `conversation_id` (e.g. `tenant=acme;user=u-123;thread=42`) and in tool closures.
No tenant column on `Session`, `SessionAgent`, or `SessionMessage` (`types/session.py`). Encode tenancy in `session_id` (`acme:user-123:thread-abc`) and/or in `agent.state`.
`SnapshotLocation` has `sessionId`, `scope`, `scopeId`, `agent.id` — none are tenant. Encode tenant into `sessionId`, `appData`, or `invocationState`.
There is no session in the SDK so no first-class tenant scope on a session object. Convention is `runtimeContext.tenantId`.

`context.Context` is plumbed through and `ctx.UserID()`/`ctx.AppName()` are available, but the framework defines no "principal" or "claims" first-class type. JWT claims must be wedged into `context.Context` values manually. The `authPreprocessor` is for OAuth-flow tools, not request-time caller identity.

AgentOS authentication propagates the JWT `sub` to `run_context.user_id` (`agno.os.routers.agents.router:587-593`); tools that need to act under user permissions read this. For RemoteAgent calls, the JWT is forwarded via `auth_token` kwarg (`router.py:101-103`). No general claims object but user_id flows.
Caller's identity does not reach the tool. Must be captured as a struct field on the tool at construction time.
Captured via Python closure into hook/tool callbacks. No SDK primitive automatically threads the caller's JWT to every tool call. CLI built-in tools execute under the subprocess's OS identity.

Caller identity does not flow into tool calls automatically. SDK-MCP tools run in your Node process so you pull identity from your own request context (e.g. via AsyncLocalStorage). CLI built-ins execute under the subprocess OS identity.

Caller's identity does not propagate to tools. For tools that call external APIs, authentication is configured per-tool-instance (`api_key` on BaseTool subclass at construction). No notion of "use the caller's bearer token". AMP's Connected Apps feature binds at the user-org level, not per-request.

Not built-in. The caller's identity reaches the tool only because you put it on `context.Context`. No automatic Okta-token-pass-through or per-tool-call STS / impersonation; instrumented in `BeforeAgent` middleware.

If you wire auth credentials into `ActionContext` from headers via a `ContextProvider`, tools that read `core.FromContext(ctx)` see them. Firebase Auth helper available (`plugins/firebase/auth.go`). No automatic IAM/RBAC layer; each tool enforces what it wants.

`runtime.context` carries the caller's identity into every tool; tools execute with whatever DB credentials the engineer wires in `runtime.context.db_conn`. So passing a tenant-scoped DB connection means all tool DB calls run under that scope. Engineer-wired but designed for it.
Auth identity is whatever you stash in `ctx.store` and read inside the tool. No built-in identity propagation from an outer HTTP handler.

`MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY` is a reserved RequestContext key explicitly for forwarding the caller's auth token into tool execution (`request-context/index.ts:51`). Tools hit downstream services (MCP/internal APIs) by reading `ctx.requestContext.get(MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY)` and forwarding. Editor uses this for MCP auth pass-through.

Caller identity is not automatically propagated; inject it via `function_invocation_kwargs` (Python) or `AgentRunOptions.AdditionalProperties` (.NET), or via custom `FunctionMiddleware`/`ContextProvider`. The `ToolApprovalAgent` mechanism only handles is-approved, not identity.

`TContext` reaches every tool, so tools can carry user OAuth tokens, tenant scoping rules, RLS predicates without ever passing through the LLM. `ToolContext` adds `tool_call_id`/`tool_arguments`/`tool_namespace` for correlation. Engineer-wired but cleanly typed.

Whatever you put in `runContext.context` is automatically reachable from every tool, lifecycle hook, guardrail, and handoff (docs/context.mdx:24: "Every agent, tool and hook participating in a single run must use the same type of context."). HTTP-auth-like checks done inside `execute`.

`ctx.deps` flows to every tool by construction. Host code that constructs `deps` (typically from the incoming HTTP request) is the auth termination point. No automatic IAM layer but the deps idiom is designed for it.
No `principal`, no `auth_token`, no per-call identity. Tools execute with whatever permissions you wired into their `call` body — typically captured on the tool struct at construction.
Whatever you stash in `invocation_state`/`agent.state` is forwarded to every tool (`tools/executors/_executor.py:138-149`). No first-class JWT/OAuth identity object — build it yourself.

Caller's identity propagates via `invocationState` only. No built-in auth principal type; tools execute under host process credentials and you pass any per-call auth via `invocationState.userId`/`scopes`/`jwt`.

Caller's identity reaches tool calls only if you put it in `runtimeContext` or `toolsContext`. Common patterns: `runtimeContext = { tenantId, userId, jwt }` for prepareStep/telemetry, and `toolsContext = { toolName: { tenantId, jwt } }` for tool execute. Typed but no automatic plumbing.

Tools/toolsets are registered in static slices at agent construction. Filtering at runtime via `FilterToolset`/`Predicate` is the only mechanism. No concept of "register this tool for tenant X only at publish time". Sub-agents are static `SubAgents []agent.Agent`. Skills via `skilltoolset.New(Source)` — tenant-conditional source must be hand-rolled.

Skills: per-Agent instance, no tenant scoping at the loader level (wrappable in callable factory). Sub-agents (Team members) and tools support callable factory pattern. No "register tool as global/tenant/user" first-class scoping at registration time.
Not provided at the framework level. Scoping must be implemented at your own registration layer (e.g. per-tenant `AgentBuilder` factory).

The SDK's scoping mechanism is the filesystem. Skills/sub-agents/slash-commands/plugins/MCP-config/CLAUDE.md all load from `setting_sources` ('user'/'project'/'local'). Per-tenant resource scoping requires a per-tenant filesystem tree under cwd plus `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. No in-memory registry to pass per-request.

Same filesystem-based scoping: skills at `~/.claude/skills/` (user) / `.claude/skills/` (project) / `<plugin>/skills/`. Sub-agents (md) and slash commands follow the same pattern. Programmatic registration via `Options.agents` is a secondary option. You cannot register a resource as "tenant X only" via an API call.

Skills: scoping is by filesystem path passed to `Agent(skills=[Path(...)])`. Sub-agents: by `Crew(agents=[...])` membership. Tools: by `Agent(tools=[...])`. No global → tenant → user scope hierarchy at registration time. AMP Agent Repositories are org-wide (one org = one tenant).

Scopes (global/tenant/user) at registration are not provided. Cannot say "register skill X as tenant=acme only" at the registry layer. Must build it yourself via a custom `skill.Backend` returning different `FrontMatter` lists per ctx tenant.

Tools, prompts, retrievers, evaluators, models all registered in a single global `*registry.Registry` per `*genkit.Genkit` instance. No `register("topicSearch", scope: "tenant:acme")`. Scoping is your job — Generate-call-time filtering or middleware. Child registries only used internally.

`BaseStore.put((namespace_tuple,), key, value)` — tuple namespace is a natural per-tenant-per-user partition (e.g. `("acme", "user-123", "preferences")`). For HTTP (LangGraph Server): `@auth.on` decorators with `FilterType` dict shape applied as SQL filter on threads/runs/assistants/crons/store, with create/read/update/delete/search/put/get/list_namespaces actions. Strong for Server tier.
Not provided. Pass tenant-scoped tool lists at agent construction or filter in your `tool_retriever`. No registry concept beyond agent-instance tool lists.

`SkillsResolver = string[] | ((ctx) => string[])` per request (`workspace/skills/types.ts:136`); sub-agents, workspaces, memory all use the same `DynamicArgument` pattern; `MASTRA_VERSIONS_KEY` pins per-call sub-agent versions. FGA permissions consume `requestContext`. No org/channel/user hierarchy — you encode it in the keys.

Tools/skills/sub-agents can be filtered at registration via `FilteringSkillsSource` (`_skills.py:AggregatingSkillsSource` + `FilteringSkillsSource`). No publish-time tenant tag — scoping happens at runtime composition of a different `SkillsProvider` for each tenant.

Per-agent at construction (pass `tools=[...]`), per-call via `is_enabled` callables filtering visible toolset, per-handoff same. No registry concept (see Q11) — you roll your own dict-of-agent-per-tenant for the registry layer.
Filtering is runtime-only via `isEnabled` / handoff `isEnabled` / `callModelInputFilter`. No registration-time scope — there's no "this tool belongs to tenant X".

Toolsets/capabilities can be scoped per-run (passed to `agent.run(..., toolsets=[...], capabilities=[...])`) or per-agent (constructor). Dynamic capabilities resolve at run time based on `RunContext` (e.g. `def user_skill(ctx): return load_skill(ctx.deps.user_id, ctx.deps.tenant_id)`). No registry layer that marks publish-time tenant scope.
No global/tenant/user scopes at registration; everything is "registered on this agent" or "registered on this `ToolServerHandle`".

`tool_registry` is a flat global dict on the agent (`tools/registry.py:32-44`). Tenant/user scoping must be enforced at the hook layer (e.g. `BeforeToolCallEvent` callback inspects `invocation_state["tenant_id"]` and blocks tools not in tenant's allowlist).
Tools, hooks, and plugins register globally on an `Agent` instance. The only "scope" the SDK knows is `Snapshot.scope: 'agent' | 'multiAgent'`. Per-tenant scope is whatever your host enforces.

Per-tool `contextSchema` declares what context each tool expects (`tool.ts:95-99`); `validateToolContext` rejects mismatches. Per-call `runtimeContext` typing via `ToolLoopAgent<...>` generics. No global/tenant/user scope on tools or skills directly — you template the agent or filter `activeTools` based on `runtimeContext.tenantId`.

No `MaxTokens`-per-tenant, no USD cap, no rate-limit middleware. Trigger controllers have a global `MaxConcurrentRuns` (`server/adkrest/controllers/triggers/config.go:30`) but that is global to the trigger, not per-tenant. Token counts available via `Event.UsageMetadata` for application-side roll-up.

Closest first-party knob is `tool_call_limit` per agent (`agent.py:169`) — a count cap, not a budget cap. `Metrics.cost` is computed in USD (`libs/agno/agno/metrics.py:48`) but reported after-the-fact; nothing enforces "stop when tenant X exceeds $5/month". Would need a pre-hook + DB-backed tenant counter.

`ExecutorConfig { max_turns }` (`executor/mod.rs:28`, default 10) — turn cap only. No USD budget, no per-tenant cost tracking. Would need to build on top of `Usage` extracted from `Event::StreamChunk(StreamChunk::Usage(...))`.

First-party per-run USD ceiling: `max_budget_usd: float | None` wired to CLI flag `--max-budget-usd` (`types.py:1659-1664`); on overrun the run ends with `ResultMessage.subtype == 'error_max_budget_usd'`. Post-call check so cost may exceed by one API call. No per-tenant aggregation — you set per run; cross-run totals are BYO. `RateLimitEvent` provides observability on Anthropic's 5h/7d ceilings.

`Options.maxBudgetUsd` is a USD ceiling enforced server-side; overrun -> `SDKResultMessage(subtype: 'error_max_budget_usd')`. `Options.taskBudget.total` (alpha) sends a token budget via the `task-budgets-2026-03-13` beta header to make the model aware. `maxTurns` is the turn cap. No per-tenant cumulative cap — aggregate `total_cost_usd` from `SDKResultMessage`.

`Agent.max_rpm` and `Crew.max_rpm` enforce a requests-per-minute cap via `RPMController` — process-local, not per-tenant. USD budget cap: not provided. `UsageMetrics` tracks token counts only; no `cost_usd` field; `LLM.completion_cost` exists but no code path populates it.

No USD budget enforcement, no per-tenant token ceiling. Token counts readable off `ResponseMeta.Usage` per assistant message; enforce yourself in a `callbacks.Handler.OnEnd` that aborts via `context.CancelFunc`.

No USD budget enforcement. Only per-call cap is `MaxTurns` (turn count). Token usage exposed on `resp.Usage` after the call but you must read it and enforce limits yourself (probably in a `WrapGenerate` middleware checking a Redis counter).
No token-budget cap, no USD-cost cap in OSS. LangGraph Platform exposes per-deployment rate limits but not per-tenant USD ceilings.

`TokenCountingHandler.token_budget` parameter raises `ValueError` if exceeded (`callbacks/token_counting.py:153, 167`) — but per handler instance, not per tenant, and counts tokens not USD. No USD budget cap.

`CostGuardProcessor` is a built-in processor that fires a tripwire when cost exceeds a threshold — but relies on caller-provided pricing (`CostContext.estimatedCost`), not built-in tables. `stopWhen` supports `maxSteps`, `tokenLimit`, custom predicates (token caps not dollar caps). Real per-tenant dollar ceiling = `CostGuardProcessor` + custom `processInputStep` that emits cost via your pricing table.
Not provided. Tokens observable via OTel histograms and `UsageDetails` but no built-in USD-cap or per-tenant ceiling.

Not provided. `Usage` (`usage.py:102`) reports tokens (input/output/total/cached/reasoning) and request counts but no dollar-cost field, no per-tenant budget cap, no "stop if usage exceeds $X". Enforce in your `on_llm_end` hook or post-hoc against your billing store.

Not provided. The SDK surfaces token usage (`RunContext.usage`) but doesn't enforce caps. You enforce ceilings in an `agent_tool_start` listener that throws, or via a custom `Model` wrapper that pre-checks usage. No USD budget cap.

`UsageLimits` caps per-run tokens, requests, tool calls (`usage.py:263-295`) — `request_limit=50` default. No USD budget cap in-tree; for USD, Pydantic AI Gateway adds project/user/key-level daily/weekly/monthly USD caps (separate product). Per-tenant rate limiting is BYO inside a hook.
Only `max_turns` (turn cap) and `max_tokens` (per-completion cap). No USD budget, no per-tenant rate limit.
Not provided. `EventLoopMetrics.update_usage` (`telemetry/metrics.py:352`) tracks tokens at the agent instance level; you must aggregate per-tenant and enforce caps yourself in a hook.

Not provided. `AgentMetrics.accumulatedUsage` gives input/output tokens but no USD cost computation and no enforcement. Enforce via `BeforeModelCallEvent` checking `event.projectedInputTokens` or by polling `agent.metrics?.accumulatedUsage`.
Not provided. `stopWhen` accepts step-count and tool-name stop conditions but no USD-cost or token-count budget cap in the SDK. AI Gateway's spend report is observational, not enforcing.

Eval framework is Python-only (adk-python); adk-go's REST routes for eval sets/results are present but return HTTP 501 via controllers.Unimplemented (server/adkrest/internal/routers/eval.go). You'd run a sister adk-python process or build your own harness.

libs/agno/agno/eval/accuracy.py ships AccuracyEval, PerformanceEval, ReliabilityEval, and AgentAsJudge as first-class types. Eval runs persist to the agno_evals table via db.create_eval_run/update_eval_run/get_eval_runs, and BaseEval is a hook target so evals can run as pre/post hooks. No formal dataset file format though.

Report explicitly says BYO. There's an internal autoagents-llm/src/evaluator/parallel.rs used for parallelism (not eval), and only standard cargo test --features full --workspace runs unit tests. No dataset format, no agent regression harness.
Report lists section 19.1 as Not provided. No dataset format, no regression harness ships in the Python SDK.
BYO. The only test-shaped artifact is examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts which is a SessionStore adapter conformance suite, not an agent regression suite.

note: crewai test re-runs but no dataset
details: crewai test [-n N] CLI runs the crew N times and CrewEvaluator (utilities/evaluators/crew_evaluator_handler.py) scores outputs. But there is no dataset format - inputs are baked into the script. For true golden-dataset regression you'd build a harness around kickoff_for_each(inputs=[...]).
BYO entirely. No Dataset, no Evaluator, no EvalRun type. Recommended pattern is Go's testing package plus mocked model.BaseChatModel.

go/ai/evaluator.go ships first-class Example, EvaluatorRequest, Dataset types. Datasets managed via the Genkit CLI (genkit-tools/cli/src/commands/eval-*). Built-in evaluators include EvaluatorDeepEqual, EvaluatorRegex, EvaluatorJsonata. Slight gap: no first-party LLM judge in Go (that lives on the JS side).
Open-source repo provides no dataset or eval primitives. LangSmith (paid) ships dataset management and evaluators. OSS-only path is BYO pytest + graph.invoke.

llama-index-core/llama_index/core/evaluation/ ships RetrieverEvaluator, RelevancyEvaluator, FaithfulnessEvaluator, CorrectnessEvaluator, GuidelineEvaluator, SemanticSimilarityEvaluator, BatchEvalRunner, plus RagDatasetGenerator and LabelledRagDataset. Heavily RAG-oriented; for general agent-behavior eval you compose primitives or use Phoenix/Langfuse/Opik.

packages/core/src/datasets/ defines Dataset types, storage/domains/datasets/ persists them, and runEvals (packages/core/src/evals/run/index.ts) orchestrates with agent+dataset+scorers+concurrency. Results land in the configured storage backend for trend dashboards. Scorers can also be wired into the agent loop via isTaskComplete - unique in this benchmark.

_evaluation.py (~1941 lines) ships EvalItem (~line 726) and LocalEvaluator (~line 1343) plus evaluate_agent/evaluate_workflow/evaluate_traces/evaluate_foundry_target. Gated by @experimental(feature_id=ExperimentalFeature.EVALS) so semantics may shift; Foundry integration is the productionised path.
Not first-party. The doc'd pattern is partner integrations (Braintrust, Phoenix, Langfuse, LangSmith) consuming the SDK's traces. The SDK itself provides no dataset/eval primitive.
vitest is used for the SDK's own tests but no agent-eval primitive ships. Community is steered toward partner integrations.

pydantic-evals ships as a first-party package: dataset.py (Dataset/Case, JSON/YAML serializable), evaluators/ (built-ins + custom + LLM judge), online.py (production traffic sampling), reports + OTel emission. This is the most complete first-party eval surface in the benchmark alongside Mastra.

crates/rig-core/src/evals.rs (feature-gated by experimental) ships EvalOutcome<Output> (Pass/Fail/Invalid), the Eval trait with eval/eval_batch, and an LLM-driven evaluator built on Extractor. It's a primitive not a dataset+harness - no first-party golden-dataset format.
Standard pytest is used internally (tests/, tests_integ/) but no built-in eval harness or dataset format ships.
BYO. SDK has unit + integration tests for its own code (strands-ts/test/integ/, src/**/__tests__/) but no dataset format or runner for agent-behavior regression.
No SDK-shipped eval dataset format. @ai-sdk/test-server (packages/test-server/) lets you mock providers for unit tests, but eval/regression harnesses are external (Braintrust, LangSmith, your own).
Not provided. No first-party rubric/scorer/judge classifier ships.

AccuracyEval (eval/accuracy.py:24-58) uses an LLM (defaulting to the agent's own model) to score outputs 1-10 against expected_output with reasoning. AgentAsJudge (eval/agent_as_judge.py) provides a generalised agent-grades-agent primitive. First-class capability.
BYO. The crates/autoagents-llm/src/evaluator/parallel.rs evaluator is for internal parallelism, not an LLM-as-judge.
Not provided. No built-in rubric scorer.
BYO. No first-party LLM-as-judge primitive in the SDK.

CrewEvaluator's TaskEvaluationPydanticOutput.quality field (1-10) is filled by a spawned Agent(role='Task Execution Evaluator') that grades each task against task.description+task.expected_output. Works out of the box but the judge prompt is hardcoded with no rubric customisation beyond expected_output. For richer judging you integrate Patronus or AMP's hallucination guardrail.
BYO. You'd write a function that calls an LLM with a rubric prompt over the agent's output. Eino ships nothing here.

BYO - you define your own Evaluator whose Evaluate function calls genkit.Generate with a judge prompt and returns a Score (which supports numeric/string/categorical). Better than nothing because the Evaluator protocol and Score type are first-class, but the judge implementation is yours. JS side ships built-in judges; Go side does not.
Not in the OSS repo. langchain has load_evaluator('labeled_score_string') etc but it's separately packaged; LangSmith ships hosted LLM judges as a paid feature.

RelevancyEvaluator, FaithfulnessEvaluator, CorrectnessEvaluator, AnswerRelevancyEvaluator, GuidelineEvaluator each use an LLM as judge against a rubric. Coverage is broad but RAG-flavoured rather than general-purpose agent behaviour.

createScorer({id,description}).generateScore(async ({ run }) => {...}) supports both code-based predicates and LLM-based rubric scoring. Built-in scorer types live under packages/core/src/evals/. Uniquely, scorers can be wired into the agent loop via isTaskComplete: { scorers, strategy: 'all' } so the agent re-iterates until passing.

Evaluator protocol (_evaluation.py:507) supports both pre-built checks (keyword_check, tool_calls_present, tool_call_args_match, ...) and custom LLM-judge functions. Still experimental and lacks a one-call LLM judge like pydantic-evals.
examples/agent_patterns/llm_as_a_judge.py shows the pattern - it's a usage example not a built-in scorer. Not first-party.
examples/agent-patterns/llm-as-a-judge.ts shows the pattern (one agent grades another) but the SDK ships no built-in judge.
pydantic_evals.evaluators.llm_judge is a built-in evaluator (docs/evals/evaluators/llm-judge.md). One-import, fully integrated with pydantic-evals datasets and reports.

Via the experimental evals module + Extractor (crates/rig-core/src/extractor.rs:31-80) you implement Eval for a struct that wraps an Extractor<M, YourRubric> returning Pass/Fail. The plumbing is there but the judge wiring is yours and the feature is experimental.
Not provided - BYO.
Not provided.
No first-party rubric primitive. Trivial to compose with generateObject({ model: judgeModel, schema, prompt }) but every project rebuilds it.
Not provided - BYO entirely.
No first-party 'pre-merge gate' CLI. You run evals via eval.run()/eval.arun() and assert on the returned score in a pytest test (e.g. result.score >= 8). No JUnit or threshold-fail flag baked in.
No agent-behaviour CI gates ship. Standard cargo test --features full --workspace runs unit tests (README.md:173).
Not provided.
BYO. Build your own eval harness over query().

crewai test prints a scores table but exit code is 0 unless an exception fires - there's no --min-score threshold-fail, no JUnit XML, no PR-gate integration in OSS. AMP markets 'Crew Testing' in its dashboard but no documented CI hook.
Not provided. The recommended pattern is BYO - run agent against a fixture set in CI, assert outputs/judge-scores above a threshold.
Not shipped first-party. Recommended pattern is genkit eval:run (JS CLI) in CI reading a JSON dataset, running an action, asserting on scores. You wire the CI yourself.
BYO. Typical pattern is a pytest job that runs a sample of graph.invoke against golden datasets and blocks merge on regression.
Not provided. You wire BatchEvalRunner into your CI yourself.

runEvals runs cleanly inside Vitest it() blocks; the pattern is documented and eval results land in the configured storage backend for trend dashboards. No separate 'ScoredTest' macro or first-party CI gate command, but the integration is the smoothest in the benchmark.
Not packaged. You wire it yourself into CI - run evaluate_agent and fail on score. FoundryEvals provides a managed alternative.
BYO entirely.
Not provided.

Datasets run under pytest directly. The framework's own test suite uses inline-snapshot + pytest-recording + vcrpy for replay-based LLM testing (AGENTS.md:107-115) and you can integrate the same in your CI. Closest to a turnkey pre-merge gate after Mastra; still no dedicated 'gate' CLI.
Not provided as a turnkey CI gate. You write a cargo test that calls eval_batch(...) and asserts on EvalOutcome counts.
Not provided - BYO.
Not provided.
BYO. Eval is your CI's responsibility - the SDK ships nothing for pre-merge gating.

The `adkgo` binary walks for `root_agent.yaml`, launches Web UI, REST, A2A, and a Vertex Agent Engine emulator. Sub-launchers include `web`, `webui`, `api`, `console` (TUI REPL), and `agentengine`. Strong multi-surface coverage but not as polished as Mastra Studio or Genkit Dev UI.

`python run.py` starts a uvicorn AgentOS on port 7777 that the hosted os.agno.com UI points at; `ag`/`agno` CLI handles scaffolding and `Agent.print_response`/`cli_app()` provides a rich terminal REPL. Strong, but the polished UI is hosted rather than local.

No first-party local runner ships with the core SDK; users run `cargo run --example <name>` for the 20+ examples. A separate `AutoAgents-CLI` repo exists but is explicitly out of scope for this benchmark.

The `claude` binary the SDK spawns is itself a full TUI you can run on a laptop, and `examples/quick_start.py` is a one-shot headless script. No dedicated SDK web playground, but the underlying CLI is best-in-class as a local agent runner.

note: Claude Code CLI, no SDK UI
details: The underlying `claude` CLI launches an interactive REPL but the SDK itself ships no playground/TUI/web dev UI for SDK consumers; you write a script and run it with `tsx`/`bun`/`node`. Slightly weaker than the Python sibling because the report explicitly notes the absence of an SDK dev UI.

`crewai chat`, `crewai run`, `crewai install`, `crewai create crew|flow`, `crewai checkpoint` and `crewai memory` cover scaffolding, REPL chat, runs and TUI inspection. No first-party web playground in OSS (AMP's Crew Studio is cloud-only).
No `eino dev` CLI, no playground, no TUI. CloudWeGo's DevOps tooling is a JetBrains/IntelliJ plugin (mostly Chinese-documented) — there is no web-based playground.

note: Dev UI + action runner + prompt playground
details: `genkit start -- go run .` spawns the process, hits the reflection server and opens the Dev UI with an action runner, trace viewer, prompt playground for `.prompt` files, and a dataset/eval runner. One of the strongest first-party local dev UIs in the benchmark.

`langgraph dev` shells out to `langgraph_api.cli.run_server` and boots a local HTTP server backed by `InMemorySaver` plus the LangGraph Studio web UI that visualizes the graph, lets you step state and trigger interrupts. Studio itself is closed-source but the runner experience is first-class.
No CLI/playground in `llama-index-core`; agents are run in Jupyter or a script. The separate `llama-index-cli` package targets document indexing, not agent chatting.

`mastra dev` boots a local server plus Mastra Studio at localhost:3000, where you can run agents, inspect traces, run evals, iterate on skills and view memory. React-based playground packages (`packages/playground` + `playground-ui`) make this best-in-class.

`devui ./agents --port 8080` auto-discovers agents/workflows in a directory, hot-reloads, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API plus a debug web UI. Labelled a sample app rather than production, but feature-complete for local benchmark use.
`run_demo_loop` from `src/agents/repl.py` is a terminal REPL that loops on user input, streams output and surfaces tool calls — useful for smoke tests. No web playground/TUI/dev UI beyond that.
No CLI playground ships; `examples/sandbox/basic.ts` is the closest thing and it's just a file you `tsx examples/sandbox/basic.ts`. No web dev UI.

`clai` (`uvx clai`) is a model-agnostic chat CLI, `agent.to_web()` launches a Starlette + HTML chat UI at localhost:7932, and `agent.to_cli_sync()`/`to_cli()` drop an agent into the interactive REPL. Strong coverage but no graph/trace dashboard like Mastra Studio.
`integrations/cli_chatbot.rs` wraps an `Agent` in a stdin/stdout chat loop. No TUI, web dev UI or playground.
`strands-agents/agent-builder` is a sibling repo CLI scaffolder, not bundled with the SDK. Inline, `agent('...')` from a Python REPL works as a one-liner. No first-party playground or trace UI.
A `strandly` dev CLI ships in the monorepo for codegen-style developer tooling, but it isn't a TUI or playground. Ad-hoc invocation uses `tsx` against `examples/`.
No SDK-shipped CLI/TUI/playground/web dev UI; the dev pattern is to write a Next.js example, `pnpm dev` and hit localhost:3000. Compared explicitly to Mastra and LangGraph as missing.

`DebugTelemetry` buffers the last N spans/logs in memory and exposes them at `/debug/trace/...`; the Web UI consumes these to show traces of past runs, and the same `SpanProcessor` can forward to Datadog/Jaeger. Local inspection is genuinely first-class, just less polished than Studio/Dev UI.
Traces are browsed in the hosted os.agno.com UI or queried directly from the `agno_traces` table. Functional but no first-party local-only trace viewer.
Indirect — push traces to an OTLP collector (Tempo/Jaeger/Datadog) via `autoagents-telemetry` and inspect in those tools. Nothing local or replayable in-framework.

Local JSONL transcripts at `~/.claude/projects/...` plus the CLI's `/context`, `/cost`, `/status` slash commands; the SDK exposes `get_context_usage()` programmatically. Strong durable replay, just not a graphical dashboard.
Local JSONL files in `~/.claude/projects/<cwd>/<sessionId>.jsonl`; the CLI's `/transcript` and `/usage` commands render formatted versions. Inspect with `cat`/`jq` or build your own viewer.

TUI commands (`crewai memory`, `crewai checkpoint`) plus rich-formatted console output when `verbose=True`; 18 observability integrations (Langfuse, Arize, Datadog, Weave, MLflow…) for remote dashboards. AMP adds a Traces dashboard.
No built-in local trace inspector; rely on Langfuse / LangSmith / APMPlus / CozeLoop dashboards via `eino-ext`. The optional CloudWeGo visual-debug IDE plugin is third-party.

Dev UI ships a trace viewer (timeline of generate iterations, tool calls and middleware) and exposes traces via the reflection API at `/api/traces`. Among the best in the benchmark for local trace inspection.

LangGraph Studio (closed-source web UI) when running `langgraph dev` lets you step through state and inspect runs; LangSmith (paid cloud) for production traces. Excellent UX but the Studio is closed-source.
Trace inspection happens through the OTel exporter into Phoenix/Jaeger/Langfuse/etc. No local TUI viewer ships.

Mastra Studio has a built-in trace inspector showing spans/metrics from `observability/` queryable end-to-end; Langfuse/OTel exporters are also wired. Strongest end-to-end local trace experience in the benchmark.
DevUI surfaces OTel traces via the `--instrumentation` flag and a dedicated trace viewer panel; ADR 0003 describes the OpenTelemetry instrumentation. Close to Studio in capability.
Inspection via the free OpenAI Traces dashboard (hosted) or 25+ partner exporters. Functional but nothing local-first.
Default exporter ships traces to platform.openai.com/traces (hosted only). Local inspection requires switching to `ConsoleSpanExporter`.
Logfire UI for hosted inspection; any OTel backend (Jaeger/Tempo/Honeycomb) for self-hosted. No bespoke local trace UI ships.
Tracing logs go through `tracing-subscriber::fmt()` and you ship them to OTel for inspection. No replay primitive.
Traces export to OTel; inspection happens in whichever viewer you wire up.
`AgentResult.traces` exposes an in-process tree, but there is no GUI; pipe to OTel for visualization.
Wire `@ai-sdk/otel` to Jaeger/Tempo/Honeycomb yourself. Nothing first-party.
The Web UI doesn't switch tenants natively; the workaround is hitting the API directly with different `appName`/`userId` to simulate tenants.
Not first-class — you'd run multiple AgentOS instances or pass different `user_id`/`dependencies` from the client. No tenant picker.
Not provided. Tenant switching is entirely the host's responsibility.
